22811-the-staircase-at-the-heart-s-delig:
Police headquarters supplies the frame for The Staircase at the Heart's Delight, a detective story dated 1894. The narrator looks back on his younger self, a man full of ambition who refused to drop a case when his colleagues moved on. He kept watching and waiting, certain another victim would be reported.

His patience shapes the whole tale. Because he alone stays with the puzzle, he is ready when fresh word arrives, and the odd results he promises begin to unfold. The story belongs to the early years of modern detective fiction, when dogged legwork mattered more than clever gadgets. It suits readers who enjoy a murder inquiry told by the man who would not let it go.
23177-the-inmate-of-the-dungeon-1894:
W. C. Morrow published The Inmate of the Dungeon in 1894, a grim work of fiction about prison life. A guard brings a convict into view. The man shuffles with pain, holding up by a string the heavy iron ball chained to his ankles so it will not drag on the floor.

The prisoner is about forty-five years old and worn down to skin and bone. Yet his frame still shows that he was once a man of rare bodily strength. Morrow dwells on that contrast, giving readers a stark picture of what long confinement in a dungeon can do to a human body.
a-spirit-in-prison-pg2994: Robert Hichens's 1908 A Spirit in Prison: an Italian romance of passion. Lush and dramatic in his best manner. The Garden of Allah author's romance. An Italian passion in Hichens's lush prose, romance behind bars, Hichens's lush Italian romance.
alchemy-and-chemistry-1894: Alchemy and Chemistry is an 1894 paper by Herbert McLeod, the English chemist. McLeod wrote when the new profession of chemistry was taking stock of its own past. His paper sets the old art of alchemy beside the modern science that grew out of it, comparing the discarded parent with the disciplined successor. It is a short Victorian period piece on that descent, written by a working chemist rather than a historian.
arxiv-2510-00194:
Prasanna Parthasarathi and four colleagues published this 2025 paper improving how language models learn from rewards. The popular GRPO method trains models on reasoning tasks with a single score per answer. That design cannot tell which tokens in a long answer earned the score. The team's GRPO-lambda extension restores fine-grained credit using ideas from eligibility traces.

Their method rebuilds a lambda-return from token-level log-probabilities after each answer is generated. A critic-free estimate of the prediction error guides how credit flows backward. Several weighting variants were tried, and every variant beat plain GRPO in training. Gains during training ran between thirty and forty percent on the reported curves. Final scores rose by more than three points on average across five math benchmarks. The largest model tested, at seven billion parameters, gained the most.
arxiv-2510-00394:
Zhouyang Liu and four colleagues published this 2025 paper on judging how similar two graphs are, quickly. Measures like maximum common subgraph and graph edit distance are exact but NP-hard to compute. Neural approximations either compare every node pair at great cost or lose the graph's structure and size. Their method, Graph2Region, embeds each node as a closed region in space.

A whole graph becomes a summary region whose shape encodes structure and whose volume encodes size. Overlap between two graph regions then approximates their maximum common subgraph score. The leftover disjoint parts serve as a proxy for edit distance, so both scores come out together. Across fifteen datasets, the method improved MCS similarity accuracy by up to about sixty percent over leading rivals. Training and inference both stayed efficient in their benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-00494:
Julian Coda-Forno and eight colleagues published this 2025 paper on whether language models reason better with a separate thinking partner. Psychologists split thought into a fast, fluent system and a slow, deliberate one. The authors test dual architectures where a fluent base model trades latent messages with a coprocessor. Two fixes are on trial: widening the channel, and training both models jointly.

Experiments on GPT-2 and a Qwen model used matched budgets of latent tokens. Joint fine-tuning won consistently, while extra channel capacity helped only modestly. A single-model baseline with soft embeddings nearly matched the best dual system. That parity suggests today's dual designs mostly add compute, not better reasoning. Raising the latent budget past small values failed to harden performance on stress tests. Latent spaces overlapped heavily, with little sign of clean specialization between the partners.
arxiv-2510-00594:
Lauri Kurki, Yaniel Cabrera, and Samu Karanko published this 2025 paper on whether rain forecasts mean what they say. A neural weather model that promises seventy percent rain should be right seventy percent of the time. Standard calibration scores miss errors that only appear at specific rainfall thresholds. The authors introduce a threshold-aware error metric built for ordered precipitation classes.

They also import post-processing tricks from computer vision into forecasting. Their selective scaling adjusts confidence only where a classifier flags likely mistakes. Conditioning the adjustment on forecast lead time sharpened the fix further. Calibration error fell by up to about twenty-four percent in their tests. Forecast quality itself did not degrade under the correction, they report. The authors suggest future calibrators should also condition on place and season. Honest probabilities matter when farmers and flood managers act on them.
arxiv-2510-00694:
Abu Shairah and seven co-authors introduce ALARB in this 2025 arXiv paper, a benchmark for testing how well large language models reason about Arabic law. Existing Arabic benchmarks mostly test reading and recall, not the step-by-step reasoning that court work needs. ALARB fills that gap with real commercial court cases from Saudi Arabia.

The dataset holds more than thirteen thousand cases, each with the facts, the court's reasoning chain, the verdict, and the legal clauses cited. Tasks include predicting verdicts, completing missing reasoning steps, and finding the rules that apply to a case. Reasoning-focused models scored best, though all left clear room to grow. Fine-tuning a modest twelve-billion-parameter model on ALARB brought its verdict scores close to those of GPT-4o in their tests.
arxiv-2510-00794:
Morel, Moulin-Frier, and Barla build interactive tools for exploring complex systems in this 2025 arXiv paper on artificial life and generative methods. Simulations of complex systems produce rich self-organized patterns, which scientists and artists mine for discovery and art. The parameter spaces are huge, and the map from parameters to patterns is strongly nonlinear, so blind sampling wastes effort. Explorers arrive with expectations, wanting patterns of a particular kind rather than any diversity.

The authors define constrained diversity: maximize the variety of patterns found inside a user-specified region of interest. Users state that region as system-agnostic constraints on measurable pattern features. Their method then steers exploration toward the region while keeping global diversity alive in the background. The search stays sample-efficient, needing fewer simulations than random sampling to stock the target region. Interactive guidance lets the user redirect exploration as their taste develops.
arxiv-2510-00994:
Chakravarthy and Groman relate two blow-up constructions in symplectic geometry in this 2025 arXiv paper. Blowing up a symplectic four-manifold removes an embedded ball and collapses its boundary, a standard surgery. On a manifold carrying an almost toric fibration, a different surgery replaces a triangle in the base with a nodal singularity. Both operations change the second cohomology in the same way, yet a direct map between their outputs was known only through global classification arguments.

The authors construct a symplectomorphism between the almost toric blow-up and the ordinary symplectic blow-up. Their map is the identity outside the affected region, so it works for non-rational and non-compact manifolds too. Under a compatibility condition on the ball embedding, the map can also preserve the induced symplectic log canonical divisors, which matter in current classification programmes.
arxiv-2510-01194:
Barrientos and co-authors build a telemedicine system that helps midwives capture useful fetal ultrasound images in low-resource clinics. Rural areas often lack sonographers, so specialists never see most pregnancies at all. Their setup pairs a cheap handheld scanner with an AI guide and remote review.

Midwives follow blind sweep protocols while the model picks out diagnostically key frames. Specialists then review selected frames through a web platform instead of whole videos. Field tests with briefly trained midwives showed good usability and low mental workload. The system found standard fetal planes reliably from non-expert sweeps. Asynchronous review respects specialists' scarce hours across distances. Brief instruction sufficed, which keeps training costs low for clinics. Standard planes are the checkpoints of a competent scan. Human judgment stays in the loop at the interpretation step. Access, not automation, is the goal here.
arxiv-2510-01294:
Tian, Dokyeesun, and Klavžar study how graph invariants about point placement shift when a vertex or an edge is deleted. General position numbers measure the largest set of vertices with no three on a common shortest path. Three flavors, total, outer, and dual, behave very differently under surgery.

Removing a non-cut vertex moves the total number only within a proved band. The outer and dual numbers, by contrast, can jump arbitrarily in either direction. Membership in an optimal set restores one-sided control for those wilder variants. Edge removal receives its own bounds, completing a map of fragile and stable cases. Cut vertices are excluded because their removal disconnects the graph entirely. Degree of the removed vertex caps the total number's rise. Constructions prove the wild jumps are genuinely attainable. Stability results tell engineers which measures survive damage.
arxiv-2510-01394:
Kalayci, Raman, and Dughmi decide when a language model should stop generating candidate answers and settle, using a classic economics puzzle. Each new sample costs compute and might beat the current best, a Pandora's box dilemma. Their framework treats stopping as the decision, not the sample count.

An optimism-based algorithm nearly matches the optimal strategy that requires knowing the reward distribution. A reward-normalization trick adapts thresholds per prompt, inspired by paired-comparison modeling. Dialogue experiments matched fixed-sample quality while using notably fewer generations. Larger budgets widened the adaptive method's advantage rather than shrinking it. Weitzman's classic solution is the benchmark the new algorithm chases. Fifteen to a third fewer generations saved real compute in tests. Two reward models and two datasets confirmed the trend was robust. Best-of-many sampling is the incumbent practice being outsmarted. Stopping well is a skill in itself.
arxiv-2510-01494:
Gupta and co-authors explain a puzzle in adversarial machine learning: why some attacks hop between models while others die at the border. Image tricks and text jailbreaks transfer famously, yet image jailbreaks between vision-language models reportedly failed. Their hypothesis splits attacks by where they live.

Attacks crafted in input data space transfer; attacks crafted inside a model's representation space do not, absent geometric alignment. A proof in a toy setting shows identical functions with different representations already separate the two. Constructed attacks on classifiers and language models confirmed the pattern empirically. Representation geometry, not attack strength, decides portability. Four settings carry the theoretical and empirical evidence jointly. Adapter-style vision-language models bound the study's scope explicitly. Similarity metrics in use remain heuristic, the authors concede. Earlier failed jailbreak transfers get a retrospective explanation here. The winning move is attacking the input, not the insides.
arxiv-2510-01594:
Jones attacks a stubborn conjecture in the representation theory of p-adic groups using the geometry of a special building. The conjecture links two ways of describing a group's representations, and it matters for the local Langlands program. Beyond rank one, the statement has resisted proof for years.

The approach ties the conjecture to exactness of a chain complex built from data spread over the building. For the rank-two group over a ramified extension, the paper marshals strong evidence for that exactness. New combinatorial tools for picturing the building carry much of the argument. A sequel aims to finish the proof. Buildings here are geometric homes for the group's symmetries, tiled by chambers. Coefficient systems spread representation data across that tiling. Rank two is the first case where rank-one intuition fails. Totally ramified extensions supply the arithmetic setting. Evidence, carefully assembled, moves conjectures.
arxiv-2510-01694:
Wong, Cho, D'Orsogna, and Chou model how T cells find their targets in this 2025 mathematical biology paper. Inside a lymph node, T cells wander and bump into antigen-presenting cells. Only a rare presenting cell carries the matching antigen that can activate a given T cell. Meanwhile, T cells can die or leave the node before any match happens.

The authors build a stochastic model that couples diffusion with a multistage recognition chain. A T cell activates only if it completes every step of the chain on a matching cell. From the model they compute both the chance of successful activation and the average time it takes. Wrong-match cells, cell death, and node exit all enter the calculation. Adding kinetic proofreading, which resets partial matches, sharpened the system's preference for true matches. The framework gives concrete numbers for how fast an adaptive immune response can begin.
arxiv-2510-01794:
Schildbach presents a design procedure for controlling large systems under uncertainty in this 2025 control paper. Model predictive control plans inputs by forecasting a system's behavior over a short horizon. Robust versions also guard against bounded disturbances and model errors. Until now, robust methods stalled at roughly five states, because their safety sets explode in size as systems grow.

A recent variant, Deadbeat Robust MPC, drops the need for that invariant set entirely. Schildbach shows its online optimization problem costs exactly as much as ordinary nominal control. The offline setup also becomes cheaper for the same reason. Full theoretical guarantees from the deadbeat approach carry over to the procedure. A numerical study on random large systems confirmed the method works at several hundred states and inputs. That scale opens robust predictive control to plants, buildings, and energy networks.
arxiv-2510-01994:
Yang and five co-authors clean up example tests so language models learn better from them in this 2025 software paper. In-context learning can generate unit tests, but messy examples teach messy habits. Poorly structured or unclear tests drag down the generated output. Their technique, CLAST, refines existing tests for semantic clarity before they serve as examples.

CLAST splits complex tests into logically simpler ones and rewrites them with program analysis plus model assistance. Across four open-source and three industrial projects, it fully retained the original tests' effectiveness. The rival refinement method degraded compile success, pass rates, coverage, and mutation scores by sizable margins. In a user study, over eighty-five percent of participants preferred the clarity of CLAST-refined tests. Feeding refined examples into two generation systems raised compile success by about a quarter and coverage by nearly half.
arxiv-2510-02094:
Amiri, Barrenechea, Georgoulis, and Pryer keep numerical solutions inside physical bounds on messy meshes in this 2025 numerical analysis paper. Elliptic problems often demand solutions that respect known upper and lower bounds, such as nonnegative concentrations. Standard discontinuous Galerkin methods can overshoot inside each element. Their composite method enforces the bounds exactly where users ask.

Starting from an interior penalty form on polygonal meshes, they overlay a simplicial submesh inside each element. A nonlinear iteration enforces the bounds at the submesh nodes. The construction adds no global degrees of freedom beyond the baseline method. It also preserves the method's order of accuracy by design. Where no limiting is needed, the scheme reverts to the standard Galerkin method. Bound preservation at user-chosen points, not just nodes, is the distinctive gain.
arxiv-2510-02394:
Patwardhan and co-authors give text-to-SQL systems a tidy library of domain facts. Their 2025 paper targets a hidden weakness in query translation. Business questions use special vocabulary tied to each database. Models must map those terms onto the right tables and columns. Older benchmarks paste ad hoc hints onto each question. Such hints are impractical for real enterprise use. The team attaches structured domain statements to the whole database instead. A simple substring match retrieves the statements each question needs. Tests used eleven realistic database schemas from varied domains.

Five language models, open and proprietary, took part in the tests. Database level statements proved more practical than per question hints. They also produced more accurate SQL overall. Substring retrieval beat fancier retrieval approaches clearly. The dataset came from the BirdSQL benchmark family. Enterprise databases change often, so updates matter next. Shared domain knowledge makes language interfaces trustworthy.
arxiv-2510-02594:
Chen and co-authors give underwater robot operators touch feedback inside virtual reality. Their 2025 robotics paper presents a framework called SubSense. Piloting a subsea vehicle usually means flat camera feeds. Operators lose depth cues and any sense of contact. SubSense pairs a VR headset with a haptic glove. The glove reports grip force and grasp status in real time. A simple add-on upgrades a standard one joint gripper. Live camera views stream into the immersive display. The whole control chain runs through their software stack. Experiments and user studies tested the full setup.

Delicate manipulation tasks benefited most from the feedback. Operators handled fragile targets with fewer mistakes. Awareness, efficiency, and safety all improved over plain interfaces. The test vehicle was a common commercial subsea robot. Feeling a grasp from the surface changes teleoperation. Inspection and repair work underwater could adopt the pattern.
arxiv-2510-02894:
Lisowski and co-authors speed up a popular tool for medical image analysis. Radiomics extracts numbers that describe tumors in scans. The open-source library PyRadiomics is a standard for that work. Its three-dimensional shape features can be slow to compute. Large scan collections make the delay painful. The team's extension, PyRadiomics-cuda, moves the heavy geometry work onto graphics cards. It keeps the exact same interface as the original library.

Existing scripts run unchanged and finish in a fraction of the time. Tests covered cluster machines, budget rigs, and home devices. Output quality matched the original library. The project began with a lung study of about forty thousand CT scans. Faster extraction cut costly computing time for that study. The code is free under a permissive license. The release should help AI pipelines that screen images at high volume.
arxiv-2510-03094:
Choudhary, Shen, and Shrivastava bound a two-input averaging operator over spheres. The operator takes the largest spherical mean of two functions jointly. Only radii from a chosen dilation set are allowed. Fractal dilation sets make the ranges delicate to pin down. The authors measure the set with upper Minkowski dimension. That fractal size then sets the exact range of bounds. Their theorem covers general sets, not just tidy ones.

One case settles a question left open for years. Lacunary dilations grow in a sparse, geometric pattern. At the borderline exponents, earlier work stalled in higher dimensions. For dimension four and up, the new result closes that gap. The maximal bounds follow the pattern known from the one-input theory. Dilation shape, not just count, drives the outcome. Harmonic analysts use such bounds to control singular averages. The proof mixes Fourier tools with geometric covering tricks.
arxiv-2510-03594:
Wu and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on keeping wireless links secret in fluid antenna systems, where an antenna can slide among ports to find a spot. Predicting secrecy needs a model of how the ports' signals correlate, and correlation guesses skew the answer. Their variable block correlation model tunes correlation block by block to match channel behavior. From it they derive formulas for secrecy capacity and secrecy outage probability. Two optimization algorithms adjust settings to raise secrecy.

Against simulations, the model's secrecy predictions missed by under five percent, while constant models missed by ten to fifteen percent. The edge is largest for antennas with fewer than twenty ports, where correlation is hardest to capture. The two optimizers suit jobs, one for offline design and one for adjustment. Fluid antennas are a leading candidate for wireless hardware. Trustworthy secrecy math helps engineers build eavesdropper resistance in from the start.
arxiv-2510-04094:
Wang, Liao, and Luo present this 2025 arXiv paper on making kernel methods for differential equations fast enough for long simulations. Least squares support vector machines solve ordinary differential equations accurately, but their cost grows with the cube of the number of time points. Long or finely resolved problems become impractical. The authors reformulate the equations as constraints in a primal feature space instead.

Their key step is an explicit Nyström mapping that lifts one-dimensional time points into a modest feature space, derivatives included. Cost then depends on the small number of features rather than the full time grid. On sixteen benchmark equations, the method ran from ten to several thousand times faster than classical solvers and physics-informed neural networks. Accuracy matched the classical kernel solver closely and beat the neural approach on error measures. Kernel solvers with this profile become viable for large scientific computing tasks.
arxiv-2510-04194:
Thulasidharan, D'Onghia, and Benjamin present this 2025 arXiv paper on reading a galaxy's merger history from the twist of its warped disk. Disk galaxies commonly bend into warps at their edges, and mergers are a suspected cause. Using high-resolution Milky Way analogs from the IllustrisTNG50 simulation, the authors compare galaxies with and without major mergers. They measure the warp orientation separately for stars born before and after each merger.

Merged galaxies show a characteristic azimuthal misalignment between the two populations' warps. The offset survives correction for differential rotation, marking it as a dynamical imprint rather than a kinematic artifact. Galaxies without mergers show no such offset between age groups. Physically, the infalling satellite torques the outer disk, and later stars form in a resettled plane tilted from the old one. Applied to the Milky Way, the signature could test whether the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger built our warp.
arxiv-2510-04494:
Ningzhi Tang and six coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on a new way to edit computer code. Editing code demands that a developer grasp the code, plan a change, state the intent, and check the result. The team built NaturalEdit, a system that turns summaries into living documents. A summary stays linked to the code it describes.

Readers can slide a summary between broad overview and fine detail as their needs change. Clicks move both ways between summary text and the matching code lines. When a user edits the summary, the system updates the code to match the stated intent. A technical evaluation confirmed that the machinery works as designed. A user study with twelve developers then tested the workflow in practice. Users understood code faster and stated their intent with more clarity. They also checked results with greater confidence and control.
arxiv-2510-04694:
Lucas Bandarkar and coauthors at UCLA and Fudan University wrote this 2025 paper on how multilingual models route words. Mixture of experts models send each token to a few specialist subnetworks chosen by a router. The team compared routing across texts in many languages. Early and late layers routed each language in its own way. Middle layers, by contrast, routed languages through the same experts.

How a language followed English routing in those layers tracked how well the model performed in it. Languages the model knows failed to use the shared English experts. The team steered routers toward the middle layer experts that English favors. That push lifted scores by one to two points. The gains held across two tasks, three models, and more than fifteen languages. Steering outside the middle layers, or toward language specific experts, hurt. The findings say skill depends on sharing experts, not on ones per language.
arxiv-2510-05194:
Anni Tziakouri and Filippo Menolascina train an AI to order the right medical scans in this 2025 arXiv paper. Unnecessary imaging exposes patients to radiation and clogs busy systems. The American College of Radiology publishes evidence-based appropriateness criteria for choosing scans. Busy clinicians underuse those criteria today.

Their reasoning agent learns with reinforcement learning, using group relative policy optimization. Reasoning-focused rewards teach it to follow the criteria like an expert would. The resulting 8B model, MedReason-Embed, raised macro F1 by 18 percent over baseline. It beat larger and differently trained models on reasoning alignment. A surrounding pipeline maps diagnoses to codes, retrieves PubMed evidence, and recommends procedures. The system can even generalize beyond the written guidelines.
arxiv-2510-05394:
Ahmad Alsheikh and Andreas Fischer predict heating patterns inside plastic bottle preforms in this 2025 arXiv paper. PET preforms are microwave-heated before blow molding into bottles. Temperature fields decide whether the final bottle forms correctly. Models usually need retraining for every material or shape change.

Their framework pretrains specialized neural regressors on separate conditions, like recycled PET or varied geometries. Model fusion then merges those specialists into one global model. Skip connections stabilize the architecture and sharpen accuracy. With only 450 to 550 samples per category, the fused model beat models trained from scratch. Two case studies confirmed stronger generalization across material and geometry changes.
arxiv-2510-05494:
Cao and colleagues ask how much computing power crystal-focused neural networks really have. Equivariant graph neural networks respect the symmetries of crystal structures. That makes them popular for predicting materials properties from atomic layouts. Their 2025 paper measures the networks' limits through circuit complexity, a theory of computing depth.

Under realistic limits on precision, width, and depth, the authors prove a ceiling. Any such network can be simulated by a family of shallow threshold circuits. That placement caps which prediction problems these networks can ever solve. Older yardsticks for graph networks do not transfer cleanly to periodic crystals, the authors note. Their analysis instead tracks nodes, coordinates, and lattice data through each layer. Beating the ceiling would require deeper models, wider layers, or richer geometric parts. The result gives materials modelers a firm map of what current designs cannot do.
arxiv-2510-05794:
Miao and colleagues experimentally test how fast multiparticle quantum systems can evolve. Quantum speed limits bound evolution speed through energy-time uncertainty. Whether many particles and entanglement truly accelerate observable dynamics lacked experiments. Their 2025 two-photon platform measures those limits with ultrahigh precision timing.

Maximum speeds grow across single, product, and maximally entangled initial states. The team verifies that both multiparticle structure and entanglement accelerate evolution. Initial state choice proves critical for entangled systems' speed limits. Tighter speed limits than earlier versions frame the whole experiment. Upper and lower speed bounds also hold in a nonunitary Markovian open system. The two-photon results generalize to more particles by design. Controlling large systems' transient dynamics is the practical payoff. Applications range from metrology state choice to quantum battery charging. Speed limits also guide optimal quantum control design.
arxiv-2510-05894:
Kirn and colleagues unify three characterizations of NP over abstract machine models. Their machines run Turing-like programs augmented by a first-order structure's operations. Classical theory links NP to verifiers, complete problems, and Fagin's logical description. The 2025 paper extends that trinity to machines over general structures.

Under weak conditions, polytime verification on such machines defines the class. A satisfiability problem over the structure is complete for it. Existential second-order metafinite logic captures exactly the same class. Some infinite-vocabulary structures admit no complete problem at all. Even there, the logical characterization survives intact. Analogous trinities hold for the constant-free Boolean part and both hierarchies. Oracle machines characterize the polynomial and Boolean hierarchies directly. Real vector spaces are the motivating infinite-vocabulary example throughout. Descriptive complexity looks especially suited to such abstract settings.
arxiv-2510-05994:
Deng and co-authors present a 2025 mathematics paper on Bayesian inversion, a method for estimating unknown quantities from observed data. Their work reframes the posterior distribution, which summarizes what the data imply, as the intensity measure of a Poisson point process. That process is a standard model for random points scattered across a space. Inverse problems of this kind arise when direct measurement is impossible.

The authors approximate the posterior density with kernel density estimation, a smoothing technique that builds a curve from sample points. They then use the superposition property, which lets separate point processes merge into one, to draw samples from each kernel part. Their numerical tests show that the method produces independent samples from the posterior. The approach gives researchers a simpler way to explore uncertainty in inverse problems from imaging and geophysics.
arxiv-2510-06094:
Bittner of the University of Houston asks whether noise can shelter exotic quantum particles in a 2025 theory paper. Anyons live in two-dimensional systems, and swapping two multiplies the quantum state by a phase set by an angle. Real devices jitter, so that angle should wobble rather than stay fixed.

Bittner promotes the exchange phase to a fluctuating quantity and derives a Lindblad equation from a stochastic Liouville equation. The result is a dephasing channel whose rates depend on the particles' statistics. A correlation matrix for the noise picks out which collective exchange currents stay protected from dephasing. Those protected modes form decoherence-free zones, and some noise patterns create exceptional points. In the simplest two-site model, the safest angle is always the same halfway value, whatever the noise details. The rule gives experimenters a design target for ultracold-atom anyon platforms.
arxiv-2510-06194:
Schueler and thirty-two co-authors introduce OASIS, an overlap-aware segmentation framework. Separating overlapping objects challenges scientific imaging. Segmentation models predict pixel intensities yet treat all regions equally, ignoring overlap zones where attribution is most ambiguous.

OASIS adds a weighted loss focusing training on overlap regions, extending an instance segmentation idea into regression. They demonstrated it on the MIGDAL experiment, which images the rare Migdal effect in an optical time projection chamber. There a faint electron recoil track hides inside a far brighter nuclear recoil track. The overlap weight proved the single most important training weight for reconstructing the faint tracks. Across eight training campaigns, median intensity errors for low-energy electrons improved from −41.1% to −13.3% on average. The method should transfer wherever a weak signal sits buried under a stronger overlapping one.
arxiv-2510-06494:
Noll, Basu, and Hekker use seismology to test what happens at red clump star cores in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Red clump stars burn core helium, but core mixing and nuclear rates remain poorly constrained. Their mixed gravito-acoustic oscillations probe the interior directly. Period spacing senses the structure around the core.

The team computed MESA grids spanning masses and metallicities. Each grid assumed a specific mixing scheme or carbon-alpha reaction rate. Monte Carlo sampling with observed metallicities and seismic masses produced predicted distributions. Kepler's observed distribution judged the candidates. A maximal overshoot scheme fit best, mimicking modes trapped outside a semi-convective region. Without mode trapping, no mixing scheme matched observations at all. Extending the core worsened the fit, while cutting the carbon-alpha rate by about fifteen percent improved it. One mismatch remains: models overpredict early red clump stars near two hundred fifty seconds of spacing.
arxiv-2510-06594:
Sowmya Kadali and Evangelos Papalexakis look inside language models for signs of attack. Their 2025 paper studies jailbreaking, where crafted prompts trick a model into giving restricted answers. Defenses keep improving, yet attackers keep inventing new prompt tricks. No current model is fully resistant.

The authors examine the hidden layers of two open models, GPT-J and Mamba-2. They compare how those layers respond to jailbreak prompts and to harmless ones. Distinct layer-by-layer patterns separate the two prompt types. For GPT-J, attention representations carried more signal than raw layer outputs. For Mamba-2, its mixer representations beat plain block outputs. Tensor methods helped uncover the hidden structure behind those patterns. The study is early, but it points to a cheap detection route. Watching a model's insides may flag attacks before harmful text appears.
arxiv-2510-06694:
Jipeng Lyu, Jiahua Dong, and Yu-Xiong Wang build tools for filming scenes that can be replayed from new angles. Their 2025 paper works with 3D Gaussian Splatting, which represents a scene as many soft blobs. Moving scenes are harder, because every blob must deform correctly over time. Tracking those deformations accurately while staying fast is the core problem.

Their framework, SCas4D, exploits a pattern in real motion. Groups of blobs on the same body part tend to move together. Optimization therefore proceeds in a cascade, from coarse part-level fixes to fine point-level tweaks. The method converges within about a hundred steps per frame. That is one twentieth of the training steps of a leading rival method, with competitive quality. The structure also yields articulated object segmentation as a side benefit. Extensive tests cover rendering quality and point tracking across dynamic scenes.
arxiv-2510-06894:
Tsofar Maniv and Vladimir Zhuravlev offer a new theory for a long-argued transition in thin superconducting films. Their 2025 paper studies what happens when a magnetic field drives a disordered two-dimensional film from superconducting to insulating. The effect was found in the early 1990s and has stayed controversial. The standard story leans on a duality between charges and vortices.

Their scenario starts from fluctuations of Cooper pairs, the bound pairs that carry superconductivity. As the field rises, those pairs condense into scattered puddles and get stuck there. The puddles shrink as the surrounding normal regions grow. Transport then runs through pairs tunneling between puddles and breaking apart. That picture matches transport measurements on amorphous indium oxide films, the case they analyze. It also fits earlier data from a strontium titanate interface system. A quantitative theory that avoids the usual duality gives experimentalists a fresh lens on old data.
arxiv-2510-07094:
David Rytz, Kim Ly, and Ioannis Havoutis search for training recipes that make one walking policy fit many four-legged robots. Their 2025 paper studies sampling strategies for quadrupedal locomotion policies. A universal policy must survive different body masses and joint settings. Training in simulation is cheap, but policies often fail on real hardware.

The team varied how joint controller gains are sampled during training. Three strategies competed in their experiments. One mapped body mass to gains through fixed curves. One filtered configurations adaptively by performance. One sampled gains uniformly at random. Biasing the samples with nominal reference models improved robustness further. Policies trained in the RaiSim simulator transferred to simulated robots. The best recipe deployed zero-shot onto an ANYmal robot. Range-based sampling produced unstable controllers that failed on hardware. The results argue that randomization of joint gains is essential. Larger robots benefit most from the sampling.
arxiv-2510-07394:
Aron and Kulkarni show that randomly restarting a chaotic system can freeze the spread of information inside it. Their 2025 paper studies extended many-body systems, whose chaos normally scrambles information at exponential rates. Stochastic resetting interrupts that scrambling by snapping the system back at random times. Above a critical reset rate, the whole spectrum of growth exponents collapses to zero. The transition is sharp. At criticality, a key exponent function suddenly loses its smoothness, marking the change of regime mathematically.

Below the threshold, information races outward in a ballistic front. Above it, information stays trapped near its origin over a length that diverges at the transition with a square-root exponent. Numerical tests on coupled map lattices confirm the analytic picture. Both the singular edge of the spectrum and the localization exponent trace back to the small-velocity behavior of the original exponent function.
arxiv-2510-07494:
Murff and Arsiwalla bound the number of colors needed to paint a hypergraph's edges so that overlapping edges never share a color. Their 2025 paper works with linear, loopless hypergraphs, where edges are sets that intersect sparingly. The target is the Berge-Furedi conjecture, a long-standing generalization of Vizing's classic graph theorem. Their first bound comes from symmetry: a color-preserving group acting on a minimal coloring partitions edges into orbits, and that finer partition caps the chromatic index. The argument is deductive, extracting a bound from structure that any minimal coloring must possess.

A second, constructive family of theorems ties the chromatic index directly to a degree-like quantity of a squared version of the hypergraph. Within that framework the authors give three sufficient conditions under which the conjecture holds. The conditions involve the Helly property, a classic intersection pattern in combinatorics.
arxiv-2510-07794:
Wu and six coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on teaching search agents when to search. Retrieval-augmented agents fetch outside facts while they reason. Many search too often, wasting effort on things they already know. Others skip searches they need. Outcome-only rewards cannot fix such step-level habits. The authors add a process reward that judges each search decision as it happens.

Their method, HiPRAG, first breaks the agent's reasoning into discrete steps. A hierarchical reward then pays a bonus tied to the share of optimal choices. On seven question-answering benchmarks, HiPRAG beat agentic baselines. Its over-search rate fell from over twenty-seven percent to just over two percent, and under-search dropped too. Accuracy averaged about sixty-five percent for the smaller model and about sixty-seven percent for the larger one. Step rewards made agents both thriftier and more reliable.
arxiv-2510-07994:
Hancart wrote this 2025 economics note on when commitment has no value for a principal. Economic theory usually treats commitment power as an advantage. A principal who can commit to a mechanism can copy any uncommitted behavior, so commitment should never hurt. Hancart asks when it also never helps. The setting covers mechanism design, principal-agent problems, and sender-receiver games, all written as constrained maximization.

He gives a sufficient condition called stable preferred strategies. Roughly, near the optimal mechanism, some strategy that achieves the principal's best payoff must remain feasible. When that stability holds, the principal gains nothing from commitment. In principal-agent problems, the condition follows when the agent's strategy space is finite and the principal's value varies continuously with the mechanism. The note also simplifies modeling practice. Where the condition holds, analysts can ignore commitment timing and study best replies directly.
arxiv-2510-08394:
Mustafa Yaldiz and co-authors teach neural fields to blur correctly at any scale in a 2025 arXiv paper. Neural fields store images or shapes as continuous functions learned by a network. They usually work at one fixed resolution, so zooming out creates aliasing artifacts. Prefiltering, which smooths a signal before sampling, is the classic cure.

Their method folds the filter into training, so one forward pass yields the filtered signal. They scale Fourier feature embeddings by the filter's frequency response, in closed form. This trick extends beyond Gaussian filters to Box and Lanczos filters never seen in training. Training uses Monte Carlo estimates, drawn from single samples, of the filtered signal, keeping things fast. The approach adds no constraints on network architecture, they stress. Both quantitative and qualitative results improved over existing neural-field filtering methods.
arxiv-2510-08894:
Gupta and co-authors compare two ways to run one quantum program across several linked machines, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A single quantum processor holds too few qubits for big programs, so work must be split across modules. The standard trick, circuit cutting, chops the program and rebuilds the answer from many runs, but its cost explodes as cuts multiply. The rival approach teleports operations between machines over entangled links, avoiding that explosion if the links are clean enough.

The team modeled the noisy hardware that converts signals between superconducting chips and light, since that conversion dirties the shared entanglement. They simulated building a shared quantum state across modules both ways and tracked accuracy as errors varied. Their maps show where each method wins. Cutting the converter noise tenfold, they find, would tip the balance to teleported gates, whose rival drowns in repeated sampling.
arxiv-2510-08994:
Teng and co-authors speed up image generators that build a picture one token at a time, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such autoregressive models are powerful but slow, needing thousands of sequential steps per image because each token waits for the last. Their framework borrows two ideas at once. Jacobi iteration, a classic method that refines all unknowns in parallel, supplies the parallelism. Denoising supplies the stability to make those parallel guesses converge.

A light round of fine-tuning teaches the model a new trick: accept a noise-roughened token and predict the next clean one. Generation then starts from pure noise and repeatedly cleans the whole sequence in the embedding space. A probabilistic check accepts the tokens that look settled and sends the rest through another round. Experiments showed generation accelerating through far fewer model passes, while the visual quality of the images held steady.
arxiv-2510-09294:
Ilyas Varshavskiy and six co-authors study model drift in finance in a 2025 arXiv paper. Model drift means a prediction model loses accuracy as the data it sees slowly changes. The problem is sharp in Central Asia and the Caucasus, where sudden economic shocks often shake financial data in places like Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, and Azerbaijan.

The team tests whether adding fake outlier records, meaning rare extreme cases made by a computer, can steady a model against shocks. They built a two-level test that measures both how much accuracy drops and how strong each shock is. Adding a small share of these synthetic outliers generally made models more stable than plain baselines, though the best amount differed by dataset and by model.
arxiv-2510-09494:
Nico Bistolfi, Andreea Georgescu, and Dave Hodson argue for a new way to control access to company data in a 2025 arXiv white paper. In cloud systems, standing permissions give workers and software constant access to data, and the authors tie that habit to catastrophic breaches, citing a Cloud Security Alliance deep dive report from 2025. Tools guard networks and interfaces well, but granular data access stays exposed.

Their answer is the data enclave: access is granted on demand through temporary data contracts instead of static permissions. Separation is built around the exact records requested, with precise access and real-time monitoring per record rather than per dataset. The design follows zero standing privilege and just-in-time principles at the data level. The authors say it shrinks the attack surface, blocks privilege creep, and makes auditing simpler for firms that hold valuable data at scale.
arxiv-2510-09594:
Nathan Quiblier, Roy Friedman, and Matthew Ricci present MODE in a 2025 arXiv paper, a model for systems that keep switching behaviour. In the life sciences, cell populations may cycle steadily, rest at equilibrium, or branch toward different fates. These overlapping regimes switch noisily, which breaks traditional flow-based models that assume smooth local dynamics.

MODE, short for Mixture Of Dynamical Experts, uses a neural gating mechanism to split complex dynamics into sparse, interpretable components. Each expert captures one governing law, and components can jump between laws, matching the noisy transitions seen in real data. The framework supports both unsupervised discovery of behavioural regimes and long-term forecasting across switches. On synthetic benchmarks it classified snapshot data well, even with noise and few samples. It also forecast simulated cycling and branching processes, and on human single-cell RNA data it separated proliferation from differentiation.
arxiv-2510-09794:
Lianghuan Huang and Yingshan Chang separate two ideas that interpretability research often confuses, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Decodability asks whether information can be read out of a network's hidden states. Causality asks whether those states actually drive the output. The authors test their relationship in vision transformers fine-tuned to count objects in images.

They use activation patching, transplanting activations between matched clean and corrupted images, to measure the causal role of spatial tokens and the special CLS token. In parallel, linear probes measure how decodable the count is at each depth. Systematic mismatches appear. Object tokens in the middle layers exert strong causal influence while being weakly decodable, and final-layer tokens decode accurately yet are functionally inert. The CLS token becomes decodable in the middle layers but gains causal power only at the end. The authors argue the divergence between the two measures can expose hidden computational circuits.
arxiv-2510-09894:
Liu and co-authors push past AlphaEarth in this 2025 arXiv paper on spatial representation learning. AlphaEarth builds global embeddings, compact numeric summaries, of the Earth's surface at ten-meter detail from many Earth observation sources. Those embeddings capture physical patterns such as land cover and terrain.

The team argues that place is also about human activity, not just physical form. Their method uses points of interest, mapped sites like shops and schools, to guide contrastive learning, a method that pulls similar places together and pushes unlike ones apart. The aim is a spatial representation that reflects how people use space. Such human-centered embeddings could transfer better to tasks about cities and communities.
arxiv-2510-09994:
Yimin Xiao and co-authors study machine translation literacy in this 2025 arXiv paper on how lay users handle imperfect translations. Machine translation is now an everyday tool, yet its output often carries errors. The authors ask how ordinary people perceive those errors and how much they rely on flawed output anyway.

Their work frames translation literacy as a practical skill: knowing when a translation can be trusted and when it needs a check. The findings bear on how researchers should judge translation systems in real use, not just in lab scoring. If users over-trust smooth but wrong output, design must warn them better. The study connects user behavior to the design of translation tools.
arxiv-2510-10294:
Peng and co-authors study heavy quark transport in hot QCD matter in this 2025 arXiv paper in nuclear theory. Heavy quarks, charm and bottom, are probes of the quark-gluon plasma created in heavy-ion collisions. How they diffuse and lose energy reveals the plasma's properties.

The work extends the soft-hard factorized model, a perturbative framework, into the region near the critical temperature, where non-perturbative effects grow strong. Near the transition temperature, simple perturbation theory fails, so both kinds of physics must be handled together. The authors investigate transport in that blended regime. Better transport coefficients sharpen what collision data can say about the plasma's viscosity and structure.
arxiv-2510-10394:
Cheung, Mona Berciu, and Kyle Monkman build a controllable dissipator in this 2025 arXiv paper in quantum physics. Dissipation, the loss of energy or coherence to an environment, is usually the enemy of quantum devices. Here it is engineered as a tool that drives a target system to a chosen steady state.

The authors present a microscopic Hamiltonian evolution on a combined ancilla and target system. The ancilla, an auxiliary system, shapes the dissipation the target feels. Depending on the target's energy scale, the system reaches the intended steady state or stays partly trapped in its initial state. Spectral control of dissipation could help prepare quantum states and stabilize quantum hardware on demand.
arxiv-2510-10494:
Martina G Vilas and four co-authors look inside reasoning models to predict which chains of thought will succeed, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such models solve hard problems by generating long intermediate reasoning, but much of that computation is wasted on paths that fail. The team defines signals drawn from how the model's internal representations change during reasoning, which they call Latent-Trajectory signals.

They track three things: the total change from start to finish, the change built up across steps, and how far the changes move toward the final state. These signals predicted solution accuracy better than cross layer metrics and better than the model's own output confidence. Used to pick answers among sampled attempts, they cut token use by up to 70 percent compared with majority voting, while raising accuracy by 2.6 percent on average. The signals also appear early, so compute can be steered sooner.
arxiv-2510-10894:
Maria Vasilyeva, James Brannick, and Ben S Southworth shrink large diffusion problems on graphs down to coarse models, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The target problems are heterogeneous and anisotropic: conductivity varies from place to place and with direction. Their reduction first partitions the domain into balanced local subdomains. Inside each piece, spectral clustering on the signed graph Laplacian identifies the key small scale features the coarse model must respect.

The splitting feeds two energy minimizing strategies for building coarse basis functions, one unconstrained, one constrained in the style of nonlocal upscaling methods. They test the algorithms on graph Laplacian problems including perforated domains, channelized media, and discrete pore network models. Numerics and theory both indicate the coarse models approximate the fine system accurately. Early results for a two level solver using the reduction with a block smoother are also reported.
arxiv-2510-11394:
Retrieval-augmented generation lets a language model answer with sources, but the citations it attaches are often wrong, missing, or attached to claims they do not support. Haosheng Qian and co-authors present VeriCite in this 2025 arXiv information retrieval paper, a framework that checks supporting evidence carefully before finalizing an answer. It targets the weakness of both fine-tuned citation generators and post-processing citation matchers.

VeriCite works in three stages. It first drafts an answer from all available context and verifies its claims with a natural language inference model. It then scores each retrieved document and keeps the evidence that is actually useful. Finally it refines the answer by merging the draft with the collected evidence. Experiments across five open-source language models and four datasets show VeriCite clearly improves citation quality while keeping the answers correct, and the code is publicly available.
arxiv-2510-11594:
Boron and beryllium are forged almost nowhere; they are chipped off carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen nuclei by cosmic rays. Their abundances record the history of cosmic ray activity in the early Galaxy. M. Spite, B. Barbuy, and K. Tan measure boron in metal-poor stars with unprecedented precision in this 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. They use Hubble's STIS spectrograph to observe a boron line in the far ultraviolet.

The line they identify, at about 209 nanometers, is free of blending lines in their metal-poor sample. Across stars with iron abundances between about minus 2.6 and minus 1.0 relative to solar, boron rises with iron more steeply than one-to-one, and steeper than beryllium, so their ratio climbs slightly. Since boron at the top of that range is already near its solar value, they infer a break in boron enrichment around that metallicity.
arxiv-2510-11694:
Machine learning engineering, the grind of exploring data, tuning models, and shipping experiments, is usually automated by teams of specialized agents that must coordinate. Operand Research bets on the opposite design in this 2025 arXiv paper: Operand Quant puts the whole lifecycle inside one context-aware agent working in its own development environment. The claim is that multi-agent orchestration pays for its parallelism with coordination costs, fragmented context, and synchronization errors that a single linear agent avoids.

On MLE-Bench, a seventy-five-problem benchmark of autonomous machine learning tasks run in isolation without internet access, Operand Quant achieved a medal rate of about 0.40, reported with an uncertainty of about 0.06, the highest recorded among evaluated systems at the time of the study. The agent loops through observing, planning, editing, executing, and evaluating. The authors present this as evidence that one strong agent can beat elaborate orchestration.
arxiv-2510-11894:
Jesús A. De Loera and three co-authors ask how often a convex polytope is positively curved. Polytopes are higher-dimensional cousins of polygons and polyhedra. Their skeleta, the graphs of corners and edges, can carry discrete notions of curvature. The team's 2025 arXiv paper studies two: Forman-Ricci curvature on edges and resistance curvature on vertices.

For Forman-Ricci curvature, they prove a formula for the average edge curvature through flag counting numbers. They construct endless families of positively curved polytopes in every dimension six and up. In dimensions three and four, however, only finitely many exist, and they prove the same for simplicial five-dimensional ones. Resistance curvature behaves unlike it, appearing endlessly in every dimension from three onward. A degree-based barrier shows that a vertex whose neighbors all have low degree cannot be positively curved. Positive curvature is rare and tightly constrained.
arxiv-2510-11994:
Yinan Wang leads a fifteen-author team pushing acoustic resonators into the millimeter-wave frontier. Acoustic resonators sort radio signals in phone front ends, but designs top out below next-generation frequencies. Their 2025 arXiv paper shows a solidly mounted resonator, a device built on a solid mirror stack rather than a suspended membrane, resonating at sixty-two point six gigahertz.

The device sandwiches a scandium aluminum nitride piezoelectric film, under seventy nanometers thick, on a buried platinum electrode. Beneath lies an acoustic Bragg reflector of silica and tantalum oxide layers in turns that traps the sound. A third-order thickness vibration does the resonating. The built device shows a coupling of zero point eight percent and a maximum quality factor of fifty-one near sixty-three gigahertz. That is the highest frequency reported for this resonator type, a step toward millimeter-wave filters.
arxiv-2510-12094:
Heng Zhang and eight colleagues pull graph embeddings toward home base to sharpen zero-shot predictions. Text-attributed graphs promise zero-shot learning through graph-text alignment, but fine-grained tasks, especially on heterophilic graphs where neighbors differ, defeat current methods. Their 2025 arXiv paper diagnoses an over-abstraction problem in hyperbolic space, the curved geometry used to embed hierarchies.

Embeddings pushed to large hyperbolic radii compress multi-scale structure into uniform high-level abstractions, erasing the local patterns predictions need. Details survive better near the origin. Their framework, H4G, shrinks embedding radii with learnable block-diagonal scaling matrices, together with Möbius multiplication, a hyperbolic arithmetic. Global reach is kept at minimal computational cost. Experiments deliver state-of-the-art zero-shot results: improvements of twelve point eight percent on heterophilic graphs and eight point four percent on homophilic ones.
arxiv-2510-12194:
Linyi Yang and Yixuan Weng refuse to let research agents run unsupervised. Deep-research systems typically work fire-and-forget: launch one and you cannot fix its errors or inject expertise mid-run. Their 2025 arXiv paper presents ResearStudio, an open-source framework built around real-time human control, organized as a collaborative workshop.

A hierarchical planner-executor writes every step into a live plan-as-document. A communication layer streams every action, file change, and tool call into a web interface. There the user can pause at any moment, edit the plan or the code, run custom commands, and resume, sliding between AI-led and human-led modes. Control costs nothing in capability: in fully autonomous mode the system achieves top results on the GAIA benchmark, surpassing OpenAI's DeepResearch and Manus. Code, protocol, and evaluation scripts are public.
arxiv-2510-12394:
Kang, Park, and Taniguchi construct an exotic diffeomorphism on a contractible four dimensional manifold that stays exotic after two stabilizations, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Such a map is a symmetry of a manifold that cannot be smoothed into the identity map, even when the manifold itself is simple in shape. Contractible manifolds, which can be shrunk to a point, are a sharp test case.

Stabilization adds a standard building block to the manifold and usually kills the exotic effect, so surviving two rounds is notable. The authors develop a refined algebraic tool: an equivariant version of the lattice homotopy type that respects a symmetry group combining Pin(2) and a two element group. This refinement lets them compute equivariant Seiberg Witten Floer homotopy types, which detect exotic behavior. With these tools, they produce a relative exotic one on a compact contractible four manifold. Its exoticness provably survives two rounds.
arxiv-2510-12494:
Liu and co-authors redesign split learning between two groups with a publisher subscriber design, in a 2025 arXiv paper. In vertical federated learning, two parties holding different features for the same users train a model together without sharing raw data. The standard design forces the parties to work in lockstep, wasting resources, and hardware and data differences make training uneven.

Their PubSub-VFL decouples the parties through a publish subscribe pattern. It adds data parallelism borrowed from parameter server designs, forming a hierarchical asynchronous mechanism that cuts latency. To handle heterogeneity, they formalize an optimization problem over the participants' profiles that selects hyperparameters while preserving privacy. Theory shows stable convergence and fit with differential privacy. Across five benchmark datasets, PubSub-VFL trained two to seven times faster than leading baselines without losing accuracy, and pushed resource use above ninety percent in the best case.
arxiv-2510-12594:
Schootemeijer and colleagues find that the brightest cool supergiant stars shine at the same maximum brightness even in a galaxy devoid of heavy elements, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. Stellar winds are usually assumed to weaken at low metallicity, so models predict metal poor massive stars keep their hydrogen layers and become brighter cool supergiants. Earlier studies across a moderate metallicity range found no such dependence, puzzlingly.

Adding four galaxies observed with the Hubble and Webb telescopes extends the test to the metal poor dwarf galaxy I Zw 18, at about one fortieth the Sun's metallicity. In every galaxy the upper luminosity limit of cool supergiants sits at the same constant value. The authors argue late stage mass loss, independent of metallicity, is the likeliest mechanism stripping stars above that limit. For the early universe this caps black hole masses and links massive stars to its surprising nitrogen enrichment.
arxiv-2510-12694:
Wimarsson, Ferrari, and Jutzi simulate how small moons of asteroids get their odd shapes by merging gently with other moonlets, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Direct observations have revealed satellites with unexpected forms: the flattened Dimorphos and the two lobed Selam. Classical formation theories explain mainly the elongated population.

Using a discrete element N-body code that treats the moons as rubble piles of many grains, the authors collide moonlets below their mutual escape velocity. They follow the merged body in its tidal environment. The resulting shapes depend strongly on the shapes and initial orientations of the colliding moonlets, because each largely retains its own structure through the gentle impact. Tidal stripping of a two lobed body happens in discrete distance regimes. Close in, the inner lobe is torn off completely. Farther out, only a small piece is lost. Modeling satellite formation must therefore track moonlet shapes, not just masses.
arxiv-2510-12794:
Chen and colleagues ask whether rocky planets in compact systems are born dry or wet in this 2025 arXiv paper. They model systems like TRAPPIST-1, where several small planets orbit close to a dim red dwarf star. Earlier estimates of planet water content usually treated collisions and air loss separately, which may have distorted the picture.

The authors coupled impact delivery, impact erosion, and exchange between a planet's mantle and atmosphere inside one model that follows random collision histories. They also included the young star's long bright phase before it settles down. Inner planets in their TRAPPIST-1 analogs ended with very little water, while outer planets often kept more than an Earth ocean. That gradient, they argue, explains why the space telescope JWST found no atmospheres on the inner two planets.
arxiv-2510-12894:
Li, Tan, Gucev, and Lidar probe memory effects in quantum computer noise in this 2025 arXiv paper. Most qubit analysis assumes Markovian noise, meaning the environment forgets instantly, but real processors show correlated noise from qubit coupling and long-lived environmental effects. Such non-Markovian behavior matters for reaching fault-tolerant quantum computing, where errors must stay below strict thresholds.

The team used the post-Markovian master equation, a modeling framework built to capture those memory effects, to study how the noise behaves. They validated the framework experimentally on superconducting qubits running on an IBM Quantum device and saw clear non-Markovian behavior during circuit execution. An information-theoretic analysis of crosstalk, unwanted interaction between qubits, showed that crosstalk can dominate the memory effects seen in current hardware.
arxiv-2510-13094:
Pandey and co-authors develop certified machine unlearning for high-dimensional models in this 2025 arXiv paper. Unlearning removes selected data's influence from a trained model while preserving generalization, and certification gives that removal a rigorous guarantee. In high dimensions, where parameter counts rival sample counts, the standard assumptions of strong convexity and smoothness rarely hold together, blocking earlier theory.

The authors propose a Gaussian certifiability notion built for high-dimensional regimes, which they argue captures a broad class of noise-adding mechanisms best. Studying a popular unlearning algorithm, one Newton step followed by calibrated Gaussian noise, they show a single step suffices for both privacy and accuracy under their notion. That contrasts with the only prior high-dimensional analysis, which required at least two steps under a different certifiability notion. They attribute the gap to that notion's suboptimality and poor fit with noise addition.
arxiv-2510-13194:
Chen, Song, and Nakamura preserve emphasis in speech-to-speech translation in this 2025 arXiv paper. Translators usually chase semantic accuracy, but emphatic stress, the highlighting of particular words, carries focus and intent, and losing it flattens meaning. Their system, StressTransfer, aims to carry word-level emphasis across languages.

The method uses a large language model to convert source-language stress into tags in the target language, which then steer a controllable text-to-speech model when the translated speech is synthesized. Because aligned training data with stress labels are scarce, the authors built a pipeline that generates such data automatically, and they use a language model as judge for evaluation. Experiments showed their approach substantially outperforming baselines at preserving emphasis, while translation quality, speaker intent, and naturalness stayed comparable. They argue prosody deserves first-class treatment in translation systems.
arxiv-2510-13294:
Kempf and Latter analyze the magneto-thermal instability globally in this 2025 arXiv paper. In the dilute plasma filling galaxy clusters, heat flows almost only along magnetic field lines, and when temperature rises outward against gravity this anisotropy drives an instability that stirs the plasma. Most earlier analyses treated the instability locally, yet its natural length scale can rival the cluster's scale height, undermining the local approximation.

The authors perform a global linear analysis in a spherical, stratified cluster model under a standard dark matter potential, combining Sturm-Liouville theory and WKBJ approximations with two independent numerical solvers. They obtain scaling laws and approximate growth rates for the global modes, whose shapes are confined inside a turning point, with the most unstable local modes living near that point. The phenomenology mirrors global magneto-rotational modes in accretion discs, and the results benchmark codes using the Braginskii heat flux.
arxiv-2510-13794:
Peng releases MimicKit, an open-source toolkit for training motion controllers by imitation plus reinforcement learning. His 2025 arXiv paper serves graphics and robotics labs that animate virtual figures and robots. Motion imitation builds agile, natural skills, but each lab rebuilds the same plumbing from scratch. Small design choices, hard to copy, make results hard to compare.

MimicKit gathers common imitation methods and learning algorithms into one shared code base. Standard formats for worlds, agents, and motion data keep tests comparable across projects. The design is modular and driven by settings files, easing tweaks and add-ons. New figures and tasks plug in without redoing the training loop. Demos show virtual human-like figures learning dynamic moves like a spinkick from source motion. The author aims to lower the bar for imitation research that others can rerun and check. The code is public for anyone to build on.
arxiv-2510-13894:
Tresp, Li, Harjes, and Ma ask whether quantum measuring or Bayesian updating better describes how the brain reasons, through their Tensor Brain model. Their 2025 arXiv paper recasts some quantum systems in purely chance-based language. State vectors become probability vectors, and unitary steps become special stochastic matrices. Brains might exploit the same math, they propose.

Pro-bits, chance-based cousins of qubits, carry the recast quantum algorithms. Controlled shortcuts then turn that machinery into neural network dynamics. The Tensor Brain models perception and memory with a cognitive brain state that measuring feeds back into. Looking gives an outcome and at once changes the state, like quantum measuring does. One special case reduces exactly to Bayesian reasoning, they show. In general, though, direct Bayes becomes too hard where the quantum-style algorithms stay cheap. Echoes of transformers close the paper: memory works like lookup, skip connections act as priors.
arxiv-2510-14094:
Haotian Feng proves results about how well neural networks can approximate solutions of reaction-diffusion equations, in this 2025 arXiv paper. These are partial differential equations that describe systems where substances spread out while also reacting. Such equations model everything from chemical patterns to biological invasion, and neural solvers are often used to solve them without a theory of when they work.

Building on the universal approximation theorem, Feng shows that a two-layer neural network can approximate the solution of the one-dimensional reaction-diffusion equation. A three-layer network suffices for the two-dimensional case. Results cover both homogeneous media, where properties are the same, and heterogeneous media, where they vary. Feng notes the framework extends further, to elliptic and parabolic equations. It gives neural differential-equation solvers a firmer foundation. It also highlights what even shallow networks can express for such problems.
arxiv-2510-14494:
Ziad Akram Ali Hammouri and co-authors build neural-network methods for judging biomarkers while adjusting for patient covariates, in this 2025 arXiv paper. They apply them to the question of whether physical activity predicts death. The receiver operating characteristic curve measures how well a biomarker separates two groups, and its covariate-adjusted version tailors that judgment, but machine learning had rarely been used for the adjusted analysis.

Their framework models the adjusted curve with neural networks, and simulations under dependency structures check its behavior. In the case study, total activity counts, a proxy for step count, serve as the biomarker for mortality at three, five, and eight years. Analyses split by sex and adjusted for age and body mass index reveal how the activity-mortality relationship changes across groups. This shows why a single plain curve can mislead clinicians comparing patients of other ages.
arxiv-2510-14594:
Markoff and Galaktionovs, in a 2025 arXiv paper, describe a system that sharpens the labels given by animal recognition software. A leading model, SpeciesNet, can name thousands of species. To stay safe, though, it often falls back on broad labels like mammal or animal, which are of little use to conservation workers who need the actual species.

Their system adds a five-stage pipeline on top of the original predictions. High-confidence labels pass through, bird detections get a special override, and the rest are re-examined using image embeddings, learned cluster centers, and a metric learning step. On a desert lion conservation dataset with over fifteen thousand detections, the pipeline rescued hundreds of bird detections from blank labels. It then reclassified hundreds more vague detections with 96.5 percent accuracy in the reported test, reaching species-level names for about two-thirds of them.
arxiv-2510-14694:
Nabi, Bhattacharya, Shpitser, and Robins reply, in a 2025 arXiv paper, to four published discussions of their earlier work on missing data. Missing data plague real studies: values go unrecorded for reasons tied to the values themselves. The original paper recast the problem in causal and counterfactual terms, using graphical models to state exactly when the complete-data distribution can be recovered from what is observed.

The response first restates that contribution. Identification of the full-data law becomes identification of a joint distribution over counterfactuals, the variables as they would look if nothing were missing. This yields a counterfactual analogue of the g-formula, and the Markov properties of a missing-data graph can turn it into a formula in observed quantities, giving nonparametric identification. The authors then answer each discussion in turn: those by Levis and Kennedy, Luo and Geng, Wang and van der Laan, and Yang and Kim.
arxiv-2510-15194:
Tianchen Zhao and four colleagues improve a trick for enlarging image training sets with AI-generated pictures, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Generators steered by an example image and a text prompt often mix the two badly. Background details survive even when the prompt asks to change them, while key subject features get lost. The result is extra training data that can mislead the very models it should help.

Their framework embeds images through a model trained to keep the class-defining features and downplay irrelevant surroundings. That produces new images that vary in controlled ways while staying true to their category. Across eight fine-grained vision datasets the method beat leading augmentation approaches, lifting classification accuracy by about 0.73 points in standard settings and 6.5 points when some classes had very few examples. The gains were strongest exactly where extra data is hardest to collect.
arxiv-2510-15494:
Lirong Yi, Gregory Gay, and Philipp Leitner test whether language models can make real software run faster, not just write plausible code. Their 2025 experimental study mines sixty-five tasks from open-source Java projects where human developers had achieved significant speedups. An automated pipeline then asked two leading models, under four prompt variations, to patch the same performance problems.

Careful benchmarking against the original code and the human solutions gave a mixed verdict. The models' patches did improve performance over the baseline in most cases. Human patches still won by a statistically significant margin, showing the models rarely find the truly optimal fix. In about two-thirds of cases the model's idea matched or resembled the developer's own optimization. The remaining third proposed something more original. Those original ideas, however, only occasionally produced large gains, suggesting current models imitate good optimization better than they invent it.
arxiv-2510-15594:
Antoine Bourgois and Thierry Poibeau build a resource for tracking who is who across entire French novels. Their 2025 arXiv paper tackles coreference resolution, the task of linking every mention of a character, by name or pronoun, into one chain. Datasets of fully annotated long documents are rare, so models are seldom tested on the long chains that fiction creates.

Their corpus holds three full-length French novels totaling more than two hundred eighty-five thousand tokens, annotated throughout. A modular resolution pipeline processes them, built so errors can be traced to specific stages. The authors report the approach is competitive and scales to full books without breaking down. As a demonstration, they use the resolved chains to infer the gender of fictional characters automatically. That example shows the corpus serving literary analysis as well as core NLP evaluation, a bridge the authors want to strengthen.
arxiv-2510-15794:
Rachna Raj and Diego Elias Costa wrote a 2025 paper for open source maintainers. Maintainers keep widely used libraries stable and evolving. Yet they get little feedback from users. They rarely see which interfaces projects actually use. They also miss which changes break downstream code. Testing priorities stay unclear as a result.

The authors propose community-based analytics. Usage would be mined across all projects that depend on a library. An empirical study supports the idea. Such analytics can guide testing strategy. They can reveal the real impact of a change. Library evolution could then rest on evidence, not guesswork.
arxiv-2511-00194: Jovial Cheukam Ngouonou, Ramiz Gindullin, Claude-Guy Quimper, Nicolas Beldiceanu, and Remi Douence present a short report on picking and proving conjectures. Their improved method selects conjectures step by step, building on a selection algorithm from earlier work. The conjectures chosen are the most-filtering ones, in the sense of the title. The authors then prove every conjecture their method selects. Readers get both the selection procedure and the completed proofs in one compact paper.
arxiv-2511-00294:
Lucas Almeida and Maycon Peixoto propose Tetris, a strategy for placing application modules across edge and cloud resources. Edge sites sit close to users and cut delay, while the cloud offers raw power for heavy tasks. Placement must match user demands with limited capacity at each site, without overloading the system or breaking service-level agreements.

Tetris uses a heuristic that ranks services by urgency under their agreements and by how efficiently they use resources. In tests, it cut service-level violations by about seventy-six percent compared with a baseline method. For operators running delay-sensitive apps across mixed edge and cloud sites, the result promises better quality of service without wasteful over-provisioning.
arxiv-2511-00394:
Yuto Nogata completes a classification in finite group theory. The groups in question are the projective special linear groups in two dimensions, the Suzuki groups, and the first Janko group.
