All are finite simple groups, families with no normal shortcuts in their structure. For set ranges of the size parameter, earlier studies had classified their pronormal subgroups, subgroups with a special conjugacy property, and open cases remained.

Building on those works, Nogata settles the remaining cases under the same parameter conditions. For each group family, the pronormal subgroups turn out to be closed under joins but not under meets, two lattice operations on subgroup families. Replacing the meet with a suitable operation repairs the failure, and the family becomes a lattice. The result closes a tidy chapter in subgroup structure theory.
arxiv-2511-00694:
Uthman Jinadu and six co-authors sharpen personalized search for online shopping. Big catalogs hold many near-identical items, and models must learn subtle differences while respecting each shopper's history. Training data for that skill usually comes from sampling schemes that are expensive or logistically painful. Their model embeds queries and products in one shared vector space.

A taxonomy-based hard-negative sampling strategy mines training examples that are relevant yet challenging, using the product taxonomy as the guide. User-level personalization layers each customer's purchase history and behavior on top. Offline tests beat keyword and neural baselines on recall, and live A/B testing lifted conversion, add-to-cart rates, and average order value. Taxonomy-driven negatives also cut training overhead and sped convergence at deployment scale.
arxiv-2511-01494:
M. Murabito and colleagues measure plasma flows inside a solar filament, a cool, dense ribbon of gas suspended in the Sun's atmosphere above an active region. Flow measurements in such filaments are rare, above all in the infrared and ultraviolet ranges that probe the chromosphere and transition region, and earlier work mostly studied filaments near the solar limb.

Their filament sat on the solar disk and was observed over two days in November 2020. It combined spectra from the IRIS satellite with ground based infrared spectrograph and imager data covering helium and hydrogen lines. Steady blueshifts inside the filament indicate upflows, fastest in the silicon lines, while red shifted emission at the footpoints of a new dark bundle suggests chromospheric downflows. The measurements benchmark models of filament support and mass loading.
arxiv-2511-01694:
Hossein Abdi, Mingfei Sun, and Wei Pan fine-tune CLIP, the vision-language model. They work in the hard regime. Labeled examples are scarce there, and test data may drift from training data. First-order optimizers converge slowly there and are touchy about step size, while CLIP's loss landscape is non-convex with sharp critical points, exactly where curvature information should help.

Natural gradient descent uses that curvature by scaling the gradient with the inverse Fisher information matrix, but the matrix is far too expensive for large models. The authors approximate the natural gradient in a Bayesian way, using a Kalman filter, which also yields uncertainty estimates as a byproduct. Experiments on diverse image datasets test whether the second-order, uncertainty-aware updates generalize better both in-distribution and under distribution shift.
arxiv-2511-01794:
Vi Retault and Yohaï-Eliel Berreby attack catastrophic forgetting, the tendency of a fine-tuned language model to lose skills it had before training on a new task. Their method, RIGSA, starts from randomly initialized full-rank adapters, switches them on with a ReZero-style gate, and prunes them iteratively by weight magnitude until only a sparse adapter remains.

The testbed is SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct learning a new vision-in-text task, reading MNIST digits presented as text, where it starts near chance. Forgetting is then measured on the PIQA, HellaSwag, and GSM8k benchmarks. RIGSA learned the new task. Despite having more trainable parameters than the 4-bit QLoRA baseline, it forgot less, particularly on GSM8k math problems. It performed only comparably to a simple random masking control, though.
arxiv-2511-02094:
Michel Ma, Takuma Seno, Kaushik Subramanian, Peter Wurman, Peter Stone, and Craig Sherstan automate one of the fiddliest parts of reinforcement learning: the writing of reward functions. A reward function tells an agent what good behaviour means. In complex settings like racing, hand-crafting rewards is slow and error-prone. Their testbed is the Gran Turismo 7 racing game, and the only human input is instructions written in plain text.

Foundation models search the space of reward functions, with a large language model proposing candidates, a vision-language model judging preferences, and human feedback steering the process. The resulting agents rival GT Sophy, a champion-level racing system, and also display novel behaviours the team did not program directly. The authors present this as a step toward practical automated reward design beyond games.
arxiv-2511-02194:
Yibo Zhao, Yang Zhao, Hongru Du, and Hao Frank Yang model how individuals make high-stakes personal choices, using travel mode and vaccine uptake as test cases. Personal decisions often diverge from what a population-level optimum predicts, because each person weighs numerical factors like cost and time alongside personal preferences and constraints expressed in words. Classical utility theory captures the numbers but not the language.

Their framework, ATHENA, works in two stages. First it uses a language model to help discover robust symbolic utility functions at group level. Then it adapts those functions to each person through semantic templates shaped by the optimal utility. On real-world data the method beat utility-based, machine learning, and other language-model approaches, raising the F1 score by at least 6.5 percent over the strongest rival, and removing either stage clearly hurt performance.
arxiv-2511-02394:
Zibin Zhao and six co-authors, including Boris Malomed, measure how springy a droplet made of quantum fluid is. Quantum droplets are self-bound puddles of ultracold atoms held together by the Lee-Huang-Yang correction, a quantum fluctuation effect, and earlier work on their breathing vibrations and collisions hinted they have well-defined elasticity. This study derives the droplet's bulk modulus, the property that resists compression, in three dimensions.

Theory and numerical simulation together link the bulk modulus to the frequency of the droplet's own vibrations. The analysis shows how the elasticity depends on the number of particles in the droplet and on the strength of the interactions between them. The authors also give a realistic numerical estimate of the modulus for an actual experimental system, intended as a reference value for future measurements. They point to elastic materials governed by this quantum effect as a longer-term possibility.
arxiv-2511-02594:
Bahareh Afshari, Giacomo Barlucchi, and Graham Leigh bound how long a certain kind of logical recursion can run before it settles. In the modal mu-calculus, formulas can define functions by least fixed points, and the closure ordinal counts the iterations needed to reach that fixed point. The authors prove that across all countable structures, functions definable in the alternation-free fragment always settle in strictly fewer than omega-squared iterations, where omega is the first infinite ordinal.

The result corrects and extends an earlier claim by two of the authors. The proof revives Kozen's well-annotations, a bookkeeping device from the finite model theory of the mu-calculus, in a conservative form that guarantees minimal annotations. Parts of the structure then locally determine the closure ordinal, and a direct pumping argument rules out any closure ordinal between omega-squared and the limit of countability.
arxiv-2511-02694:
A tablet touchscreen can sense more than fingers, as Siqi Zhang, Mayank Goel, and Justin Chan show in a 2025 paper. Their system, DropleX, turns a stock tablet into a tool that detects tiny liquid samples. The trick is turning off the screen's built-in filters, which normally ignore drops like rain, with no change to the hardware.

The team models how the screen senses, then builds a signal and learning pipeline for liquid tests. In lab trials, DropleX spotted adulteration in soda, wine, and milk with accuracy from 89 to 99 percent, using samples of a few microliters. It also traced faint chemical levels and worked through container walls. Such screens could serve labs and food safety checks.
arxiv-2511-02794:
Chenyu Zhang and six colleagues study a failure mode in models that reason across text, image, and sound together. Sometimes one stream, confident but wrong, drags the whole answer down. Their 2025 paper names that failure modality sabotage and builds a light diagnostic layer to expose it in multimodal language models.

The layer treats each modality as an agent that offers a label plus a short self-assessment. A simple fusion step then merges the offers, marking which streams backed the right answer and which misled it. In a case study on emotion recognition, the method revealed steady reliability profiles for each stream. The authors offer the scaffold as a general audit tool, to tell whether faults come from data quirks or model limits.
arxiv-2511-02894:
W. K. M. Mithsara and four colleagues defend wearable health sensors against poisoned data. Activity recognition in homes, clinics, and factories depends on clean sensor streams, and attackers who corrupt the training data can quietly wreck it. Older defenses need large labeled sets and heavy retraining, which suits shifting Internet of Things settings poorly. Their 2025 framework hands the defense to large language models.

The models work in zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot modes. Role-play prompts cast the model as an expert judging sensor anomalies, and step-by-step reasoning guides it to spot poisoning signs and suggest cleaned values. The team measured detection accuracy, cleaning quality, delay, and communication cost. They report the approach is practical for real-time use and adapts without curated data sets.
arxiv-2511-03394:
Harry Desmond, Richard Stiskalek, Jose Antonio Najera, and Indranil Banik argue that statistical habits quietly skew cosmic distance work and may feed the Hubble tension. Distances in the ladder method are hidden values that need a prior guess in Bayesian work. The usual flat prior on distance steps pulls distances low, because objects spread evenly through volume, and that pull inflates the expansion rate.

A second trap comes from selection: samples favor bright or near objects, and Bayesian math must add factors for that favoring. Classic fitting stays unbiased only in narrow cases, though simulation-based fixes can repair the bias. The authors urge ladder studies to audit their statistics as carefully as their telescopes.
arxiv-2511-03494:
Amir Bahador Javadi and Philip Pong test data-driven ways to learn the behavior of a grid-following power converter from its own traces. Renewable sources and smart grids are making power systems harder to model by hand. Methods that read equations straight from data, including sparse identification and deep symbolic regression, promise a shortcut.

Their test rig swaps a classic generator for a converter resource on a lossless line tied to a vast grid. Synthetic traces from that rig, run in grid-following mode, feed each learning method. Scores show how faithfully each method recovers true dynamics. Trustworthy learned models would help operators predict converter behavior as grids fill with inverter-based sources.
arxiv-2511-03794:
Aqeel Ahmed, Juan P Garces, and Manfred Lindner present a new version of Dirac leptogenesis set during reheating, the hot phase just after inflation in the early universe. An imbalance first forms in the scalar sector through decays of the inflaton that violate CP symmetry and occur out of equilibrium.

Yukawa interactions then carry that imbalance to chiral neutrinos, and electroweak sphalerons convert part of it into the baryon imbalance seen now. A minimal version of the setup naturally allows small neutrino Yukawa couplings. It also leaves effects on the effective number of relativistic species that upcoming cosmological observations could test, giving the idea a clear observational handle.
arxiv-2511-03894:
Martin Guillot is the lead author among eleven authors reporting the first direct measurement of the non-Abelian quantum geometric tensor in a multi-gap photonic lattice. Multi-gap semimetals host band nodes with non-Abelian braiding behaviour, and probing those phases requires geometric tools beyond the standard Abelian tensor.

Orbital-resolved polarimetry recovered the full Bloch Hamiltonian of a six-band, two-dimensional synthetic lattice. From it the team read off non-Abelian quaternion charges, Euler curvature, and the non-Abelian quantum metric for all bands. Quantum geometry shapes responses from flat-band superconductivity to transport and metrology, so a direct probe opens experimental access to a wide class of multi-gap phenomena.
arxiv-2511-04394:
DORAEMON is an open-source PyTorch library presented by Ke Du and four colleagues. It unifies visual object modeling and representation learning across many scales in one system. A single workflow driven by simple config files covers classification, retrieval, and metric learning tasks.

The library exposes more than one thousand pretrained backbones through an interface compatible with the timm library. It adds modular losses, data augmentations, and tools for training across many machines. Its recipes match or beat reference results on ImageNet-1K, MS-Celeb-1M, and Stanford Online Products. One-command export to ONNX or HuggingFace helps move models from research into real use.
arxiv-2511-04494:
Alper Kalle and three colleagues compress convolutional networks by respecting the data distribution. Trained networks can shrink a lot, but classic low-rank methods judge error in weight space alone. That can keep weights close while the network's actual outputs drift.

Their tensor method instead measures error in function space. It weighs weight changes by the covariance of each layer's inputs, so busy directions count more. The goal is a smaller network whose output distribution barely moves. Smarter compression like this matters for running vision models on phones and other limited hardware.
arxiv-2511-04594:
Utkarsh U. Chavan and two colleagues set regret lower bounds for decentralized multi-agent shortest path problems. Fleets like robot swarms and traffic systems must coordinate without a central controller. Shortest path models capture that decentralized control task well.

Learning in the single-agent version is well studied, but the multi-agent case is nearly untouched. The team works under linear function approximation for dynamics and costs. Symmetry arguments reveal the structure of optimal policies in this setting. Their main result bounds how well any learner can do, giving the young field a firm floor to measure algorithms against.
arxiv-2511-04694:
Zishuo Zheng leads five authors teaching language models to reason about instruction priority. Real prompts mix orders from several sources, and higher-level rules must win. Rather than hard-coding the hierarchy, the team treats resolving it as a thinking task.

The model first reasons about how a user request relates to stronger instructions. Only then does it write its response. Their VerIH dataset trains this skill with checkable constraint-following tasks. It pairs aligned and conflicting system and user instructions side by side. Lightweight reinforcement learning on that data aims at models that stay controllable in high-stakes roles.
arxiv-2511-04894:
Hui-Fei Zhai leads four authors reporting that mixed valency disrupts magnetic order in a cerium compound. Mixed-valent lanthanide materials often show odd transport, magnetism, or superconductivity. Their compound joins cerium, iron, and gallium in a quasi-one-dimensional structure.

Diffraction and photoelectron tests show cerium in two charge states on one site. Mössbauer spectroscopy finds the iron sublattice nonmagnetic, contrary to a recent report. Low-temperature resistivity and heat capacity show no sign of magnetic ordering either. The mixed cerium valence appears to suppress the order that simpler readings of the structure would predict.
arxiv-2511-05294:
Shaolong Wu and co-authors study how often people go online, and how that ties to income and job search in the United States since 2010. Surveys tend to log use counts alone, and skip the gear, skills, and support that make digital life possible.

Using a youth cohort tracked over years, they focus on the 2011, 2013, and 2015 waves, with 2017 as later context. Daily use marked higher income and firmer job attachment in each cross-section. Less-than-daily use tracked lower outcomes, which the authors read with care about what use counts can and cannot prove.
arxiv-2511-05394:
Alexander Htet Kyaw and co-authors build an augmented reality aid for assembly work, guided by AI object recognition. A worker sees a box drawn around the part needed for each step, placed in the real scene, plus where that part should go.

By tying each instruction to the live spot of its part, the system cuts the need to hunt, sort, or label parts by hand before each step. The team tests the flow for feasibility on a real assembly task. Such aids could cut errors and training time on factory floors.
arxiv-2511-05494:
Haichao Zhang and co-authors present CRAGRU, a method to make a recommender system forget one user's data without harming picks for others. Privacy laws grant a right to be forgotten, but plain unlearning can skew picks for users who act like the one removed.

Full retraining kills that bias but costs too much at scale. CRAGRU uses retrieval-augmented generation tuned per user to patch the gap at low cost. Tests weigh how close it comes to retrained quality. The work seeks a middle path: honor a delete request and keep the service sharp.
arxiv-2511-05694:
Anirudh Satheesh, Keenan Powell, and Vaneet Aggarwal tackle a training problem in reinforcement learning: agents that shine in the lab often fail when the real world shifts. Robust training guards against the worst case within a set budget of change. But a fixed budget forces a bad trade-off between everyday performance and safety.

Their method turns the budget itself into a curriculum. The budget grows or shrinks with the agent's progress, a self-paced schedule that steadies training. Across several test environments the method improved the balance between robustness and performance. Returns under disturbances rose by about twelve percent over fixed or hand-set schedules, and roughly doubled the scores of plain algorithms.
arxiv-2511-05894:
Fei Yu and co-authors build scene graphs of 3D spaces that robots can query in plain language. A scene graph lists objects and their relations. Open-world settings break the fixed label sets such systems usually need, since new objects and relations appear freely.

Their framework pairs vision-language models with retrieval-based reasoning. One module builds the graph on the fly, detecting objects and inferring relations without a closed vocabulary. The graphs are stored in a vector database, so text or image queries can pull relevant scenes for question answering, grounding, retrieval, and task planning. On two benchmarks the method generalized well and beat rivals. The authors pitch it as a scalable route to interactive 3D understanding.
arxiv-2511-06094:
Daniel Beechey and Özgür Şimşek explain reinforcement learning decisions with Shapley values, a fair-credit idea from game theory. Agents that learn by trial and error are powerful but opaque, which blocks their use where safety matters. Shapley explanations assign each feature its fair share of a decision, yet computing them exactly is ruinously expensive.

Their method, FastSVERL, approximates Shapley values at scale. It is built for the quirks of reinforcement learning: effects that unfold over multi-step trajectories, data gathered by a different policy than the one explained, and agent behavior that shifts over time. The authors present it as a practical, scalable route to principled explanations. Rigorous interpretability, they argue, should not wait for exact computation.
arxiv-2511-06194:
Muhammad Usama and colleagues introduce NURBGen, a system that turns plain text descriptions into editable three-dimensional CAD models. Earlier text-to-CAD tools produced fixed meshes or depended on rare design-history data. NURBGen instead generates models built from NURBS, the smooth mathematical surfaces that professional CAD software uses.

A fine-tuned large language model writes surface parameters such as control points, knot vectors, and weights as structured text, which converts directly into standard CAD format. A hybrid scheme adds simple solid shapes to handle trimmed surfaces cleanly. The authors also built partABC, a captioned dataset of single CAD parts, and expert checks favored NURBGen on shape fidelity and dimensions.
arxiv-2511-06694:
Jose Marie Antonio Minoza and colleagues measure what machine learning inference really costs the planet, framework by framework and chip by chip. Inference runs at planetary scale, yet its carbon, energy, heat, and water footprints are seldom counted, especially on modest hardware. Their tool, ML-EcoLyzer, instruments models across processors, consumer graphics cards, and data center accelerators.

A new Environmental Sustainability Score counts effective parameters served per gram of carbon dioxide emitted. More than nineteen hundred configurations were measured across text, vision, audio, and tabular tasks. Quantization improved the score, giant accelerators wasted effort on light jobs, and even small models proved costly when deployed carelessly, giving practitioners a yardstick for greener choices.
arxiv-2511-06794:
Lisong He, Yi Yang, and Xiangyu Chang work on machine unlearning, the task of removing certain data from a trained model so it behaves as if that data was never used. Laws granting a right to be forgotten make such updates necessary. Most current methods, they note, treat every deleted point as equally key.

Their system, Data Value-Weighted Unlearning, weights each point by how much it contributed to the model's performance, so valuable and worthless data are unlearned differently. The weighting can be added to many current methods, and the authors build certified versions using a one-step Newton update with added noise. Tests on synthetic and real data showed better accuracy and robustness than uniform deletion.
arxiv-2511-07094:
Necati Sefercioglu, Mehmet Ozan Unal, Metin Ertas, and Isa Yildirim make low-dose CT reconstruction serve the diagnosis, not just the image metrics. Deep learning reconstructions already score well on signal-to-noise and structural similarity, yet they often erase the fine anatomical detail clinicians need, which limits real clinical use. Their system adds a frozen, pre-trained task network as a regularizer inside the reconstruction loss, guiding training without letting the task model pull the images astray.

The test task is segmentation of the liver and its tumors. Task-adaptive models reached Dice scores up to 0.707, approaching full-dose scans at 0.874 and far ahead of joint training at 0.331 and standard reconstruction at 0.626. Because the change is only to the loss function, the system can be added to current reconstruction models.
arxiv-2511-07194:
Kristoffer Eggestad, Benjamin A D Williamson, and Sverre M Selbach compute the behavior of domain walls and point defects in the only known ferroelectric inorganic halide perovskites, the cesium germanium halides. Using density functional theory, they examine how walls between oppositely polarized regions interact with common vacancies. The most stable defects are halogen and cesium vacancies, and the halogen vacancies migrate easily.

Unlike oxide ferroelectrics, defects here barely notice domain walls: the structural distortions at the walls are subtle, so nothing pins a moving wall, and wall formation and migration energies are small. The band gap stays constant across walls, which makes conducting walls for nanoelectronics hard to realize, but shallow p-type defect levels suggest strong p-type conductivity is possible. Low wall energies make the family promising as soft ferroelectrics for fast, low-loss switching.
arxiv-2511-07394:
C Tegkelidis, J Larsson, and D Alp pin down the exact position of Supernova 1987A, the nearest supernova of the modern era, in the Large Magellanic Cloud. A precise position anchors readings of the kick given to its compact remnant and of the ejecta and shock velocities. Using multi-epoch Hubble Space Telescope imaging, the team modeled the early ejecta and the famous equatorial ring, then registered everything onto Gaia's third data release to get absolute celestial coordinates.

The averaged position sits at about five hours, thirty-five minutes, twenty-eight seconds of right ascension and sixty-nine degrees, sixteen arcminutes, eleven arcseconds south. The early ejecta center lies slightly offset from the ring center, greatly so, which may reflect instrument systematics or a real offset of the explosion. Comparing with the JWST-observed compact source implies a three-dimensional kick of roughly four hundred seventy kilometers per second.
arxiv-2511-07594:
Leonardo Abbrescia, Pieter Blue, and Jan Sbierski build a wave that breaks in a fully controlled way. Their model quasilinear wave equation in one space dimension starts from smooth data chosen so elementary methods solve it. Even so, the classical solution blows up in finite time and a shock forms.

A weak solution with a supersonic shock then interrupts the smooth development. Because the model stays tractable, geometric and analytic shock phenomena appear in miniature. The maximal smooth region and its breakdown can be described exactly. Such prototypes help relativists and analysts test ideas about singularities before facing harder equations from physics.
arxiv-2511-07894:
Shihao Li, Jiachen Li, and Jiamin Xu turn plain-language control requirements into checked controllers. Writing robust controllers by hand demands scarce skill, and language models alone cannot guarantee stability. Their S2C framework chains five agent roles from spec extraction through solver, tester, and code generator.

Linear matrix synthesis based on the bounded-real lemma produces the controller, while Monte Carlo and frequency checks verify it. A guardrail tied to settling time keeps the search stable. That proof separates this from casual code generation: the output ships with hard evidence that performance bounds hold, the standard safety work requires.
arxiv-2511-08094:
Kaicheng Zhang, David Reynolds, Piero Deidda, and Francesco Tudisco introduce a graph neural network built on Stuart Landau oscillators. Deep graph networks often suffer oversmoothing, where node features blur together, and vanishing gradients. Oscillatory designs borrow physics to fight both problems, but phase only models discard amplitude information that can carry useful signals.

The Stuart Landau model keeps amplitude and phase together, with tunable settings for the Hopf parameter and coupling strength. Node features then evolve with richer behavior, including amplitude control and multistable synchronization. Across node, graph, and regression tasks, the network beats earlier oscillatory graph models and sets a grounded new framework.
arxiv-2511-08194:
Antoine Monier and colleagues study how soap films drain inside a centrifugal thin film balance that can reach one hundred times normal gravity. Surface bubbles feed aerosols that affect climate, so film thinning matters beyond the laboratory. Interferometry gives time resolved thickness maps across a wide range of effective gravities, from below normal to extreme.

Drainage is governed by capillary suction and marginal regeneration, where thin elements born at the meniscus replace thicker film. The thickness ratio between new elements and nearby film stays near zero point eight to zero point nine, matching earlier work. Strong gravity also stretches the film, sets meniscus size, and drives a shift from inertial to viscous motion.
arxiv-2511-08294:
Laura Bragagnolo, Leonardo Barcellona, and Stefano Ghidoni present SkelSplat for estimating three dimensional human poses from several camera views without three dimensional ground truth labels. Multi view methods usually learn view fusion from large annotated sets and then generalize poorly to new scenes. SkelSplat models a pose as a skeleton of three dimensional Gaussians, one per joint, fitted through differentiable rendering.

A one hot encoding scheme lets each joint Gaussian be optimized independently, adapting a scene reconstruction tool to sparse skeletons. The method beats rivals that avoid three dimensional labels on standard sets and cuts cross dataset error sharply versus learning based methods. Occlusion tests show robustness without scene specific fine tuning.
arxiv-2511-08494:
Hongyu Guo rebuilds Euclidean geometry on a single distance function, extending Tarski famous first order axiom system for the subject. Tarski system is complete and decidable, yet it cannot state the Pythagorean theorem directly because distance is not a primitive notion in its language. The new system works in a two sorted language where a two place distance function is the only geometric primitive, making numerical distance directly expressible.

An extension adds a three place angle function as well. The axiom of similarity does double duty: it grounds proportion and similarity theory rigorously and implies the parallel postulate, acting as a quantitative form of it. Pythagoras theorem and other quantitative similarity results can finally be stated inside the system.
arxiv-2511-08594:
Stewart Slocum, Asher Parker-Sartori, and Dylan Hadfield-Menell argue that standard alignment training quietly makes language models less diverse. Methods such as RLHF and DPO narrow word choice and reasoning styles. They also shrink the range of social views in model outputs. The authors blame the KL penalty that keeps models near a reference.

Their fix, Soft Preference Learning, splits the entropy and cross-entropy parts of that penalty so diversity can be tuned directly. Models trained this way score higher on hard repeated-sampling tasks and produce richer, more varied text. They also represent a wider spread of societal viewpoints and show better calibrated confidence. The method even improves on plain temperature scaling, the usual diversity knob.
arxiv-2511-08694:
Leonard Jung and three co-authors make a graph sparsification method practical for long-running state estimation. The method, Maximization of Algebraic Connectivity, trims a graph's edges while protecting estimation accuracy. Algebraic connectivity ties directly to estimation error. But the method has been too slow and too manual for online use.

Three upgrades close the gaps. A specialized solver for algebraic connectivity doubles the average runtime speed. Better step-size rules inside the optimization improve both convergence and the quality of the final graph. Automatic schemes now guarantee the trimmed graph stays connected, removing the need for users to hand-pick a backbone edge set first. Together the changes target real-time estimation on large graphs that evolve over long periods.
arxiv-2511-08794:
Boya Liu and Weinan Wang solve an inverse problem for a semi-linear wave equation posed on a Lorentzian manifold with boundary, the curved-spacetime setting of relativity. The unknown is the equation's time-dependent nonlinear term, and the only data is a partial Dirichlet-to-Neumann map taken on a part of the boundary as small as one likes.

Despite the tiny data set, that map pins down the nonlinear term of order three or higher in exactly one way, up to the natural limits the geometry imposes. No size or shape limits are placed on where data is taken. The proof combines a higher-order splitting trick, which peels the nonlinear response apart order by order, with Gaussian beams that bounce off the boundary to probe the interior. Such results matter wherever waves are used to infer hidden material or spacetime properties.
arxiv-2511-09194:
Simon König, Lukas Epple, and Christian Becker rethink synchronization for coroutines and other tasks scheduled entirely in user space. User-space scheduling avoids heavy system calls, which is a major draw for parallel and asynchronous programs. Yet current tools borrow kernel-level thinking and add delays on the app's key path.

The team proposes Combine-and-Exchange Scheduling, which keeps contended critical sections on the same thread of execution. Work that can run in parallel spreads evenly across the remaining threads instead. The approach adapts to many existing languages and libraries. It delivers about three-fold gains in application benchmarks and up to eight-fold gains in microbenchmarks, according to their measurements.
arxiv-2511-09294:
Yanli Li and eight co-authors defend federated learning against attacks that damage accuracy and fairness at the same time. Federated training keeps data on client devices, but malicious clients can poison updates. Earlier work studied attacks on utility or on fairness separately, leaving combined attacks unexplored.

The authors define the dual-facet attack, with synchronous and split variants matching different collusion patterns, and show existing defenses fail against it. Their GuardFed framework keeps a fairness-aware reference model on the server, trained with clean and synthetic data. Each round it scores clients on both utility deviation and fairness damage, then aggregates only trustworthy updates. Experiments show GuardFed preserves accuracy and fairness across varied conditions.
arxiv-2511-09494:
Octave Mestoudjian, Matt Wilson, Augustin Vanrietvelde, and Pablo Arrighi extend the diagrammatic theory of quantum subsystems beyond the usual tensor-product picture. Real subsystems can be non-factor von Neumann algebras, which standard process theories handle badly. The authors introduce splitting maps inside dagger symmetric monoidal categories as a basic notion of subsystem.

Splitting maps generate subsystems that can be compared through a preorder called comprehension. They also support an adapted categorical trace. The authors prove comprehension exactly captures how von Neumann algebras include one another, and their trace matches the natural algebraic one. As a payoff, the known equivalence between semi-causality and semi-localisability extends from factor subsystems to all subsystems. The tools give quantum information a cleaner foundation.
arxiv-2511-09694:
Munazza K. Alam and two co-authors document a Jupyter notebook for exoplanet transit analysis. It covers observations taken with Hubble's WFC3/UVIS G280 grism. Transit spectroscopy measures how a planet's atmosphere filters starlight, but the raw grism data need careful reduction first. The notebook lives in the Space Telescope institute's public hst_notebooks repository.

The workflow runs from calibrated, flat-fielded spectra to light curves ready for fitting. Steps include background subtraction, cosmic ray correction in space and time, spectral trace fitting, and spectral extraction. Its end products, broadband and spectroscopic light curves, feed public fitting tools that extract planetary transmission spectra. The paper explains each routine so users understand, not just run, the pipeline.
arxiv-2511-09794:
Wasique Islam Shafin, Md Nakhla Rafi, Zhenhao Li, and Tse-Hsun Chen test whether giving teams of language models a formal software process helps them write whole classes, not just single functions. They simulate a Waterfall cycle of requirement, design, implementation, and testing stages, with three different models playing the roles. The test bed is one hundred Python tasks from the ClassEval benchmark.

Multi-agent workflows reorganized performance rather than consistently improving it. Code came out cleaner and easier to maintain, yet functional correctness fell sharply for two models, while Claude-3.5-Haiku gained instead. Process discipline cut structural failures such as missing code but raised semantic and validation errors. Testing was the most influential stage, improving verification while also introducing new reasoning failures.
arxiv-2511-09894:
Keshara Weerasinghe and seven co-authors introduce EgoEMS, a dataset of emergency medical work recorded from the responder's own point of view. First responders face heavy mental load in high-stakes moments, and AI assistants that could help with data collection and decisions need realistic training material. No end-to-end, high-fidelity egocentric dataset for this setting existed before.

EgoEMS captures over twenty hours of simulated emergency care across 233 scenarios, performed by 62 participants including 46 EMS professionals, using a low-cost open-source rig built with expert input and national standards. Annotations cover key steps, diarized speech transcripts, action quality scores, and object boxes with masks. The authors add benchmarks for recognizing key steps and estimating action quality in real time.
arxiv-2511-09994:
Xiaohan Cai, writing alone, proves Liouville-type uniqueness theorems for positive harmonic functions on compact Riemannian manifolds. The setting assumes nonnegative Ricci curvature and a strictly convex boundary. Such theorems say that positive solutions of the Laplace equation are heavily restricted, often forced to be trivial. The results confirm several cases of a conjecture posed by Wang in a 2021 geometry journal article.

Cai further studies Wang's conjecture on warped product manifolds and verifies it in part, which also yields a new proof of the Gu-Li resolution for the ball case. The method rests on the P-function technique, with special weight on the closed conformal vector fields these manifolds carry. The paper ties a classical PDE rigidity question to modern curvature geometry.
arxiv-2511-10094:
Yiming Tang, Abhijeet Sinha, and Dianbo Liu built a way to find and name the ways image and video generators break the rules of physics. New generators follow prompts well and look real, yet they still make objects bend, fall, or meet in ways that cannot happen, and stock checks miss most of these faults. Their system learns sparse traits at coarse and fine scales from the hidden states of a physics check model.

Large multimodal models then read those traits and state each fault in plain words, with no hand-built trait list. The team says the traits beat past methods on relevance and truth. They used the found patterns as a test set for eight top generators, mapping how each one breaks physics, so builders know what to fix.
arxiv-2511-10294:
Sebastian Knauer and seven co-authors report spin waves that travel far in a material with no magnetic order: the organic free radical known as TEMPO. Above its Néel temperature the sample is paramagnetic, where spin excitations called paramagnons were thought to survive only over tiny distances. Using all-electrical propagating spin-wave spectroscopy in external magnetic fields, the team excited coherent paramagnon-polaritons at low energies.

These waves propagated about eight millimeters, a large distance, at supersonic group velocities above one hundred kilometers per second, at frequencies up to twenty-three gigahertz. The result shows long-range coherence can persist without long-range order in this organic radical. The authors frame the finding as widening where spin-wave tools might operate.
arxiv-2511-10494:
Stanislav Selitskiy tackles a stubborn problem in stock forecasting: neural networks that predict prices far ahead often produce unrealistic jumps, especially when new data fall outside the range seen in training. His answer is a loss function for Kinematic-Informed Neural Networks, which learn velocity relations between time-series points alongside the prices themselves.

The loss penalizes not only errors against the true values but also any mismatch between a predicted next point and the previous point plus the predicted velocity. Tested across several popular and exotic autoregressive network designs on about fifteen years of Dow Jones data, the method gave statistically meaningful improvements. The gains were clearest for normalization-sensitive activation functions that tend to misbehave on out-of-distribution data.
arxiv-2511-10694:
Aditya Pola and Vineeth N. Balasubramanian ask where inside a language model following an instruction actually begins. Processing a prompt mixes several subprocesses, reading the content, reading the instruction, executing it, and answering, and the authors want the layer where reading gives way to doing.

They built three simple datasets, covering key-value lookup, quote attribution, and letter selection, plus two-hop compositions of them. Using activation patching on minimally different prompt pairs, they measure a layer-wise flip rate showing when swapped activations stop changing the answer. Across Llama family models, a clear inflection point appears, which they call the onset, and multi-hop tasks show a similar onset location. The method offers a simple, replicable way to locate instruction following inside a model.
arxiv-2511-10794:
Jourdan Waas and seven co-authors ask whether the supermassive black hole at a galaxy's center can sterilize its planets. Winds from active galactic nuclei, especially ultrafast outflows, have been little studied as a habitability factor, even though black hole masses span about five orders of magnitude across galaxies.

Using simplified models, they trace how atmospheric heating, thermal velocities, and mass loss scale with black hole mass and with a planet's distance from the center. Energy-driven winds hit harder than momentum-driven ones. Ozone depletion grows with black hole mass and shrinks with distance. For the largest black holes, at or above a hundred million solar masses, the energy-driven case destroys nearly all ozone on galactic scales. The authors argue black hole growth over cosmic time has reshaped habitability very unevenly.
arxiv-2511-10894:
Luciano Araujo Dourado Filho and five co-authors propose a lean recipe for probabilistic rainfall nowcasting, the short-horizon prediction of accumulated rain with honest uncertainty. Their system keeps a large pretrained satellite vision encoder completely frozen, avoiding the cost of training a weather model from scratch.

A video projector built on a vision transformer reads the encoder's tokens. A lightweight probabilistic head turns them into a discrete distribution over four-hour accumulated rainfall, trained end to end against the ranked probability score. On the Weather4Cast 2025 benchmark, the system posted a continuous ranked probability score of about three and a half. That is roughly a 26 percent effectiveness gain over the best 3D-UNet baseline the authors trained. They present frozen-encoder nowcasting as both competitive and computationally cheap.
arxiv-2511-11094:
Lu-Meng Liu, Jinhui Chen, and their colleagues propose a new probe for the stiffness of hot quark-gluon plasma, the soup of quarks and gluons made when heavy nuclei collide. How that soup expands along the beam line is still poorly known, and its stiffness, summed in its equation of state, is the key unknown. The probe tracks how mean sideways momentum wobbles from event to event.

In large three-dimensional flow simulations, the linked wobbles at two points along the beam react strongly to stiffness. They barely react to how sticky the soup is, which makes the signal a clean stiffness test. The results also shed fresh light on the soup's lengthwise layout.
arxiv-2511-11294:
Bertille Tierny, Arthur Charpentier, and François Hu present a post-processing frame that splits the bias of a fairness-adjusted linear model into direct and indirect parts. Linear models are prized in high-stakes decisions for their clarity, but adding a demographic parity constraint reshapes every coefficient in ways that are hard to read. Prior work often assumed too much or ignored the sensitive attribute's own role.

Applied on top of any trained linear model with no retraining, the method shows exactly how parity shifts each coefficient, for sensitive and ordinary features alike. That feature-level view lets auditors see where bias persists or migrates through correlated variables. Tests cover synthetic and real data.
arxiv-2511-11394:
Bruno Mera and Tomoki Ozawa propose a microscopic mechanism by which generic Chern bands relax toward ideal Chern bands when coupled to a bath. Chern bands are energy bands with a topological twist, and ideal ones have a special quantum geometry sought for building fractional Chern insulators. The bath here is an Ohmic bosonic reservoir of the Caldeira-Leggett kind, coupled weakly to interacting electrons.

Under a Born-Markov treatment, the authors show analytically that states of a Chern band evolve toward states of the matching ideal band. A simulation of a massive Dirac model with Hubbard interaction confirms the picture: Berry curvature and quantum metric co-evolve toward the ideal trace condition.
arxiv-2511-11594:
James McCammon introduces TimeStampEval, a benchmark for finding the exact moment a spoken quote occurs in a long transcript when the written quote does not match the transcript word for word. Official records and speech-to-text output differ in small ways that defeat ordinary fuzzy matching.

Given a sentence-timestamped transcript and a slightly drifted target quote, the task is to return precise start and end times in milliseconds. A simple two-stage method improves retrieval accuracy sharply while cutting inference costs by over ninety percent. The motivating project assembles Congressional Record clips into an automated long-form podcast, a use case where cheap, accurate quote location is essential.
arxiv-2511-11794:
Miguel Correia and three co-authors map the analytic structure of the black hole S-matrix. The S-matrix encodes how waves scatter off a Schwarzschild black hole. The map is drawn in the plane of complex frequency. Analyticity is where causality leaves its mark on scattering. So the map has physical meaning, not just math interest.

The gravitational potential is continued to complex values. The singularity behind the horizon plays a key role. In the lower half-plane, the partial-wave amplitudes are analytic, with two exceptions. They are quasinormal mode poles and a branch cut from late-time tails. Stokes effects give the elastic amplitude its own upper half-plane cut. Wave scattering near black holes gains a firmer causal base.
arxiv-2511-11894:
Lingxiao Li and three co-authors generate molecules from written descriptions in stages. A chemist should be able to name functional groups, scaffolds, and property limits in words. Structures that honor all of them should come back. One-shot conditioning encodes the whole prompt once. It routinely drops some of the stated requirements.

Their frame, Chain-of-Generation, applies the description step by step. Each part of the prompt guides its own phase of generation. Three failures of the one-shot style are named. They include poor clarity of generated parts and missing substructures. Stepwise conditioning gives better compliance with the prompt. It also gives a clearer view of which words built which part.
arxiv-2511-11994:
Paulo Henrique Foganholo Biazetto and three co-authors design an extremum-seeking controller for Schrödinger-type systems. The dynamics are governed by complex-valued partial differential equations. The goal is to maximize a measured output, where the map that defines the optimum is unknown. Actuation sits at one boundary.

The goal value is the squared norm of the complex state at the far, free boundary. A two-step backstepping boundary control offsets the actuation dynamics. A small-signal Hessian estimate powers a Newton-style seeking law. The complex state space is viewed as a two-dimensional real one to make this work. Model-free optimization enters genuinely infinite-dimensional territory here.
arxiv-2511-12094:
Víctor A. Vicente-Benítez constructs a tool for solving Schrödinger equations whose potential is rough, given as the derivative of a square-integrable function. Such equations model quantum particles, and a transmutation operator can turn simple solutions into solutions of the harder equation. Building that operator for rough potentials needs a new route.

The construction uses a regularization based on a factorization named for Pólya, tied to a solution that never vanishes on the interval. The author shows such a solution exists and can be computed. Related results cover the impedance form of the problem, a Darboux transform, and series forms for solutions that expand in powers of the spectral parameter.
arxiv-2511-12294:
Bodhisatwa Chatterjee and four co-authors present ProofWright, a system that formally verifies code for graphics processors written by large language models. Models can generate fast CUDA kernels quickly, but the code often holds subtle correctness bugs. Testing misses cases, and manual verification cannot keep pace with the rate of generation.

ProofWright pairs automated formal verification with the generation process to give end-to-end guarantees on memory safety, thread safety and semantic correctness. On a standard kernel benchmark it verifies safety for a large share of generated kernels, finds errors that testing missed, and proves equivalence for a class of simple kernels. The overhead reported is a few minutes per kernel.
arxiv-2511-12594:
Rongkun Zheng and five co-authors present Seg-VAR, a framework that rethinks image segmentation as generating a mask step by step, in the autoregressive style used for image generation. Segmentation needs precise, low-level spatial perception, and visual autoregressive methods had not been explored for it. Their design borrows the multi-scale spirit of leading mask models.

Three parts work together. An image encoder makes latent priors. A second encoder turns masks into discrete latent tokens. It uses a location-sensitive color mapping to separate instances. A decoder then rebuilds masks from those latents. Training proceeds in stages, first learning the mask representation jointly with images, then refining latent changes, then aligning the two latent sources.
arxiv-2511-12694:
Mohamed A. Mabrok and Yalda Zafari introduce X-VMamba, a framework for explaining how vision state space models make their decisions. Mamba-style models have become strong alternatives to transformers. But unlike attention-based models, they offer no built-in map of which image patches mattered. The authors borrow an idea from control theory, controllability, to measure how each patch influences the model's internal state as an image moves through it.

They give two methods: a Jacobian-based one that works for any state space model, and a faster Gramian-based one for diagonal models, both running in a single forward pass. Tests on three kinds of medical images show early layers spread influence over broad textures while deeper layers focus on clinically meaningful patterns. Scanning order also shapes the patterns. The tools aim to make this model family easier to audit.
arxiv-2511-12994:
Debjit Basu studies when a layer of relations among a variety's defining equations is forced to be empty. Syzygies are the relations among equations, and relations among relations, that make up a projective variety's minimal free resolution; Koszul cohomology sorts them by weight. Basu finds when the weight one Koszul cohomology vanishes. That vanishing is not an end in itself: as spin-offs of more general results, he obtains claims about property (M_q), which controls higher syzygies, for minimal surfaces and for larger projective varieties.

By weighing properties (M_q) and (N_p) together, the analysis sharpens what is known about the shape of minimal free resolutions. A vanishing theorem gives geometers a test: check the terms, and a whole stratum of the resolution is known to be absent before anyone computes.
arxiv-2511-13494:
Jae Joong Lee probes how steadily vision-language models match images and text when the wording changes. Models such as CLIP score well at zero-shot tasks, but their response to careful language tweaks was unclear. The new LGIP benchmark separates harmless rewording from edits that truly change meaning.

Using forty thousand COCO images with human captions, the study auto-generates paraphrases and rule-based flips of object, color, or count. Nine models are scored on paraphrase stability and on favoring true captions over flipped ones. Some large models balanced both well, while SigLIP versions often preferred flipped captions, a flaw that standard retrieval scores miss entirely.
arxiv-2511-13594:
Masaaki Nakamura and Masanori Yamanaka derive the condition for the integer quantum Hall effect in interacting lattice fermions using spiral boundary conditions. That wrapping turns the system into a single long chain, which lets force and response directions be controlled cleanly. Their argument blends Lieb-Schultz-Mattis and Laughlin style reasoning.

It ties magnetic flux, Chern number, and electron density into a single integer link. Earlier derivations with periodic boundaries reached the same link only by a roundabout path, with extra dependence on system size cluttering the proof. The spiral approach removes that clutter and gives the Hall result directly for lattice systems.
arxiv-2511-13694:
Jay Bartroff and Asmit Chakraborty extend the Push algorithm to compute the shortest fixed-width confidence intervals for a bounded parameter. A confidence interval trades width against coverage, and for a fixed width the shortest valid one is the best a data analyst can report. The earlier Push method handled only the binomial case.

Their version works for any discrete bounded value, and for continuous ones whose interval probabilities have a quasiconcave shape. The Push result is provably the shortest non-decreasing one at its level, and its absence proves no such interval exists. Demonstrations on binomial, hypergeometric, and normal cases beat standard intervals, and an application uses World Health Organization tobacco data.
arxiv-2511-13994:
Yilun Zhu, Nikhita Vedula, and Shervin Malmasi improve product search for queries built on superlatives like best or most popular. Answering such queries means comparing items across several traits at once, which takes language understanding and domain knowledge. The authors show large language models can extract the hidden intent as structured attribute-value hints.

Their framework generates those hints alongside retrieval and feeds them into the ranking pipeline. Because calling a big model to re-rank directly is too slow, they transfer the superlative interpretations into lightweight models for deployment. The method raised standard search quality scores by clear margins over baselines, and the study explains how superlative meaning can be passed between models.
arxiv-2511-14094:
Hien Phan-Thanh, Nguyen Nguyen-Duc, Thuy Le-Quang, and two co-authors built SPECTRUMMATE, a compact spectrometer for small telescopes. Small scopes are cheap, portable, and easy to set up, making them ideal for schools and amateur astronomers, and they can still do useful science on bright objects. The design adapts the Sol'EX spectrograph and uses optics on hand at a Hanoi university laboratory.

The instrument covers visible light from 4000 to 6600 angstroms, capturing a few hundred angstroms per image with resolving power above twenty-five hundred. The team selected and aligned a collimator, grating, and objective lens to keep dispersion low and the unit compact, aiming at detailed spectral analysis for low-budget observatories.
arxiv-2511-14294:
Morgane Dumont, Ahmed Alsaloum, Julian Ernst, and two co-authors ask what drives the doubt in spatial micro forecasts. These models project people and homes, with their traits, over maps and years. Each run is a guess, and the spread of guesses is rarely checked. The team ran a variance-based test on the jobs module of MikroSim, a model of Germany, and split direct from indirect effects.

The usual sources of doubt, the values of weights and inputs, turned out to matter less than plain choices about how to build the model. Short summary scores also failed to show the full spread of doubt. The authors urge builders to weigh such choices with care and to state the doubt plainly in their reports.
arxiv-2511-14494:
Guoliang Tang and Jiaqun Wei characterize a special class of modules over tensor rings. Tensor rings combine a base ring with a bimodule in a standard construction. The modules in question are Gorenstein flat modules with an added projective coresolution property. Such modules play a role in relative homological algebra.

The pair give a precise test for when a module over the tensor ring has the property. The test reduces to two checks on its structure map and quotient. They also describe a related class of Gorenstein flat modules in explicit form. Applications cover trivial ring extensions and Morita context rings, two common ring constructions.
arxiv-2511-14694:
Rui Zhu, Xiaopu Zhou, and three co-authors present FOCUS, a compression module that lets DNA language models read much longer sequences. Models trained on DNA from many species learn the grammar of the genome, but attention costs grow fast with length. Stores of past keys and values also swell during generation, forcing crude cutoffs that drop distant information.

FOCUS squeezes the context in stages while keeping the features that matter, and it plugs into already trained models. The authors report near-lossless quality with far longer reach than window tricks allow. Longer context means gene regulation and other far-apart genomic signals can finally be modeled together in one pass.
arxiv-2511-14994:
Yue Yu, Xiaobo Zheng, and Shaoming He design a trajectory planner for drone swarms that keeps working when radio links are poor. Splitting the planning across the swarm saves central computing, but dropped messages and tight bandwidth make coordination fragile. Their framework, CA-ADTO, is built in two tiers for exactly that setting.

Each drone refines its own path with a parameterized dynamic programming method, while swarm-level agreement is reached through an asynchronous multiplier method that tolerates late updates. The design cuts communication overhead sharply compared with lockstep schemes. Swarms that can plan through bad links are a step toward real missions in disaster zones and contested airspace.
arxiv-2511-15194:
Jian Deng, Yuandong Wang, and four co-authors present Eq.Bot, a wrapper that gives robot manipulation policies a proper sense of geometry. Learning-based robot hands often stumble when objects are rotated or shifted, because their training never guaranteed consistent behavior under such moves. Hand-built fixes inside each network are costly, complex, and hard to port.

Eq.Bot instead canonicalizes: it rotates and shifts each observation into a standard frame, runs whatever policy is already in use, then maps the chosen action back to the real frame. The scheme rests on symmetry theory for planar motions and is meant to wrap any existing policy unchanged. Inspired by how people normalize a scene mentally before acting, it promises steadier manipulation with no retraining.
arxiv-2511-15394:
The BESIII Collaboration reports a search for a forbidden decay that would break a sacred rule of particle physics: lepton number conservation. The target process turns a Xi-minus baryon into a Sigma-plus plus two electrons, with no neutrinos to balance the lepton count. Seeing it would prove leptons can be created from nothing, a clue to why the universe holds more matter than antimatter.

Working blind on about ten billion J/psi events recorded at the BEPCII collider, the team finds no signal above the expected background. They set an upper limit on how often the decay can occur, at ninety percent confidence. Each null search of this kind tightens the space where lepton number violation can hide.
arxiv-2511-15594:
Koen Scheres and Rodolphe Sepulchre ask whether a circuit built to mimic neurons can be described as a sequence of discrete events. Excitable neuromorphic circuits are physical devices whose smooth electrical paths naturally break into event-like steps, much as neurons fire in spikes. Turning a continuous physical model into a discrete-event model is the goal of their study.

A discrete description would let engineers analyze and design such circuits with tools made for event systems rather than full continuous simulation. The authors discuss how to extract that model from the physical one and weigh what the method could offer neuromorphic control systems. The work is a short conceptual study of modeling method, scope, and promise.
arxiv-2511-15694:
Medha Kumar, Zifei Xu, Xin Wang, and Tristan Webb test how quantization, the compression of model weights into fewer bits, affects reinforcement learning in large reasoning models. Strong reasoning can now be trained by large-scale reinforcement learning without supervised fine-tuning. Quantization after training and quantization during training are well studied for fine-tuning, but their effect on this kind of reinforcement learning was an open question.

Systematic experiments on math benchmarks found a significant reasoning gap. Models quantized after reinforcement learning kept far more performance than counterparts whose reinforcement learning was itself quantization-aware, which seemed to harm the learning process. Post-training quantization and a low-rank adapter method for quantized models both performed better in their tests.
arxiv-2511-15794:
Pouya Asadi, David Cyncynates, and Stefania Gori argue that a crowd of axion-like particles solves two problems at once for the QCD axion. Axions are hypothetical light particles proposed to explain a symmetry puzzle and to serve as dark matter. A mechanism called axiogenesis could also create the cosmic excess of matter over antimatter, but the minimal version makes too few baryons or too much dark matter and strains axion quality.

In the axiverse picture, the QCD axion is a blend of several axion-like fields. New dissipation channels prevent overclosure of the universe, and extra symmetries keep the axion high quality. A two-axion toy model illustrates the fix, and the framework predicts signals within reach of dark matter, astrophysics, and collider experiments.
arxiv-2511-15894:
Shuang Guan and Kasso A. Okoudjou study when a signal can be uniquely recovered from its short-time Fourier spectrogram without phase information. Phase retrieval matters because many sensors record only magnitudes, and uniqueness guarantees that no other signal could produce the same recording. Their setting uses window functions whose Fourier transforms decay faster than any exponential, a very strong smoothness condition.

For such windows, they derive sufficient conditions on discrete sampling sets that ensure unique phase retrieval for square-integrable signals. The result generalizes earlier uniqueness guarantees that were proven only for Gaussian windows, the classic bell-shaped case. Knowing which sampling patterns suffice helps design measurement schemes where reconstruction is provably unambiguous.
arxiv-2511-15994:
Deepthi Potluri and six co-authors study the gap between search and thinking in medical question answering with CARE-RAG. Giving a language model the right evidence does not guarantee correct thinking with it. That gap is dangerous in medical settings governed by structured protocols. Written exposure therapy guidelines serve as the testbed for curated, clinician vetted questions.

Errors persist even when authoritative passages are supplied to the model. The proposed framework measures accuracy, consistency, and fidelity of thinking separately. Search can constrain outputs, results show, but not ensure safe logic. Safe deployment therefore needs thinking assessed as rigorously as search itself. The study offers an evaluation template for other protocol driven medical tasks.
arxiv-2511-16194:
Antoniadis and three co-authors study online interval scheduling when an advance hint from a learned model is at hand. Slots arrive one by one. Each must be taken or rejected at once, and taken slots may not overlap. The aim is the largest total length of taken slots. Hints promise better results, but a method must stay safe when hints err. Good design balances doing well under good hints against safety under hostile inputs.

Their SemiTrust-and-Switch frame unifies hint-based and classic methods, for both fixed-rule and random cases. Lower bounds prove the frame is tight in some settings. One random method blends smoothly between trusting hints and falling back on safe behavior. It stays robust, and its results degrade in a smooth way as hint quality drops.
arxiv-2511-16394:
The CMS Collaboration reports a search for Higgsinos, the hypothetical partners of the Higgs boson, in proton-proton collision data collected at 13 TeV during 2016 to 2018. The target scenario has four nearly equal-mass states, so the heavier neutral particle decays to the lighter one plus a virtual Z boson, leaving very soft leptons.

The analysis hunts events with large missing momentum plus either two muons, or one lepton and an isolated track, which recovers cases where a soft lepton was missed. Multivariate discriminants suppress backgrounds from standard processes and fake tracks. Mass gaps between the two neutral states were probed down to about one and a half GeV for a 100 GeV Higgsino, and Higgsino masses up to 115 GeV were excluded.
arxiv-2511-16594:
Bradley E. Schaefer and six co-authors report an unusual nova, FQ Circini, whose companion star is a massive hot Be star of about thirteen solar masses. The nova itself was an ordinary fast helium-nitrogen event, but its eruption amplitude of about three magnitudes is the smallest known for a classical nova. The quiet counterpart is a flickering blue emission-line star.

Photometry from TESS and amateur observers shows a coherent period of about two days from the companion's ellipsoidal shape. The Be star's decretion disk feeds mass across the Roche lobe into an accretion disk around a white dwarf of about one and a quarter solar masses. It is a disk-to-disk transfer seen in no other system. The authors name this a new class, high-mass cataclysmic variables, and note the white dwarf can never grow into a Type Ia supernova.
arxiv-2511-16794:
Victor Sanchez and seven co-authors use hierarchical Bayesian model selection to study soft, tissue-like materials slammed at ultra-high strain rates, a regime key for injury biomechanics and protective design. Laser-induced microcavitation can probe such materials, but noisy bubble data and uncertain parameters make picking the right constitutive model hard.

Their method explores competing models' parameter spaces with informed priors that penalize needless complexity. It adds a redundancy prior, an information-criterion-motivated prior, and a noise model that measures uncertainty in how plausible each model is. Synthetic tests recover the true models and values. On gelatin, fibrin, polyacrylamide, and agarose data, the credible models' best fits match the experiments, and a comparison across institutions on gelatin selects the same model, a reassuring check.
arxiv-2511-16994:
Changyu Zhou carries out a close analysis of the Riccati hierarchy, a chain of related equations in maths that is studied through its series solutions. The focus is a classic test that probes how solutions behave near singular points, and the numbers that come out of that test. Zhou works out every case for this chain and sets down the full set of test numbers.

A rigid pattern turns up in how free values enter the series solutions, level by level. Zhou also finds a special flow that works alongside the whole chain and uses it to write all solutions through a single polynomial formula. Where poles of solutions collide, the formula shows lower cases emerging as limits, and negative test numbers gain a clear reading through series used on ring-shaped regions.
arxiv-2511-17094:
He Huang and four co-authors question an expensive habit in video anomaly detection: examining every frame. Their system, ReCoVAD, watches surveillance-style video for unusual events but reasons in depth about only a small share of frames. The design copies the human nervous system, which pairs a fast reflex pathway with a slower, conscious one.

A light module first scores frames quickly, consulting a memory of past frames and their scores. Only novel frames go to a vision-language model, which writes event descriptions and refined scores, while a large language model periodically reviews those descriptions to catch new anomaly types and fix mistakes. On two standard datasets the system matched the best training-free results while processing roughly a sixth to a quarter of the frames rivals used. Sparse reasoning, the authors argue, is enough.
arxiv-2511-17194:
Zhiyuan Xu and three co-authors demonstrate an attack on large language models that works by nudging their internal activations rather than their inputs. Decoder-only transformers contain attention sinks and compression valleys, regions where, the authors show, small perturbations can be amplified as generation proceeds. Their method, Sensitivity-Scaled Steering, anchors a perturbation at the first token and reinforces it at the most sensitive layers and positions.

Instead of forcing an abrupt change, the attack drifts the model's behavior gradually, so early outputs still look fluent and harmless. Across several open-weight models and four kinds of target behavior, it achieved high success rates with little damage to general capability. The authors argue these internal structures should be treated as genuine hidden-state weaknesses, especially where models pass through supply chains that others can tamper with.
arxiv-2511-17394:
Jean-Pierre Delmas surveys elliptically symmetric distributions, a broad family of laws for random vectors used throughout signal processing and machine learning. These distributions generalize the multivariate Gaussian and, at the same time, extend symmetric one-dimensional laws to many dimensions. Delmas covers both the real case and the complex versions, circular and noncircular, that engineers use for complex-valued signals.

The chapter defines the family in two matching ways, through characteristic functions and stochastic representations, showing how the laws arise from spherically symmetric distributions under affine maps. It collects results on moments, marginals, conditionals, and stability under summation, gives well-known examples with their properties. A final part discusses estimation of the center and scatter matrix, from simple sample estimators to robust M-estimators and Tyler's estimator. A closing section touches on the Slepian-Bangs formula, a workhorse for detection tasks.
arxiv-2511-17794:
Zhao Song, Ndidi Bianca Ogbo, Xinyu Wang, Chen Shen, Matjaz Perc, and The Anh Han ask how cooperation survives in evolution when players can talk before they act. Earlier models used only a hand picked subset of possible strategies, which may hide important paths.

Expanding to the complete set of eight strategies changes the outcome greatly. Cooperation becomes stronger and more varied, driven by a new cyclic pattern sparked by suspicious cooperation. A role once credited to strategic defection turns out to be fragile. Long term behavior can include up to seven strategies living together, showing why full models matter.
arxiv-2511-18194:
Faheem Nizar, Elias Lumer, Anmol Gulati, Pradeep Honaganahalli Basavaraju, and Vamse Kumar Subbiah improve how multi agent language systems find the right specialized agent and tools for a job. Existing retrieval matches a query against one agent description, hiding the fine grained abilities of its many tools and leading to poor selection.

Their method represents tools and their parent agents as nodes in a knowledge graph. Vector search first finds candidate tools and agents, a weighted fusion reranks them by type, and graph traversal returns the parent agents. On a live benchmark of protocol based tools, recall and ranking quality improve clearly over the best prior retrievers.
arxiv-2511-18294:
Mengchun Zhang, Kateryna Shapovalenko, Yucheng Shao, Eddie Guo, and Parusha Pradhan decode brain signals for people the model has never seen. Reading EEG, the scalp signal of brain activity, fails most when a new subject's patterns differ from the training group. Past fixes fake new subjects or pad data in plain ways, and neither scales well.

MultiDiffNet skips fake data growth. It learns a compact code space tuned for many goals at once, and decodes straight from that space. Scores top prior work across tasks when test subjects and sessions are held apart from training. The team also release a shared test suite of four EEG tasks, from steady visual response to imagined speech, with a clean split protocol.
arxiv-2511-18394:
Chinmay Karkar and Paras Chopra test how well large language models forecast real-world events, and find the skill unevenly spread. Models show partial competence on social, political, and economic questions, but performance swings sharply with the kind of question and how it is framed. The team uses questions about events that happened after each model's training cut-off, so answers cannot be recalled from memory.

They vary the context supplied, the question type, and the addition of factual news material, then watch accuracy and calibration shift. Adding news changes how models form beliefs and where they fail. The headline lesson is in their title's borrowed line: forecasting ability depends heavily on what is asked and how, so a single forecasting score for a model can mislead.
arxiv-2511-18494:
Furen Deng, Yidong Xu, Fengquan Wu, Yanping Cong, Bin Yue, and Xuelei Chen map the radio sky from lunar orbit. Below a set low band, Earth's air and human noise block ground dishes. A line of small satellites around the Moon, the DSL or Hongmeng mission, can listen in that quiet band by combining signals.

The sky map rebuild is in form a linear inversion: a beam matrix links sky pixels to the joint measures. The team probe two error sources: sub pixel noise from cutting the sky into finite cells, and bias from the smoothing used to tame the inversion. Both can warp the global map if left unchecked. Their checks guide how to build a sound map of the dark radio sky.
arxiv-2511-18594:
Ahmad A Aziz El-Banna and Octavia A Dobre propose a light autoencoder for predicting the best beam in millimetre-wave systems that sense and communicate at once. Such waves form narrow beams that must align precisely, and finding the right beam normally takes heavy training traffic. Knowing the user's position can shortcut that search, and the authors feed position into the prediction problem for sixth-generation network settings.

Their network squeezes its input through a narrow middle layer, which cuts the computation the trained model needs. In simulations it matches the beam prediction accuracy of a standard deep network baseline while cutting complexity by more than four fifths. For dense future networks, a cheaper predictor could save both energy and airtime on every alignment.
arxiv-2511-18794:
Zhongtao Wang and 10 co-authors rebuild places that change across photo sets taken years apart. Cities are rescanned, build sites revisited, and wild zones watched for change. Past rebuild tools assume one fixed geometry, or smooth motion, and both fail when change is long term and abrupt.

ChronoGS uses a time modulated Gaussian form set on one shared anchor scaffold. All periods rebuild in that single frame, while stable parts and changing parts are split apart. The split yields consistent builds across eras, where a wall may stand in one and fall in the next. A new benchmark set backs the work. Long term change mapping is the use.
arxiv-2511-18994:
Christian Haase and Zongpu Zhang compute multigraded Betti numbers for Veronese embeddings of projective spaces. A Veronese map re-embeds a projective space by all monomials of a set degree, and its Betti numbers grade the relations among those monomials. Hochster's formula turns those numbers into homology of set simplicial complexes.

By studying those complexes with Forman's discrete Morse theory, the pair prove where the numbers vanish and where they do not. Morse matchings collapse most of a complex, which exposes its true homology at low cost. A graded census of Veronese relations guides work on syzygies, the chains of relations among relations in algebra.
arxiv-2511-19194:
C. D. Leonard and colleagues, writing with the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration, assess a test of gravity planned for the Rubin Observatory's LSST survey. The statistic involved, called E G, mixes galaxy lensing and clustering measures to probe gravity with few assumptions about the dark universe. Lens galaxies would come from the DESI instrument.

The authors update the error framework for this pairing and show the test stays nearly model-free when only large scales are used, if galaxy bias is handled with care. A forecast method also folds in uncertainty about the present matter density. With existing microwave background priors, the full survey data should give the test real power.
arxiv-2511-19294:
Phurtivilai Patt, Leyang Huang, Yinqiang Zhang, and Yang Lei improve three-dimensional Gaussian splatting by densifying the scene before optimisation starts. Standard splatting grows its points adaptively during training, which can leave floating artefacts and waste resources on redundant blobs. Their method combines sparse LiDAR measurements with depth estimates from matching photos to build a dense starting cloud, using a sampling scheme that favours regions important in meaning or geometry.

Starting dense lets the optimisation skip adaptive density control entirely and focus on the other attributes of each blob, reducing overlap while raising visual quality. The authors report results comparable to leading techniques with significantly lower cost. For scanning teams with a LiDAR unit at hand, the approach promises cleaner scenes for less compute.
arxiv-2511-19394:
Rachit Saluja and five co-authors argue that medical image models fail on small lesions partly because of how they treat the background. Standard training lumps every non-lesion pixel into one background class, throwing away anatomy: the tissues and organs around a lesion carry useful context. Their fix is to split that background into finer labeled parts.

Called BackSplit, the scheme trains with those detailed labels while costing nothing extra when the model runs. A theory result shows the richer labels raise expected Fisher information, tightening error bounds and steadying training. The authors present background splitting as a cheap, general boost for lesion segmentation.
arxiv-2511-19694:
Chin-Chia Michael Yeh and seven co-authors build a foundation model that classifies time series without fine-tuning.
