The review will run from May to October 2026 and search many databases plus registries and government sources for work since 2000, with no language bar at the search stage. Outcomes include patient survival, how long the method lasts, infections, hospital use, heart outcomes, and tube problems. Findings will be mapped by outcome and by country, with local context noted. The data set and search plans will be shared where journal policy allows.
pmc-13264994:
Yan-Min Xu and Bao-Liang Zhong published a 2026 narrative review of the link between body image and depression, tracing fifty years of research. Unhappiness with one's body is common in depression, and the pair set out to show how the field's ideas shifted and what the proof now says about direction and treatment.

They screened literature from 1972 to 2026 and kept 266 records. Across cultures, ages, and clinics, negative body image, above all body dissatisfaction, tied steadily to depressive symptoms. Long-term and twin studies suggest each can feed the other over time. How people judge their looks mattered more than measured body mass. Proposed drivers include self-objectification, social comparison, rumination, and low self-esteem. Treatments that target body image improved it and may ease depression too. The authors urge adding body image checks to depression care.
pmc-13265594:
Xudong Rao and co-authors wrote a 2026 perspective arguing that controlled environment agriculture, high-tech indoor and greenhouse farming, should be treated as public city infrastructure rather than a private tech fix. Venture money has driven its growth, they say, yielding few sites, narrow crop choice, and little thought for fair spread across neighborhoods.

The authors propose judging such farms by public value: food justice, public health, and climate resilience. They highlight geospatial AI and high-performance computing as underused tools that could adapt crop care, guide site choices, and find underserved communities for targeted help. Joined with urban data methods, these tools could embed farms in fair, climate-ready city systems. The paper ends with priorities for a public-interest agenda for this farming sector.
pmc-13269294:
Waheed Idowu and co-authors published a review in 2026 on treating poor dry-season feed for cattle, sheep, and goats in warm dry regions. Treating straw and crop leftovers with ammonia or urea can unlock fiber and add nitrogen. The review pulled together studies mainly from 2015 to 2025.

Treating feed raised intake by 10 to 40 percent and digestion by 5 to 20 points in the studies reviewed. Animals generally performed better, though gains depended on matching nitrogen release with energy in the diet. Better feed use may also cut emissions per unit of product. The authors note uneven results, nitrogen losses, and slow uptake by farmers as limits still to solve.
pmc-13271494:
Maryam Farooqui is lead author of a 2026 cross-sectional survey on how Saudi households dispose of unused and expired medicines, and on the regulatory gaps around that disposal. Throwing medicines in household bins can harm people and the environment, so the team surveyed residents of Qassim about awareness and habits.

Among 877 adults who answered an online questionnaire, 70 percent kept unused medicines, most often in the refrigerator. A striking 88 percent threw unused medicines in household dustbins, as did 92 percent for expired ones. Most, 86 percent, had never received formal education on safe disposal, and 60 percent said pharmacies should be responsible for teaching it. The authors call for awareness campaigns and clear rules.
pmc-13271594:
Io Chi-Yan Hui is lead author of a 2026 scoping review, a broad mapping study, on putting digital respiratory technologies into routine care for people with lung conditions. Digital health is a strategic priority for the European Respiratory Society, but lasting rollout into real clinics is complex and guidance for health systems is thin.

Searching ten databases for work from the past decade, plus crowdsourced additions, the team charted which technologies were used, what rollout strategies were tried, and what challenges and supports appeared. They sorted lessons by equity, patient-professional relationships, the patient journey, and environmental impact, using standard implementation frameworks. As a scoping review, it maps the field rather than judging how well the technologies work.
pmc-13273394:
Chuyao Yu leads a 2026 study asking whether gut microbes cause retinal disease and poor vision. The method uses inherited gene variants as tools to test cause, which cuts confounding. Exposures covered 211 gut microbe groups and 28 related chemicals. Outcomes covered six eye diseases, including diabetic eye disease and macular wear.

The work found 35 microbes and three chemicals linked to various outcomes. One microbe group showed robust cause for choroid and retina disorders after strict correction, with an odds ratio of 0.874. Reverse tests found no clear effect of eye disease on gut microbes. The authors present the findings as new leads for care and prevention.
pmc-13273794:
Raimondi and colleagues pool patient-level data from four phase II trials in metastatic colorectal cancer. Their 2026 journal article covers left-sided tumors with normal RAS and BRAF genes. It compares two ways of using anti-EGFR antibody drugs.

One strategy gave the drug as steady maintenance. The other used stop-and-go dosing with planned breaks. The analysis included 378 patients. Overall survival did not differ significantly between strategies. Time without disease growth was shorter with stop-and-go. Yet time until the strategy failed was comparable. Anti-EGFR drugs block a growth signal on cancer cells. The authors say breaks may suit some patients. Survival was not harmed in this pooled group.
pmc-13274394:
Elif Bastug Guven and Ozgur Genc Sen present a 2026 journal article testing how root canal rinse changes while it sits open on a dentist's tray. Sodium hypochlorite is the standard rinse that kills germs and dissolves tissue during root canal work. Its strength depends on its chemistry, which open air and light may alter.

The team measured a five percent solution fresh, after one hour, and after two hours in clear open containers at room temperature. Acidity rose steadily, with pH dropping significantly by one hour and further by two. Surface tension did not change. Measured active chlorine was unexpectedly higher at two hours than when fresh. The authors say clinical relevance still needs study.
pmc-13274894:
Nikolas Reisecker and a large team present a 2026 journal article surveying Austrian attitudes toward anthroposophic medicine, a complementary system blending conventional care with spiritual ideas. The online survey drew 429 completed responses, weighted to match recent election results. It probed who uses such medicine, who sees it as scientific, and what mindsets travel with those views.

Women and people over fifty favored complementary medicine more, and women had used anthroposophic medicine more often. Seeing it as scientific was commoner among older, wealthier, and rural people. Low tolerance for vague answers and a strong sense of personal health control tracked with trust in it. So did authoritarian views, which also tracked preferring eminence-based over evidence-based medicine.
pmc-13275594:
Anna Fleischer and a large team present a 2026 mixed-methods study of taste damage from talquetamab, a myeloma drug known for ruining eating pleasure. Twenty-five treated patients who reported new taste changes completed questionnaires with free-text answers, analyzed independently by two coders. The team then turned the findings, with input from clinical focus groups, into a proposed care workflow and a digital companion concept.

Patients described varied problems: sweet flavors fading or turning unpleasant, bitter and sour aversions, spice burning the mouth, and simple loss of enjoyment. Dry mouth made dry or fibrous foods harder to swallow. Coping tricks that helped included mild herbs, savory umami additions, sauces and soups, temperature and plating changes, and saliva-supportive measures. Both proposed tools still await validation.
pmc-13275994:
Fuqun Wei and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on liver cancer and the cells lining its blood vessels. Those endothelial cells can change into a different cell type, a shift that helps tumors grow. The team asked which endothelial genes drive this shift and predict patient outcomes.

They combined single-cell gene data, which profiles one cell at a time, with large tumor datasets. Nineteen key genes stood out, and the team built a risk model from them. The model split patients into groups with different outlooks, immune cell mixes, and likely drug responses. In lab-grown mini tumors grown with vessel tissue, three of the genes sat in the same spots as known markers of the cell shift. The authors name them as possible drug targets.
pmc-13276594:
Linhao Jing and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on a copper-based nanoplatform meant to wake the immune system against liver cancer. Immunotherapy struggles in liver tumors because they suppress immunity and hide their antigens. One alarm pathway, cGAS-STING, can turn tumor stress into immune priming if switched on inside the tumor.

Their particles self-assemble copper ions with an immune stimulant, then wear a cloak of tumor cell membrane for homing. In the tumor's acidity they release copper, which triggers a copper-dependent death program in cancer cells. That death raised the alarm signal and switched on the pathway, while the stimulant matured dendritic cells, the immune system's teachers. In animals the particles shrank tumors and drew in killer T cells. Combined with a standard immune drug, they erased tumors completely and extended survival.
pmc-13276794:
Navya Nair and co-authors wrote a 2026 review on vaginal dilator therapy after pelvic cancer treatment. Radiation, chemotherapy, hormone blockers, and surgery can abruptly cut estrogen and scar the vagina, causing narrowing called stenosis. After cervical cancer treatment with chemo plus radiation, major narrowing may exceed thirty percent without prevention.

Dilators are smooth tubes in graded sizes that stretch tissue, prevent adhesions, and keep the vaginal canal open. Water-based lubricants matched to body chemistry are essential for comfort. The few studies done so far suggest starting early and using dilators with steady habits reduces narrowing severity and improves tolerance and sexual function. Sticking with the routine is the main barrier for many patients. The authors recommend better teaching, early access to devices, and supportive follow-up to raise adherence and benefit.
pmc-13277494:
Zishuo Huang leads a 2026 study protocol for a trial to prevent memory and thinking decline in older adults living in the community in China. Combined programs that cover heart risks, brain training, activity, and diet show promise, but scaling them is hard. The protocol, for a trial across thirteen districts of Changxing County, has no results yet.

The planned trial will enroll 1,170 older adults and 273 community health workers in three groups. Support bundles include staff training, teamwork networks, and an AI-enabled phone mini-program. Outcomes on reach, health, and upkeep will be tracked over eighteen months. The design aims to judge both whether the program works and whether it can be delivered well.
pmc-13279194:
Karlijn Scheepens and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review of bone scans in children with brittle bone disease. The disease, osteogenesis imperfecta, makes bones break often. The scan method is dual energy absorptiometry, a low dose X ray test used as a stand in for bone strength. Yearly scans often guide care, yet the test misses bone shape and fine structure.

The team searched three databases and kept ninety one studies in the review set. Close detail came from thirty eight studies with near three thousand seven hundred patients. Scan sites were not standard across sites or studies. Links between scan scores, disease type and breaks varied by method and result. The authors show a clear need for shared rules on where and how to scan.
pmc-13279994:
Morten O. A. Sommer and Christian Munck issue a 2026 author correction to their 2021 Nature Communications study that forecast spread of antibiotic resistance genes across bacterial genomes. The first study built a statistical method to spot mobile elements linked to gene transfer. It tested forecasts on a database of more than four hundred seventy thousand genomes. Thirty four of ninety four forecast transfers seemed confirmed in that check.

A later critique by Godron and colleagues found that thirty of those thirty four events likely came from contaminant DNA, not true gene gains. In one case, a claimed resistance gene sat on a DNA chunk traced to an Acinetobacter contaminant. The authors accept that contaminant DNA likely inflated their raw count of confirmed events. The correction is a clear case of post publication science repair, where a bold forecast meets a hard data check.
pmc-13280394:
Hany S. E. Mansour and colleagues present a 2026 study of high resolution solar power forecasting with machine learning. Accurate short term photovoltaic forecasts, at sub hourly scale, keep grids stable as solar grows. The team benchmarked six machine learning models against a persistence baseline, which just repeats the last value. Data came from the Yulara Solar System, resampled at five, ten and fifteen minute steps. A full preprocessing frame built time, lag and rolling features and filtered outliers.

Models held XGBoost, Decision Tree, Linear Regression, Ridge, Lasso and Elastic Net. Five error metrics scored them across train, validation and test sets, plus seasonal and stress subsets. Stress scenes held night time and wild irradiance swings. Tree based models beat linear regressors by a lot in both accuracy and robustness. The Decision Tree took the best overall performance in their tests. Fine grain forecasts can smooth solar grid work.
pmc-13280694:
Claire Emilie Bertrand and colleagues tested computer tools for rating feelings in a 2026 study on psychosis risk. Psychosis means losing touch with what is real, and flat or low drive can come first. Such signs are hard to score by eye. The team filmed one hundred one young people at high risk and forty-one healthy peers. Software read their faces during interviews, and photos tested how strongly they reacted.

The at-risk group showed more disgust on their faces than the healthy group. Face signs and feeling reactions barely matched each other. Fewer strong face displays went with weaker outward feeling. Smiling more, oddly, went with lower drive and pleasure. The authors say face software adds facts that mood tests alone can miss.
pmc-13281494:
Renfei Luo and colleagues reviewed single-cell maps of immune cells in clogged arteries in a 2026 paper. Artery plaque grows over years and can trigger heart attacks and strokes. Immune cells called T cells help steer that growth. New tools can read one cell at a time, which exposes hidden variety. The review draws on studies of mouse and human plaque. It also uses maps that show where each cell type sits in the vessel wall.

The maps reveal T cell kinds never seen before in plaque. Some cells sit between killer and calming roles, as if mid-change. Local signals in the wall seem to push cells toward one role or the other. With age, the mix of bold and calming cells shifts. The authors say joining cell maps with gene and place data could point to precise new drugs.
pmc-13281894:
Zhuochen Yu and colleagues reviewed nano platforms that fight low oxygen in tumors in a 2026 paper. Solid tumors often starve for oxygen deep inside. That starvation helps them grow, spread, and resist care. Blunt oxygen top-ups leak, fade fast, and can harm healthy tissue. Tiny engineered platforms aim to tune oxygen with precision. The review sorts them by three strategies and explains how each is built.

One family ferries oxygen in from outside the body. A second makes oxygen on site from the tumor's own chemistry. A third slows the tumor's oxygen use, stretching what supply exists. The review weighs how each pairs with other care, like radiation or immune drugs. Fitful blood flow and uneven tumor makeup still blunt all three. The authors map design rules for the next wave of trials.
pmc-13282294:
Ling Zhan and co-authors present a 2026 analysis of safety reports for robotic thyroid surgery over ten years. Robotic removal of the thyroid gland, in the neck, draws patient interest, but device problems were poorly mapped. The team searched a United States device incident database from 2016 to 2025 and hand-checked the reports. Thirty-two reports qualified, and all events happened during surgery.

Most reports involved an energy device used for cutting and sealing, and breakage or fragments were the commonest pattern. Teams often swapped the device or retrieved fragments. Most operations still finished robotically as planned, and only one switched to open surgery. No severe patient injury was recorded. Some reports reached regulators late, beyond the thirty-day window. The authors call for better risk awareness, patient counselling, rehearsed troubleshooting, and faster, standard reporting when devices fail.
pmc-13282394:
Xiaojie Wang and co-authors present a 2026 study combining two scores to predict major heart and vessel events in UK Biobank adults. One score, the metabolic vulnerability index, distils six blood markers of metabolic and inflammatory strain. The other, Life's Essential 8, grades overall cardiovascular health from habits and measures. The team followed two hundred thirty-nine thousand adults free of such events at entry.

Over a median of about thirteen and a half years, more than seventeen thousand major events occurred. Higher vulnerability scores meant higher risk, while high health scores halved risk against low scores. People with both low health scores and top vulnerability had nearly triple the risk of the reference group. The two scores interacted, adding risk beyond each alone for heart attacks and overall events. Analyses suggested better health could prevent many events, partly by lowering vulnerability.
pmc-13282994:
Acute lung injury meets a plant-and-metal nanomaterial in Xuanpeng Wu's 2026 therapy experiments with fellow researchers. Lung injury of this type is severe and often fatal, with few good treatments. The material joins the metal cerium with tannic acid from plants.

The team made the material by a simple, low-cost method and tested its traits. Tiny grains stayed stable and mopped up harmful free radicals in lab tests. Treated lung and vessel cells showed less cell death and less stress damage. In mice with toxin-induced injury, lungs showed less swelling and less tissue harm. Inflammation markers fell as well. Safety tests support more study of this approach.
pmc-13283394:
Four factors form the SEA score for triple therapy outlook in marker-negative liver cancer, Hesheng Lin's multicenter team reports in 2026. Some tumors lack both common blood markers, which hides outlook. Triple therapy mixes vessel blocking, a targeted drug, and immune therapy for these patients.

Records covered 136 patients at many centers who got triple therapy. A training group of 91 patients built the score, and 45 patients tested it. Response rates were high, with most tumors shrinking or holding steady. Four factors formed the SEA score: tumor size, surgery chance, spread, and age. The score split patients into clear risk groups for survival. It may help pick best-fit patients.
pmc-13284094:
Needle stimulation at acupuncture points eased early ovary failure in mice fed rich diets, report Lele Ling and colleagues in 2026. Early ovary failure is a leading cause of infertility in young women. The team traced benefit to a chemical mark placed on a self-cleaning gene message in egg-support cells.

Mice on high-fat, high-sugar feed developed the ovary condition for testing. Stimulation at three body points improved follicle growth and normalized cycles. Support cell death fell, and inflammation signals dropped after treatment. Single-cell sequencing mapped ovary cell groups and self-cleaning signatures in detail. A writer enzyme for the mark fell as cleaning markers recovered.
pmc-13284194:
A pinch of ceramic powder at just the right dose made plastic joint material last longer, find Ahmed Salama and colleagues in 2026. Their plastic base mimics cartilage for joint replacements. Bone-friendly mineral filler was fixed, while titanium dioxide varied across mixes.

Three blends were pressed and checked for wear, fatigue, and germ killing. Imaging and diffraction confirmed fillers spread well through the plastic base. At three percent titanium dioxide, wear resistance peaked with a dense lubricant film. That same blend also gained fatigue life and higher peak stress. Extra filler clumped and weakened fatigue performance in higher blends.
pmc-13284494:
Fengqiang Gao and co-authors report a 2026 study on sorafenib as protection against liver injury when blood flow returns after a cut-off. Such ischemia-reperfusion injury is a common problem in liver surgery and links to poorer survival. Gene and metabolite profiling pointed to a pathway that boosts antioxidant defense.

A middle dose of sorafenib cut liver cell death, swelling, and programmed cell death in the model systems used here. Blocking a key enzyme in the pathway, or raising HSP90 levels, removed the benefit, which supports the proposed chain. In human transplant recipients, high HSP90 linked to poor graft work. A new oral nanoparticle that targets liver raised the drug effect further.
pmc-13285194:
Li Chen and co-authors test a ginseng compound against artery plaque in a 2026 mouse and cell study that mimics menopause. Women after menopause face higher plaque risk, and Panax quinquefolium saponin is known to calm swelling and vessel harm. Ovariectomized ApoE-deficient mice were treated and checked at two plaque stages.

Surgery raised plaque growth, blood inflammation markers, and death of vessel lining cells, while the saponin reversed those harms at both stages. Computer and lab work pointed to estrogen receptor alpha as the key target, acting through two signaling paths. Blocking that receptor largely erased the benefit, while activating it boosted gains. The authors propose the pathway for post-menopause plaque care.
pmc-13285594:
Hidden RNA helpers in the Lyme disease germ come to light in a 2026 study by Taylor Van Gundy and co-authors. Proteins that grip RNA steer gene use in all life, yet few were known in Borrelia burgdorferi. The team fished for proteins that sink with small RNAs in gradient tubes, then tested their grip and reshaping skill.

Five proteins passed the lab tests, unwinding, pairing, and swapping RNA strands with ease. Three had been mere guesses on the gene map, while two were known from swimming and steering gear. One lead protein also held RNA inside living germ cells. The finds widen the cast of gene control in a germ with a lean toolkit.
pmc-13286194:
Somayeh Taghidoust Chahardeh, Seyyed Hossein Hosseini, and Ali Shamsi Majelan compare three warm-up styles in elite women taekwondo fighters in a 2026 randomized study. Kicks and jumps in the sport ride on a spring-like cycle in the legs, and each warm-up may tune that spring in its own way. Thirty-six athletes drew lots for active stretching, foam rolling, or band work after a set treadmill start.

Body sensors tracked drop jumps before and after each routine, and the groups parted ways on force measures. Active stretching lifted push-off force and power, while foam rolling mostly shifted how fast force built up. Band work simply held fighters near their starting marks on most counts. Plain jump height and air time barely budged in any group, which tells coaches to match the warm-up to the quality they want to sharpen.
pmc-13287094:
A de J Basánez-Muñoz and co-authors link mangrove decline to soil change on Mexico's Veracruz coast in a 2026 ecological study. Within a Ramsar-listed wetland, plots along four shore-crossing transects were classed as intact, semi-disturbed, or disturbed, and their soils and tree structure were measured side by side. The question was whether forest thinning follows the soil, pointing to where restoration must start.

Intact plots carried denser, taller, richer forest than semi-disturbed ones, while disturbed plots held no living trees at all. Statistical ordination fingered silt content and soil acidity as the main factors tracking structural change. Semi-disturbed and disturbed plots overlapped in the analysis, suggesting decline spreads as soils shift. Distance from the lagoon mattered only marginally. The authors conclude conservation must restore soils, not merely replant trees.
pmc-13287494:
Jian Xu and colleagues present an image-cleaning system in 2026 for underwater photographs, which often carry colour casts, haze, and lost detail from light absorption and scattering. Poor images weaken robot navigation, inspection, and habitat monitoring, so the team combined physics-based colour repair with a learning network.

Early steps fix colour balance and stretch contrast, then wave-based merging keeps structure. Texture maps at four angles guide a second branch that guards fine detail, while a main branch handles colour and form. Tests on three public sets showed gains across six quality scores. Downstream tasks such as edge finding also improved, the authors report.
pmc-13288694:
Ying Zhao and colleagues study a leftover cholesterol type in diabetes in 2026. The study held 26,302 hospital patients. All had type 2 diabetes. Remnant cholesterol rides in fat-rich particles. It was weighed against standard LDL cholesterol. The target was fatty liver disease.

Nearly half the group had the liver disease. That share was 48.3 percent, at median age 62. Remnant levels tracked disease more closely than LDL. Patients high on remnant but low on LDL faced more risk. The reverse mismatch carried less risk. All three check methods agreed. Cutting remnant levels may aid prevention plans.
pmc-13289194:
Michael Marll and colleagues study lung damage at TB diagnosis in South Africa in 2026. Their study ran in Johannesburg. It held 258 adults with new drug-sensitive TB. Full lung tests were done at diagnosis. HIV status split the group.

Adults with HIV and TB had better lung scores. Their odds of any odd test were lower. Tight and mixed patterns were also less common. Chest images showed less severe disease too. Yet symptom scores were alike in both groups. Breath quality of life did not split. The authors see a distinct injury pattern. HIV may blunt some lung harm at diagnosis.
pmc-13289894:
Allyson E. Shea and colleagues present a 2026 study on sugar transport in Proteus mirabilis, a top cause of complicated urinary infections. The germ uses sugars during infection, yet which import systems matter for fitness was unclear. The team built 47 mutants, each targeting a predicted sugar transporter gene, and screened growth in dishes and fitness inside the urinary tract.

Pooled sequencing flagged three genes as fitness factors in animals, confirmed in head-to-head mouse challenges. One flagged gene, thought to import xanthosine, did not do so, suggesting a wrong label in databases. A triple mutant missing three transporters copied the key single-gene defect. Raising urine sugar with a diabetes drug boosted colonization overall.
pmc-13290394:
Rainfall shapes how a serpentine-tolerant wildflower times its blooms on either side of a soil boundary, Nicole Ibañez and colleagues reported in 2026. The subject is Antirrhinum vexillocalyculatum, an annual herb that grows on and off harsh serpentine soils.

The team combined a greenhouse common garden along a moisture gradient, a water-limitation experiment, and field observation. Precipitation regime strongly shifted flowering time, and dry conditions shrank floral displays, delayed flowering, and for some traits pushed the two soil populations further apart. In the field, more plants flowered in the wetter area, and gene flow ran mainly from ordinary soil into serpentine populations. Because flowering still overlapped widely, the authors see gene flow as the dominant force, one that drought may weaken.
pmc-13291494:
Bone health is steered by talk between distant organs. Donghao Gan, Lei Qin, and Guozhi Xiao review that web in 2026. Bone loss and joint wear rise with age and weight. Other organs feed into each of these diseases.

Gut, brain, hormone, and fat signals all reach bone. Immune links braid through each of those paths. The review maps axes like gut-bone-immune in detail. Blood markers and scans can now read this crosstalk. Care teams can sort patients by axis pattern. Drug choice may then match the driver organ. Gaps in proof and open questions close the review.
pmc-13291794:
Boris Baruch S Bernatskiy's team presents a 2026 case report on rebuilding a badly damaged front upper jaw with the Bone-to-Soft Tissue technique. Their patient was a 17-year-old who lost a maxillary central incisor to trauma and had severe ridge loss. Implants and standard grafting were poor fits at that age and anatomy.

Surgeons transplanted a combined block of tooth, bone, and soft tissue into the gap, then adapted, stabilized, and restored it in stages. The graft integrated well, kept the soft-tissue shape, and restored the ridge contour on imaging. The authors suggest the method as a biology-based option for select esthetic-zone defects. They also stress that controlled studies must confirm long-term results before wider use.
pmc-13292294:
Lijun Wen and co-authors recount a 2026 diagnostically tricky case of intrathyroidal thymic carcinoma, a tumor making up under 0.15 percent of thyroid cancers. It usually betrays itself through CD5 and CD117 staining, but exceptions unsettle that rule. Their patient, a 32-year-old Chinese woman seen in 2019, arrived with hoarseness, swallowing trouble, and a firm left thyroid mass.

Imaging showed a lesion of about 4.1 cm in the left lobe plus a tiny right-side nodule, and her left vocal cord was paralyzed. After total thyroid removal and neck dissection, pathology showed CD117, p63, and p40 positivity but no CD5, still fitting the thymic carcinoma diagnosis. A separate papillary thyroid cancer coexisted. The tumor later returned in lymph nodes and, strikingly, gained CD5 expression, which the authors read as clonal evolution.
pmc-13292794:
Aroldo de Oliveira Gomes Golineli and co-authors present, in a 2026 letter, an ecological study of leprosy across towns and cities in Brazil. Leprosy has fallen yet stays clustered in poorer areas, and by 2024 new cases had fallen to 22,129, down from 31,064 in 2014, based on figures the authors report.

Town-level data came from national sources, plus the 2022 census and measures of income, schooling, housing, and social progress. The study looks at how these shared conditions line up with where cases appear. Such maps can guide health teams to places where poverty and weak services let the disease persist, even as national counts improve.
pmc-13292994:
Quan Xu and co-authors report, in 2026, a nature-inspired route to build many complex ring-shaped molecules from one starting material. Making dense three-dimensional ring systems is a long-standing hard task in organic chemistry.

Starting from a marine product idea, the team first made ocellatusone C by an acid-triggered chain reaction, then varied that path to make related bicyclic forms. Computer models guided a light-driven reshaping that reached rare ring layouts, and coupling steps grew the set further. Tests showed strong activity against malaria in the new molecules. The method shows how one precursor can seed a whole family of drug leads.
pmc-13293094:
Abdalmajeed M. Alajlouni and Wael Hananeh test, in a 2026 feeding study, whether zeolite in chicken feed changes harmful genes in gut Escherichia coli. Zeolite is a natural mineral added to feed for its soaking and buffering traits.

A total of 150 chicks were split into five groups getting feed with zeolite shares from 0% up to 30% of the mix. Lab screens checked 11 harm-linked genes in gut bacteria. At the 10% level, no sample met the set mark for the pathogenic type, and key predictor genes were least common. The authors present zeolite as a non-drug way to lower risk, pending more tests.
pmc-13293394:
Zahra Dianat Maharlouei and colleagues test, in a 2026 greenhouse study, whether treated biochar plus native bacteria can clean soils laced with heavy metals and oil waste. Such mixed pollution cuts crop yields and lets toxins enter food chains.

Soil came from industrial sites near Kerman, Iran, yielding five native bacterial types from 30 samples. In 90 pots of spiked soil, maize grew for 90 days under four plans, from plain soil to bacteria-loaded biochar. The loaded biochar cut available metals by roughly half and oil compounds by 70%, based on values the authors report. Maize also grew larger with less metal uptake.
pmc-13293794:
Agustín A. Vera and a large team show, in a 2026 study, how vitamin D helps activated helper T cells grow by feeding on glutamine rather than glucose. Vitamin D calms sugar use in these immune cells, yet early growth stays strong, hinting at a backup fuel.

Protein scans showed more glutamine-processing enzymes, and tracing showed more glutamine flowing into growth building blocks. Blocking the vitamin D receptor, glutamine entry, or its key enzyme each cut the effect. Glutamine thus powers the vitamin D growth path.
pmc-13293994:
Ellen King leads a 2026 mouse study of the first messenger RNA vaccine aimed at neuroblastoma, a childhood tumor behind 15% of pediatric cancer deaths. The vaccine uses self-assembling RALA peptides to carry RNA coding for glypican 2, a surface protein common on these tumors. Lab checks confirmed particle form, cell uptake, and function before animal dosing.

pmc-13294294:
Shin Iinuma, Takahiro Kobayashi, and Yasuyuki Fujita systematically review a rare relapsing skin vessel disease in 2026. Recurrent cutaneous eosinophilic vasculitis appears mainly in single case reports, so features were gathered case by case from three sources, last searched February 16, 2026, with structured extraction and quality appraisal.

Twenty reports gave 24 unique cases. Most people had repeated itchy purple spots on the lower legs, frequent blood eosinophil rises, and vessel damage rich in eosinophils on biopsy. Antibody tests tied to wider vasculitis were always negative in reported cases. Steroids often helped, yet relapse during dose cuts or after stopping was common. Follow-up gaps limit firm guidance.
pmc-13294494:
Areeb Mian and coauthors build a scan texture score for survival after liver metastasis surgery in a 2026 multicentre study. Outcomes after removing colorectal spread to the liver vary widely, and routine CT scans hold unused pattern data. Records from two UK centers gave 959 metastases from 399 patients, with features from tumors and background liver fed to selection tools and machine learners.

Six features formed the risk score. Texture alone predicted 3-year death with an area of 0.77, close to clinic models at 0.82 in the reported figures, and combined models nudged slightly higher. Formal tests found no clear gap between texture and clinic models. High versus low score split survival paths cleanly.
pmc-13294694:
Toru Matsui and colleagues report outcomes for a bleeding-control technique in a 2026 single-centre case series. Colonic diverticular bleeding is hard to manage during endoscopy, and their hospital uses coagulation combined with clipping. Real-world results for that combined approach had been little reported.

Among 256 patients with blood in the stool, 83 received the combined treatment for confirmed diverticular bleeding. Seven patients bled again within 30 days, and procedure-related problems arose in 3 patients, all handled without surgery. The authors present the approach as a practical option when the bleeding diverticulum can be clearly seen.
pmc-13295694:
Inês Pereira and a large team search existing drugs for new uses against gonorrhoea in a 2026 study. The germ is a top priority for fresh treatments as resistance grows. Blocking its pump systems, which throw out antibiotics, could restore drug power, especially if energy supply is also hit.

Computer matching across public databases linked 57 approved drugs to 32 predicted bacterial targets. A shortlist went to bench tests on a reference strain, where two drugs stopped growth at the lowest levels. Two others showed signs of jamming the pumps, and one helped partner drugs in combination tests, marking early candidates for resistant strain work.
pmc-13295994:
Jessica Wilkins and colleagues use health records in 2026 to study GP contact among adults with eating disorders in England. They compare visit rates before diagnosis with matched people without such disorders, and check whether ethnicity shapes referral onward.

Records covered 46,473 patients and far larger matched controls from 2010 to 2023. People with eating disorders saw their GP about twice as often in the two years before diagnosis, across all disorder types. Contact rates were lower in minority ethnic groups, and Asian and Black patients had lower odds of specialist referral. The authors urge better awareness and fairer primary care.
pmc-13297294:
Chenxi Miao and co-authors review, in 2026, CAR-macrophage therapy, a cell treatment aiming engineered macrophages at solid tumours where CAR-T cells disappoint. Macrophages naturally burrow into tumours and can flip local immunity from suppressed to attacking.

Beyond eating tumour cells directly, the engineered cells spread the alarm to other tumour targets, bridging quick innate and learned adaptive attack. The review argues macrophage-specific signal parts beat borrowed T-cell designs. Making enough cells is the big bottleneck, with stem-cell factories and in-body programming via fat nanoparticles offered as practical ways forward for the field.
pmc-13297594:
Blood signals of scarring might one day flag heart transplant rejection without a biopsy, suggests a 2026 study led by Marta Delgado-Arija. Working with 40 serum samples from transplant recipients undergoing routine biopsies, the team hunted for fibrosis-related messenger RNAs that shift during acute cellular rejection.

Several signals differed in patients with rejection, including fibroblast activators such as TNS1, FAP, and ACTA2, plus members of the TGF-β and WNT pathways. Two markers, TNS1 and WLS, separated moderate-to-severe rejection from no rejection with area under the curve values above 0.90. The authors see a path toward gentler monitoring of transplant patients and toward treatments aimed at the fibrotic process itself.
pmc-13298094:
The size of the opening at the top of the chest might help predict trouble after esophagus surgery, suggest Iskan Calli and co-authors in a 2026 study. They measured thoracic inlet dimensions on routine CT scans of esophageal cancer patients who received a neck connection after esophagectomy.

Patients with smaller inlet areas tended toward higher postoperative mortality, and leakage at the connection was markedly more frequent among those who died. The authors stop short of claiming cause, framing inlet shape as one anatomical factor among many. Because the measurements come free from standard scans, they propose adding them to future risk assessment, pending confirmation in larger prospective studies.
pmc-13299094:
An endoscopic operation through the anus spared patients with low rectal tumors the loss of anal function, report Xiaoke Hu and colleagues in a 2026 multicenter case series. Thirty-seven patients who had declined radical surgery, including older people with serious illnesses and cases that returned after earlier treatment, underwent the sphincter-preserving technique.

Most tumors were low-grade rectal cancers, with neuroendocrine and stromal tumors making up the rest. Every tumor came out in one piece with complete removal, and no severe complications occurred. Over an average follow-up near thirty-seven months, only 2.7% of patients saw recurrence. The authors present the approach as a valuable option for difficult cases.
pmc-13299194:
Natural compounds attack skin cancer through a surprisingly shared set of mechanisms, find Natalia Forno-Bell and co-authors in a 2026 systematic review of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Sixty studies covering purified molecules, crude extracts, essential oils, and combinations met their criteria.

Despite the chemical variety, activity converged on cell death programs, redox shifts, blocked growth signaling, cell-cycle arrest, and immune or light-activated effects. Purified compounds showed tighter mechanistic focus, while extracts acted more broadly and less predictably. Several agents worked both in dishes and in animals. The authors offer their mechanism-based sorting as a guide for choosing which natural candidates deserve clinical development.
pmc-13303694:
Xue Hu and co-authors share a 2026 case report with a literature review on a malignant nerve sheath tumor arising in the liver. Such tumors usually start in arms, legs, or the trunk, and a liver origin is extremely rare.

A 56-year-old woman came in with upper belly pain and swelling, while blood tumor markers stayed normal. Scans showed a liver lesion with low blood flow, and tissue testing after full surgical removal confirmed the diagnosis. No return or spread appeared during about two years of follow-up. Imaging features from this and past cases may help doctors separate this tumor from more common liver cancers.
pmc-13304094:
Paola Romano introduces a 2026 special issue on the physics and uses of superconductivity, the state where materials carry current without resistance below a set temperature. For decades the effect needed extreme cold, until layered copper materials raised the working range in the late 1980s.

Nine papers in the first edition cover low-temperature, high-temperature, and iron-based materials, their structure, electrical and magnetic traits, and theory. Making and processing methods that lift performance toward real devices also feature. The overview frames where the field stands and what practical gains may come next for energy and other technologies.
pmc-13304494:
Reuven Rasooly and Naomi Balaban develop a cell-based test for active staph food toxins in a 2026 study. Existing lab tests find the toxins but cannot tell live, sickness-causing forms from spent ones, so animal testing fills that gap.

A lab T cell line was engineered to answer active toxin by making an immune signal in proportion to dose. The test covered two major toxin types tied to food poisoning and possible misuse. Heating past a set point sharply cut one toxin's activity, while standard pasteurizing heat cut it only slightly. The method offers a humane stand-in for animal checks.
pmc-13307294:
Christophe Barbanchon tested repeated virtual motion exposure for balance in older adults in a 2026 study. Eighteen healthy participants over sixty stood quietly and faced simulated forward and backward self-motion plus tendon vibration before and after training.

Repeated optic flow in immersive virtual reality dulled the destabilising pull of moving scenes in reported results. Quiet standing with eyes closed also grew steadier, and sense weighting shifted toward more consistent visual use with weaker visual-proprioceptive coupling. The authors present short VR practice as a targeted way to keep balance strategies flexible with age.
pmc-13307794:
Claudia Maria Tucciarone and co-authors survey in 2026 DNA viruses in non native pond sliders, a turtle that has spread through ponds in northeastern Italy. Mouth and vent swabs came from 164 turtles at three sites, and lab tests hunted herpesviruses, ranaviruses, and adenoviruses in each sample.

No herpesvirus or ranavirus turned up in any turtle they sampled during the survey work. Adenoviruses were common, found in 72 of 163 turtles with full results in hand for that check. Most matched a known turtle type, while one matched a type once tied to deaths in other tortoises. What these viruses do to turtles stays unclear, yet wide carriage argues for steady watch where native species share the water.
pmc-13307894:
Dequan Guo and co-authors assemble in 2026 a disease knowledge graph to aid vet care for captive forest musk deer, a protected species farmed for musk in China. Their joint extraction model pulls core medical ideas from loose deer disease texts and links them into a web that vets can search. Tests on medical data sets showed the model could carry over well to new material of like kind. A tidy graph base could speed early spotting and care choices, while also cutting the stress that hands on checks cause shy deer.
pmc-13308594:
Ruiyang Liu and co-authors find in 2026 a driver of liver cancer growth in a metabolic enzyme called PMVK, found through a gene screen in tumour cells. PMVK tags the factor SP1 at one site, which helps SP1 grip DNA and team with fat control factors SREBP1 and SREBP2.

That team switches on fresh cholesterol and fatty acid making, which feeds tumour stem traits and spread in their tests. High PMVK in patient tumours tracked with high tagged SP1 and with poor outlook for those patients. Blocking the pair, by genes or by a known SP1 drug, curbed tumour growth in models. The axis offers a fresh drug target for liver cancer.
pmc-13309194:
Marie-Laure Oberweis, Ana C Blanchard, and Esther Vaugon lay out in 2026 five key points on hantavirus. Hantavirus is a rodent borne disease that must be reported in Canada, with four to five confirmed cases a year. Most cases arise on farms in the prairie west and British Columbia, through touch of infected rodents or their waste.

Two syndromes follow a two to four week wait: a heart and lung form in the Americas, and a kidney and bleeding form in Europe and Asia. Death rates run 12 to 45 percent for the lung form, and 1 to 12 percent for the kidney form. No vaccine or set cure exists, so care rests on support and swift transfer. Andes strain cases need strict isolation.
pmc-13309594:
Donghao Zhang and colleagues build an artificial ionic skin that also blocks electromagnetic interference in a 2026 study. Ionic skins copy human skin signal flow and softness for wearable sensors. Most versions sense well but shield poorly, leaving signals open to outside noise.

A soaking and binding strategy set a flat network of MXene sheets inside a gel while also building a charge slope through its depth. That single build gave strong shielding plus self-powered sensing, since the charge slope makes its own voltage. Stretch and self-healing traits from gel design carry over. The authors present the skin as a step toward wearables that sense cleanly in noisy settings.
pmc-13310394:
Cynthia Mmalebna Amisigo and co-authors review parasites that cause neglected tropical diseases in a 2026 article. Trypanosomatids, including Trypanosoma and Leishmania, cause sleeping sickness, Chagas disease, and leishmaniasis across Africa, Latin America, and Asia. Drugs remain toxic, costly, scarce, and more often resisted, and no effective vaccines exist.

Tactics that let these parasites hide inside cells, dodge immunity, and adapt their chemistry also blunt drug action, breeding tougher strains. New lab work on their unusual cell structures and immune tricks opens fresh attack points. Smart software is entering target and drug screening for these diseases. The authors chart control strategies and argue that drug failure and disease strength must be tackled together.
pmc-13310494:
Linna Hao and co-authors report a rare benign eye tumor in a child in a 2026 case article. Choroidal osteoma is bone-like growth inside the eye wall layer, seen in about 1 per 100,000 people, mostly young women and usually in one eye only. A child with tumors in both eyes, covering the central vision zone, breaks that pattern.

The child had no symptoms despite giant tumors involving the macula of both eyes, and full eye examinations were completed for the record. Early lesions can sit silently even over the center of vision, the authors note. Typical patients report blur, warped sight, or light sensitivity once damage advances. The case urges doctors to keep this tumor in mind during childhood eye checks.
pmc-13310794:
Kayo Sugiyama reports a 2026 case where an aorta tear worsened silently during hospital transfer. A man aged 50 years was moved for stent care of a type B tear in the lower aorta. During transfer the tear spread backward into the upper aorta, a grave turn, yet pulse and symptoms showed no change.

On arrival, open surgery replaced the arch of the aorta with a hybrid graft method. Direct ultrasound during surgery found no tear in the rising aorta, which guided the choice. The man recovered well and stayed well at five year follow up. Teams must watch for silent spread during any transfer.
pmc-13310894:
Nayoung Lee and co-authors test a seaweed pigment against Alzheimer linked stress in cells and mice in a 2026 study. Brain amyloid drives disease advance, and a reactive compound called methylglyoxal adds stress that sparks swelling through a sensor pathway. The pigment fucoxanthin may calm that chain.

Nerve cells dosed with the pigment before amyloid exposure made fewer swelling signals and kept the key switch out of the nucleus. Mice given amyloid into the brain and fed the pigment for 15 days showed lower blood stress levels and calmer brain immune cells. Synapse markers were also guarded. Human proof is still absent.
pmc-13311094:
Hina Durrani and colleagues test whether a shared growth medium changes sugar enzyme levels in parasite relatives in a 2026 study. Kinetoplastids store sugar breaking enzymes in a special compartment called a glycosome. One theory holds that storage lets cells swiftly reshuffle enzyme amounts when food or oxygen shifts.

Six species, both single host and two host types, were grown under varied food and oxygen in one medium. Enzyme levels stayed largely steady across conditions. Slow food removal and oxygen shifts caused only minor moves. Only sudden food return nudged levels down slightly. Steady levels argue against the swift reshuffle theory.
pmc-13311194:
Liufeng Mao and co-authors trace how resveratrol lifts a metabolic hormone against obesity in a 2026 study. The grape linked polyphenol fights fat gain in past work, yet its molecular route was murky. A hormone called GDF15 that steadies energy balance emerged as a key suspect.

In mouse and human cells, resveratrol raised GDF15 making and release in a dose linked way. Gene scans named a stress factor that carries the signal, switched on through a kinase path. Treated mice resisted high fat diet obesity and held higher blood GDF15. Liver, kidney, and colon levels also rose, with stronger brain signaling downstream.
pmc-13311294:
Lan Luo and co-authors present their 2026 study on how the channel protein TRPV4 drives a fiery form of cell death in lung macrophages during acute lung injury. The death pathway runs through damaged mitochondria.

The work traces a chain in which TRPV4 upsets mitochondria, raising reactive oxygen from them, which then switches on the NLRP3 inflammasome. That switch pushes macrophages into pyroptosis, a bursting death that spills inflammatory signals. Acute lung injury still lacks drugs that hit its root inflammation. Naming TRPV4 as a driver gives drug makers a fresh target to test for calming the lung.
pmc-13311794:
Kian-Hwee Chong and colleagues examine a 2026 global records study on whether the timing of sleeve gastrectomy shapes later breast cancer risk in women with severe obesity. Weight surgery can lower cancer risk overall.

The network data held over 4.4 million women with body mass index above 35 recorded from 2010 to 2019. Surgery patients were grouped by how soon the operation followed diagnosis. Early surgery tied to lower five-year breast cancer and metastasis rates, while surgery delayed one to three years tied to higher breast cancer risk in this dataset. Timing, the authors argue, belongs in counseling about the operation.
pmc-13311994:
Xiaoyan Xie and co-authors review the IL-33/ST2 signaling pathway as a drug target in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in a 2026 article. The pathway weaves through oxidative stress, immunity, and lung injury.

Levels of IL-33 and its receptor ST2 run high in patients and track with worse disease, more flare-ups, and poorer outcomes, on the reviewed evidence. Blocking antibodies and receptor inhibitors have calmed inflammation and improved lung function in early studies. How the pathway talks with other inflammatory circuits is still murky. The review maps the biology and the drug pipeline aimed at it.
pmc-13312094:
Rapin Polsook and Yupin Aungsuroch report a 2026 randomized trial in Thailand testing whether a phone-based self-management program improves blood lipids in people with coronary artery disease. Drugs often fail to bring cholesterol and related fats to target, so the authors asked whether structured self-care support could close the gap.

Forty-eight patients at a tertiary hospital were split between usual care and a four-week program run through mobile applications and telephone contact. The program group ended with significantly lower cholesterol, triglyceride, and low-density lipoprotein levels than the control group. The authors conclude that app-guided self-management can improve lipid profiles in the short term and point to a practical role for nurses in delivering this kind of support.
pmc-13312494:
Weiqian Jin and colleagues describe, in a 2026 study, a nature-mimicking nanoplatform for treating bacterial pneumonia without leaning on standard antibiotics. Their particle, called CM, wraps a copper-based metal-organic framework in macrophage membrane, using the membrane's homing ways so the platform gathers at infected sites.

Shone with near-infrared light, the platform loads copper ions into bacteria, sparks reactive oxygen species and inflammatory signals, and kills the microbes. Gene and metabolite tests showed the light-driven copper overload triggers cuproptosis, a cell death route driven by copper. The treatment also pushed macrophages toward their inflammatory M1 state and reshaped immune cell groups in the lung, so direct killing and immune activation worked together. Tests in cells and animals both backed the approach, which the authors offer as a template for other infections.
pmc-13312794:
Chang Ha Park reviews, in a 2026 article, the plant compound picroside III, an iridoid glycoside flagged for possible antileukemic activity. Its relatives picroside I and II have been studied heavily. A search of the literature from 2000 to 2026 turns up only a handful of papers on picroside III itself, a gap the review sets out to close.

The article walks through the molecule's architecture: a fused cyclopentane and pyran ring core carrying sugar units and varied substituents whose type, position, and orientation differ from its cousins. Those differences reshape its electronics and three-dimensional form. Attached sugars aid water solubility and transport but also leave the molecule open to enzymatic reshaping inside the body, while its many hydroxyl groups offer hydrogen-bonding grips on enzymes. Park argues these features make the neglected compound worth direct biological testing against leukemia.
pmc-13313294:
Shimaa El-Garf and fellow authors measure an immune brake in multiple myeloma in a 2026 study. The bone marrow around this blood cancer is full of blocked immune signals, and the PD-1 and PD-L1 pair is one such brake on T cells, though its solo role stays unclear.

The team ran a cross-sectional study of 39 patients newly diagnosed with the disease. Flow cytometry gauged PD-1 on T cells and PD-L1 on marrow plasma cells, and the values were set against clinical and lab data. PD-L1 strength on plasma cells rose with the share of T cells in marrow, with a correlation of 0.350 stated in the report, while PD-1 on T cells tracked with white cell counts. In stage III patients further links appeared. The data help weigh whether drugs that lift this brake merit trials in myeloma.
pmc-13314794:
Yunhao Zhai and a large team build a lab model of mRNA vaccination on chips in their 2026 study. Guessing how well a new mRNA vaccine will work, and how toxic it may be, still leans on animal tests that often miss human responses.

Their setup doses human muscle cells and antigen-presenting cells with fat-bubble mRNA vaccines, mimicking a shot into muscle. Plain mRNA vaccines made antigen right in the presenting cells, while self-amplifying ones needed touch between muscle and presenting cells, as the authors report. Moving those cells and fluids to a lymphoid follicle chip, a tiny fluid device, mimicked drainage to lymph nodes. The chip follicles then grew and made fresh antibodies. The human tissue model may speed vaccine screening without animals.
pmc-13314994:
Mohammed Turky and co-workers set out a privacy-safe way to train AI across dental centers, in a 2026 review. The field is endodontics, the root canal specialty, where sharp AI needs wide, well-labeled data that privacy law keeps locked in each clinic.

Their answer is federated learning: each center trains a shared model on its own data, and only model updates travel, never patient files. The review searched the literature to April 2026 in English and compared how the method works and where it has been used. Standard central training clashes with data rules, they note. The paper lays out build paths, hurdles, and research needs for diagnosis and decision support, aiming to let clinics pool smarts without pooling records.
pmc-13315094:
Quoc Phuong Nguyen, Duy Thanh Doan, and Thi Thu Huong Dinh report a brain infection case where all cultures came back empty, in a 2026 study. Subdural empyema, pus under the skull lining, is a surgical emergency that kills a share of 6 to 15 percent of patients by the range cited in the report.

Their patient was a 51-year-old man with chronic alcohol abuse, high fever of 39 degrees, severe headache, neck stiffness, and a dulled mind. Spinal fluid was thick with cells and protein yet grew nothing, like his blood, urine, and pus samples, though inflammation marks soared. A plain CT read the mass as an old blood clot, but surgery found frank pus. Drainage plus two antibiotics brought full recovery in 24 days, as reported. The case backs MRI and early surgery when cultures stay silent.
pmc-13315894:
Haisheng Lan and colleagues built in 2026 a four-gene lactate score for colorectal cancer that forecasts outlook and immune therapy response. Lactate handling reshapes how tumor, epithelial, and immune cells talk to each other and can turn a tumor immunologically cold.

Single-cell and spatial gene data fed the new LMscore. A high score marked cold tumors full of suppressive cells with poor response to immune checkpoint drugs, and signaling through EFNA1 and EPHA3 linked epithelial cells with fibroblasts. Blocking COX15 in tests slowed tumor growth and restored anti-tumor immunity, offering a target tied to the score.
pmc-13316194:
Alexandra Biácsi and colleagues describe eleven cases in 2026 of heartworm disease in Hungarian zoo animals, caused by the mosquito-borne worm Dirofilaria immitis. Affected animals included three Eurasian wolves, two Arctic wolves, a lion, a leopard, a red panda, an Arctic fox, a harbour seal, and an Asian small-clawed otter.

Post-mortem results suggested heartworm played a part in the deaths of three Eurasian wolves, the red panda, the Arctic fox, and the seal, while other infections were incidental finds. The series gives the first Hungarian records in captive felids and the first report in Arctic wolves.
pmc-13316294:
Liv Cathrine Heggebø leads a 2026 quality check for the PRO-GLIO trial, which tests radiation care for certain slow-growing brain tumors with IDH changes. Before treatment starts across centers, the team asked how much expert drawings of target areas and nearby organs differ from place to place.

Five experts first set shared reference outlines for two cases, then experts at 12 centers in two Scandinavian countries drew their own, and a deep learning tool drew its own as well. Target outlines matched closely, with a median overlap score of 0.92 in the reported cases. Nearby organs varied far more, notably the optic chiasm and memory-related hippocampi. Computer outlines fell inside the human range, hinting they may help, while organ drawing needs closer watch.
pmc-13316594:
Youn-Soo Lee, Alex Soo In Park, and Bo-Young Youn studied a 2026 question in Korean health data. Do people with normal weight but high body fat face the same diabetes risk as people with obesity? The group, called normal-weight obesity, can hide risk behind a healthy scale reading.

Using national survey data from 2019 to 2021, the team matched 684 middle-aged adults one to one by sex and background. Among men, diabetes appeared in 20.00 percent of the normal-weight obese group versus 31.03 percent of the obesity group in the matched figures, while women showed no clear gap. Measuring body fat beyond weight and height, they argue, can flag hidden risk, at least in men.
pmc-13316694:
You Jin Lee and colleagues assembled, in a 2026 study, a living bank of 41 colorectal cancer organoids grown from patient tumors, then profiled them with many molecular tools at once. Such mini-tumors let researchers sort cancers by inner state and match drugs to type.

Their reads revealed a tug between two programs, MYC and PRC, marking stem-like versus more mature tumor states. A new maturation index split the organoids into two clear subtypes along that axis. MYC-type samples ran growth programs and answered better to drugs blocking the MEK and EGFR paths. The same split held in larger organoid sets and a public cancer dataset, tying cell maturity to treatment weakness in a usable way.
pmc-13318594:
Longkang Guo and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. They study mind-body therapies for sleep in women around pregnancy and after birth. Poor sleep is common in that period. Drug options raise safety worries, so gentle therapies draw interest. Searches covered seven databases up to January 20, 2026.

Thirteen randomised trials with 782 participants qualified. Most tested mindfulness, Pilates, or yoga. Pooled results favoured the therapies over controls. Sleep scores improved by a mean difference of −2.63 points in the pooled analysis. Results varied a lot between studies, though. Country, programme length, and session length helped explain that spread. Formal grading rated the certainty of evidence as low. The authors urge caution and better trials.
pmc-13318694:
Peipei Liu and colleagues offer a 2026 genetic study of early puberty in girls. They test two variants in the estrogen receptor beta gene. The condition is idiopathic central precocious puberty, with no clear cause. One hundred affected girls from a Shenzhen hospital were enrolled.

Another hundred healthy girls of similar age served as controls. Genotyping used a standard restriction fragment method. The RsaI variant differed clearly between groups. Its R allele appeared in 41.50 percent of patients against 30.00 percent of controls, raising risk. The AluI variant showed no clear difference. A combined pattern, the Rraa haplotype, also appeared more often in patients. The authors suggest genotyping could aid early risk checks, pending larger studies.
pmc-13318794:
Mengxuan Zhang and colleagues report a 2026 nine-year field experiment on green manures before wheat in salty soils. The setting is the Hetao Irrigation District. Treatments mixed feed rape, a non-legume, with hairy vetch, a legume. Two nitrogen rates were tested, including none.

Yield stability rose by about a fifth under both nitrogen rates. Mixed planting also raised soil carbon, enzyme activity, and overall soil function. Microbes were mainly limited by carbon and nitrogen supply. The authors recommend mixed green manures to cut fertiliser dependence in saline farming.
pmc-13318894:
Arnab Purohit and colleagues present a 2026 study of gut germs in two destructive termite species, Coptotermes formosanus and Reticulitermes flavipes. Forecast microbe roles in carbohydrate use also shifted. The authors propose germ-targeted, greener termite control.
pmc-13320094: Hongyu Wang and co-authors issued a correction in 2026 to their study on finding shoulder labrum tears on MRI scans with a deep learning method. The notice itself is short and is the whole item here. It fixes the methods text, which had named only one scan type. Two fat suppressed scan types were in fact used, one based on proton density and one on T2 weighting. The restated methods also spell out the scan setup and how surgeons confirmed each tear during keyhole surgery.
pmc-13320694:
Seungjoo Lee and co-authors draw engineering lessons from desert horned lizards in a 2026 study. The lizard Phrynosoma platyrhinos gathers water through tiny channels in its skin, but how that water reaches the mouth was a long standing puzzle. The team studied jaw motion and the flow physics behind it.

Slow jaw opening paired with fast closing acts as a capillary pump that moves skin water toward the mouth. Guided by that motion, the team built a system that pulls water from damp soil and, at the same time, removes harmful heavy metals from it. The design needs little energy and suits dry regions where clean water is scarce.
pmc-13321394:
Jian-kui Du and a large team study blast lung injury and a protective protein switch in a 2026 report. Raising TFEB in models eased lung swelling, inflammation, and oxidative harm and kept the barrier intact. A new target of TFEB, the receptor IGF2R, helped control release of two tissue cutting enzymes. A hydrogen sulfide releasing nanozyme switched TFEB on by a sulfur tweak at one site, boosting cell cleanup. The chain offers fresh targets for blast injury care.
pmc-13321794:
Naoyuki Miyashita and colleagues compare two antibiotics for drug resistant lung infection in a 2026 short study from Japan. Macrolide resistant Mycoplasma pneumoniae is rising again in Japan, and minocycline is the advised first choice drug. The team tested whether the quinolone garenoxacin works as well for pneumonia caused by resistant strains.

Fever cleared within 48 hours of starting antibiotics in 90.6 percent of garenoxacin patients and 90 percent of minocycline patients in the study. Those near equal results led the authors to propose garenoxacin as a first choice option as well. A further choice matters for clinics facing resistant infections where standard macrolide drugs no longer work.
pmc-13322194:
Inbal Zigdon and co-authors profile how steroid hormone receptors choose their DNA targets in a 2026 study. Receptors lacking those domains clustered near the AP-1 motif, while full receptors also bound their classic motif far from AP-1 sites. Tests in budding yeast showed the domain can steer targeting even without mammal specific partners. The disordered head thus acts as a guide for genome choice, a lever that might one day tune hormone drug action.
pmc-13322494:
Isadora de Oliveira Lemos, Kelly Cristina Alves Silvério, and Mauriceia Cassol compare two hands-on voice therapies in a 2026 randomised trial. Voice symptoms, pain, breathing measures, and felt muscle tension were scored before and after.

All groups eased vocal symptoms, including fatigue, and muscle pain, and all lengthened maximum phonation time. Electrical treatment alone cut breathiness, manual therapy alone cut overall voice change, and the combined arm cut both overall change and vocal tension. Felt tension on examination also fell most clearly in the combined group.
pmc-13322594:
Sanjeeb Pradhan and co-authors test whether fasting time predicts low blood pressure after spinal anaesthesia in a 2026 observational study. Long fasting before surgery is feared to drain body fluid, yet natural compensation may offset that loss. The vein collapsibility index rose clearly with longer fasting. Fasting length alone separated later pressure drops poorly, while the ultrasound index did moderately well and stood as the only independent predictor in adjusted models. A one percent rise in the index raised the odds of a pressure drop slightly, which favours scanning over clock watching.
pmc-13322794:
Tim Schubert and Robert Weidner study soldier acceptance of a shoulder exoskeleton in a 2026 field study. The device aids overhead work during chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear defence tasks. Lab tests had shown muscle effort cuts of 29 to 41 percent, but field views were unknown. Twenty-seven German soldiers wore it for about 30 minutes of set tasks.

Soldiers rated ease of use at 5.15 and wearing comfort at 4.64 on a seven point scale in the survey. Fit with work routines and usefulness scored in the middle range, while felt mechanical support scored low, at 2.78 in the study. Intent to use was moderate. Stronger support and wider task coverage should lift acceptance.
pmc-13324294:
Liyan Ni and co-authors hunt for a protein that predicts sinus surgery relapse in children, in a 2026 proteomic study of chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. Nasal tissue from a discovery cohort with over a year of follow-up was screened for proteins tied to post-surgery recurrence.

Four candidates emerged from the top differing proteins, and two, SPRR3 and RAB29, ran higher in the recurrence group and sat mainly in the nasal lining. Survival and accuracy analyses supported serum SPRR3 as an early warning marker for relapse.
pmc-13324494:
Hai Zeng and Xinrong Ou present a 2026 case report on antibiotic failure after brain surgery caused by unusually fast kidney clearance. A healthy 51-year-old woman had a right cerebellar meningioma removed and then developed meningitis with no germ grown in culture.

Standard vancomycin doses left blood levels far below the target range even at 18.5 mg per kilogram. Her creatinine looked normal, yet measured clearance reached about 135 mL per minute, confirming augmented renal clearance. Usual screening scores wrongly rated her low risk. Drug level checks guided stronger meropenem dosing and a switch to linezolid, and she recovered fully by day 23 with no relapse.
pmc-13325094:
Ali H. Al-Hajooj and co-authors synthesize paired-metal Schiff base complexes and screen them for medical uses in a 2026 chemistry study. The ligand joins two metal centers, manganese, iron, or cobalt, in one binuclear frame.

Spectroscopy, mass checks, X-ray powder data, and modeling mapped how the ligand grips each metal through oxygen and nitrogen atoms. The compounds killed selected human cancer cell lines in lab screens, and the manganese and cobalt versions cut DNA strongly. The manganese complex also broke down protein fully in gel tests. Cobalt gave the strongest antioxidant action, with an IC50 of 0.0231 micromolar in the reported assay. The manganese form led against bacteria and fungi.
pmc-13327394:
Lakshmi Jogi and co-authors explore future care worries in a 2026 interview study from a large hospital in Bengaluru, India. Most earlier work came from rich countries, so an Indian view was missing.

Sixteen interviews in all, two for each of four men and four women receiving care, were translated and studied for shared themes. Worries centered on finding a trusted guardian, safety, and daily care, shaped by the adult's needs, the parents' health, sibling ties, and local attitudes. Most families had saved money, wanted kin to take over, and planned for housing and work after their own lifetimes.
pmc-13327994:
Yangjun Liu and colleagues test two exercise programs in postmenopausal women with belly obesity in a 2026 quasi-experimental study. One group did high-intensity interval Nordic walking. Its fast bouts ran at 75 to 85 percent of maximum heart rate, with slower recovery between. Another group did strength training, each three times a week for twelve weeks. A control group received lifestyle education only.

Both programs shrank waist size, the walking group by 2.64 cm from its start on the reported change, alongside checks of blood pressure, triglycerides, HDL cholesterol, and fasting glucose. Interval walking with poles offers a joint-friendly way to attack metabolic syndrome markers, and strength work gives a second route for women who prefer it.
pmc-13328194:
Nor Haji Osman and a large team measure use of electronic record data by health managers in Somalia in a 2026 multicenter study. Records systems were rolled out to strengthen routine information, but whether managers actually decide from the data was unknown. Surveys and checklists covered 405 managers across 45 public facilities in late 2025.

Only 145 managers, 35.8 percent of those surveyed, reported adequate use of record data for decisions, most often to check whether clinical guidelines were followed. Organizational, technical, and personal factors were modeled to find what helps or blocks use. Systems alone do not change decisions, the work implies: training, support, and habits must carry the data into the meeting room.
pmc-13330694:
Yangyang Zhang and a large team build a deep learning tool to predict platinum resistance in ovarian cancer in a 2026 study. Abdominal fluid drawn before treatment mirrors the tumour setting, yet its cell shapes were little used for forecasting. The OVCAP system reads whole-slide cell images at many scales.

The study held 438 patients with advanced disease. Accuracy scores stayed strong across one internal and two outside hospital groups, beating a standard clinical score in the reported values. High-risk cell patterns included bubbly cell interiors and crowded malignant clusters with immune cells nearby. Gene data linked those looks to membrane, fat, and stress pathways. Fluid checks could sort risk before first therapy.
pmc-13330994:
Justin C. Cordova, James B. Young, and James S. Huntley present a Poet's Pen piece on very short medical stories in a 2026 article. At its heart sits The Box, a 55-word story by Huntley about the mysteries of the heart. The format began in 1986 and now marks 40 years as a set writing category.

Such stories limit writers to exactly 55 words, mixing prose and poetry freely within that count. The tight frame lends itself to sharp reflections on doctor and patient bonds. Health training programmes and major medical journals have adopted the form. The authors frame it as a compact tool for narrative medicine, helping clinicians notice and act on patient stories.
pmc-13331194:
Maryo Baakliny and colleagues study routine vaccine views among adults in Lebanon after the pandemic in a 2026 case-control study. The survey ran across all regions from July to October 2023. Participants were adults who had caught COVID-19, split into 277 unvaccinated cases and 453 vaccinated controls drawn from national records.

Vaccinated adults were older, more often employed and schooled, and more often health workers in the reported profiles. They scored higher on vaccine knowledge and attitudes and kept up routine and flu shots better after the pandemic, while upkeep fell among unvaccinated adults. Schooling, age, child count, and attitudes each tied to lower odds of non-vaccination in adjusted models.
pmc-13331994:
Hendin and colleagues reported in 2026 how higher versus lower blood pressure targets affect lung circulation after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Lung artery catheters tracked pressures for 48 hours. Seven hundred thirty patients were included.

The higher target raised lung artery pressures and filling pressures. Calculated lung vessel resistance dipped slightly during the first day before the groups converged, because heart output rose proportionally more than pressures. The right side of the heart pumped more strongly under the higher target throughout, with the gap widest at 48 hours. Filling pressure fell in both groups but stayed lower early on with the lower target. The authors show pressure targets reshape lung and right-heart loads in ways standard readings can miss.
pmc-13332494:

Angiography showed a clot-blocked left anterior descending artery in a left-dominant system, treated with a stent. Four days later an ultrasound found the right ventricular clot, and cardiac MRI confirmed it, showing deep damage across the attacked territory including the tips of both ventricles and heavy small-vessel obstruction. Anticoagulation cleared the clot on later imaging, and after episodes of ventricular fibrillation he received a two-chamber defibrillator. The authors credit the wraparound artery anatomy for spreading damage into the right ventricle and stress MRI's value in spotting such complications.
pmc-13332794:
Melina Heine and colleagues examined inflammation-resolving molecules around heart surgery in a 2026 secondary analysis of a prospective study. The cohort held 319 adults who had cardiac surgery at one center, with resolvin D1 and D2 measured across the operative period and modeled against later fibrillation. Patients who developed the rhythm problem showed higher predicted resolvin D1 levels, with a mean ratio of 1.19, and lower resolvin D2 at 0.80. The D1 link ran stronger in women than men, and women also tended toward a deeper D2 drop, though that pattern missed significance. The authors read the split pattern as a sign the two mediators do different jobs, and that resolution biology differs by sex.
pmc-13333294:
