The data are freely posted through the Virginia Tech repository for skill analysis research.
pmc-13333394:
Daniela Averaimo and a team worked through a decade of Italian veterinary forensic archives in a 2026 study, trying to give the field the filing system it lacks. Italy's animal health institutes logged forensic cases with ready-made codes only for wild animal deaths and suspected poisonings, leaving everything else as free-text expert opinion.

The team took records from the Abruzzo and Molise institute between 2013 and 2023. They applied a three-step method: analyze the data, have experts label each opinion by forensic topic, then sort diagnoses into categories. Of 1,221 uncoded cases with an expert opinion, 405, or 33.16 percent, qualified as forensic cases and fell into five categories and 19 subcategories. The leading cause of death differed by animal. Pets died mostly of injury, livestock of attack, and wildlife of unlawful killing. Poisonings and road-killed wildlife were left out since they were pre-classified, so the shares describe this leftover group.
pmc-13333594:
Chi-Chieh Lee and Federico Calegari report a 2026 animal study on whether growing more new neurons in the hippocampus can ease Alzheimer's disease. New neuron growth in this brain region supports memory and mood, but it drops sharply as the disease advances.

Working in the dentate gyrus region of 3xTg-AD mice, the team used a lentivirus to raise the cell cycle proteins Cdk4 and CyclinD1, expanding their neural stem cells. Mice with stronger neurogenesis did better on some behavior tests tied to hippocampal function, including the open-field test and the Morris water maze. The results suggest the damaged niche can still respond to stimulation, pointing to neurogenesis as one part of a future combined treatment.
pmc-13335794:
Nan Meng and co-authors quantified a hidden climate bonus from tree planting in China in a 2026 environmental study. New forests stitch isolated patches together, converting former edge forest into interior forest, and that conversion itself stores carbon.

Using several high-resolution remote sensing datasets, the team estimated biomass gains and albedo losses in transformed forests. Planted forests covered 89.6 million hectares by 2015, about 35.5 percent of China's forest area, and had turned 51.8 million hectares of edge into interior. Those transformed forests gained about 1.4 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent in biomass between roughly 1980 and 2015, though darker canopy warmed the surface enough to offset part of it. Counting both effects clarifies afforestation's true climate ledger.
pmc-13336894:
Yajie Shen leads a large 2026 team that sniffs out respiratory infection by odor in mice. Infected breath carries volatile chemicals, but mixtures are faint and vary between animals. Guided by two marker compounds found in infection, they built a sensor array inside ventilated cages that samples once per second.

Over a 7-day infection cycle the system logged 3,628,800 measurements and caught clear odor shifts between infected and healthy groups. Sensor changes appeared at 7–8 hours after infection, and learning models separated the groups firmly by 9 hours in this mouse model. The best internal accuracy reached 99.88% with support from a blinded check group. Continuous smell monitoring could flag outbreaks far earlier.
pmc-13337094:
Yuan Gao and co-authors starve tumors on two fuels at once in a 2026 therapy study. Tumors switch between glucose and fat burning, the Randle cycle, so blocking one path alone rarely works. Their nanogel carries glucose oxidase, an enzyme that drains glucose, and clings inside tumors for long, deep action.

Adding etomoxir, a fat-burning blocker, imposed dual metabolic suppression and raised harmful oxygen species that killed tumor cells in an immune-visible way. The tumor immune setting reprogrammed toward attack. Adding a PD-1 checkpoint drug then achieved complete tumor regression in 60% of animals with 100% of tumor-bearing mice surviving in the reported experiment. Starvation, oxidation, and immunotherapy form one loop.
pmc-13337394:
Siyao Li and co-authors build an ultrasound radiomics model to predict lymph node spread in diabetic thyroid cancer patients in a 2026 study. Knowing spread before surgery shapes the operation, yet standard checks miss cases. The team gathered 203 confirmed patients from three centers and split them into training and two external validation groups.

Features came from contrast ultrasound timing measures around and inside each tumor. A rim of 2 mm around the tumor beat a 1 mm rim for prediction in all cohorts during testing. The combined model reached AUC values of 0.930 in training and 0.907 and 0.865 in the two validation cohorts in the reported analysis, with good calibration. Such preoperative scoring could tailor surgery for a group juggling two diseases.
pmc-13337694:
Johanna Shriver-Halligan reports a 2026 qualitative study with clinicians who counsel people facing infertility. Infertility often brings stress, anxiety, low mood, and trauma symptoms. Expressive therapies are entering counseling, yet music and imagery work had not been studied with this group.

Five clinicians, four women and one man, took part through purposive sampling. Each joined an online session with a guided music and imagery experience plus interviews. Analysis using in vivo coding and photo methods produced clinical and artistic themes. Clinicians described current symptoms and treatments, and reflected on how the arts method deepened their grasp of what clients live through.
pmc-13339494:
Thomas E. Kraft and a large team set a first human dose for a T-cell engager in blood cancer in a 2026 study. Standard minimal-effect dosing can crawl upward for long before benefit appears. Their ex vivo method used fresh patient marrow to judge the starting dose for forimtamig.

Lab dishes used a myeloma cell line and blood cells, while marrow samples came from myeloma donors. Tumor killing was chosen as the guiding signal. The most sensitive marrow sample pointed to a starting dose of 6 micrograms, adopted for the trial as reported. Activity appeared by the second dose level, supporting patient-based dose setting.
pmc-13339694:
Quanman Hu and a large team study neutrophil self-destruction in viral brain inflammation in a 2026 mouse and patient study. Coxsackievirus A6 can cause neurologic harm in hand, foot, and mouth disease. The caspase and gasdermin pathway that bursts neutrophils and casts DNA nets was the focus.

Ten-day-old normal and gene-deleted mice received a lethal virus dose, with inhibitors and cell removal as added tests. Infection raised neutrophils in brain and blood plus net markers as reported. Blocking the burst pathway or the net enzyme in neutrophils tested cause directly. Blood from patients checked that the same signals appear in human disease.
pmc-13341694:
Vaccine acceptance predicts uptake unevenly across birth regions in Sweden, in a 2026 survey by Mariam Hassan and colleagues. The anonymous cross-sectional questionnaire reached 3,281 people born in Sweden or in Western and non-Western countries, scoring six domains from trust to norms and access.

Acceptance and actual vaccination aligned strongly overall, but the link weakened for non-Western-born respondents. Vaccinated people born in Sweden scored 9.5 points higher on acceptance than unvaccinated peers, versus only 2.8 points among non-Western-born groups. Descriptive norms, what others visibly do, mattered for the Swedish and Western groups. One-size messaging, the data suggest, misses group-specific drivers.
pmc-13343894:
Catherine T. Chaton and co-authors study a wall-cutting enzyme of Enterococcus faecalis in 2026, an opportunistic germ behind hard hospital infections. The enzyme, EpaU, sits in the gene cluster that builds the cell's main surface sugar coat, and the team asked what it grips and what changes when it vanishes.

EpaU's binding end latches onto the intact teichoic acid-like decorations of that sugar coat, while the enzyme itself spreads across the cell surface snipping wall mesh during remodeling. Cells missing EpaU resisted ampicillin more and built up the messenger c-di-AMP, which helps govern internal pressure. The findings tie wall sensing to pressure control and hint at new drug angles based on such enzymes.
pmc-13347394:
Emma Dyhr and co-authors build new antibacterial peptides from the TisB toxin and test them alone and with a standard drug, in a study from 2026. Forty-four variants were trimmed, charged, linked, and scanned to map which parts drive killing, with blood cell harm checked alongside strength against six problem bacteria.

Several hits killed Gram-negative species at levels from 2 to 16 micromolar in the reported tests. While red cell bursting stayed near 20 to 30 percent at a far higher test dose. Gram-positive species needed higher doses, yet the striking gain was pairing, where gentle peptide doses cut the azithromycin needed against three Gram-negative species to useful levels. Toxin systems thus offer fresh antibiotic leads.
pmc-13347794:
Yanti Herawati and colleagues test whether massage aids early baby growth. Their study was issued in 2026. It covers babies aged one to three months. Work ran at a midwife practice. The months were February and March 2023. A total of 75 babies took part. Set rules governed who could join. A standard screening questionnaire scored each baby. Scores came before and after massage. Paired tests compared the two rounds.

Babies classed as developing well rose after massage. The share went from 41.3 percent to 61.3 percent. Mean scores rose too. They moved from 7.65 to 8.75 across the span. The shift cleared the set statistical bar. The authors back gentle massage as an early aid. Parents can learn the method at home. The first year of life is the window.
pmc-13348594:
Min-Gi Kwon and co-authors build a two-target antibody that both wakes a vessel receptor and blocks a growth signal, in a 2026 study. Eye diseases with leaky, overgrown vessels need Tie2 activation plus VEGF blocking, and indirect Tie2 help looked too weak. So a matured activating antibody was fused to five blocker modules and the fusions were ranked in vessel cells.

The lead fusion, MT-103, pairs the activator with receptor domains and was tested in two mouse eye models against a standard blocker and a rival two-target drug. Early cell work showed the activator firing Tie2 paths and matching standard care in one model, supporting direct waking plus blocking as a stronger pair.
pmc-13349394:
Jinchen Pan and colleagues build a theory of referee stress. Their interview study was published in 2026. It covers male student basketball referees in China. Twenty-eight referees gave deep interviews. Coding ran in three passes with software help. No new ideas appeared after the 26th talk. Coding yielded 979 points in total. Those points sorted into 53 first groups. Five main pressure families held them all.

Pressures spanned several sources at once. Personal traits formed one source. Crowd and coach relations formed another. Split-second calls added match pressure. Event mishaps added still more strain. Pressures fed each other in a rising loop. Moderate pressure aided learning, though. Coping leaned on self-calming and peer support. Skill growth helped as well. Stronger backing from organisers is urged.
pmc-13349894:
Kiralina Brito-Arancibia and co-authors examined how heavier job demands affect worker satisfaction in a 2026 occupational study. Modern work keeps speeding up, asking staff to do more tasks faster, with more multitasking and less downtime.

Demand growth has both quantity and quality sides, covering workload, time pressure, decisions, and learning. The authors test whether engagement sits between rising demands and satisfaction, carrying part of the effect. Within the job demands-resources model, heavier demands can either drain workers or, with enough support, spur them. Sorting out that pathway helps employers raise performance without quietly burning out their staff.
pmc-13350194:
Pengcheng Zhu and co-authors reviewed in 2026 how tiny drug carriers might rescue immunotherapy for colorectal cancer. Advanced disease responds poorly to surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation, and checkpoint immunotherapy often fails because the tumour surroundings suppress immune attack.

Nanocarriers such as fat bubbles, polymer particles, and metal particles can ferry drugs into tumours, reshape that suppressive setting, and combine with checkpoint drugs, cell therapies, and vaccines. The review pulls together how each carrier type works, where synergy arises, and what blocks clinical use. Smart delivery that wakes the immune system inside the tumour could widen who benefits from immunotherapy.
pmc-13350494:
Devina Ramesh and co-authors summarised the third annual Transplant AI Symposium, held in Toronto in 2026 by the Ajmera Transplant Center and Mayo Clinic. Clinicians, scientists, and trainees met to take stock of artificial intelligence across organ transplantation.

Talks ranged over organ matching, human and AI teamwork, and predicting survival and risk, including digital twin ideas. Speakers agreed AI helps most when tied to a concrete clinical problem, especially with mixed or time-based data. Worries persisted about data quality, fairness, fitting tools into daily workflow, and keeping clinician oversight. The meeting's message was careful testing before trust.
pmc-13350894:
Yuxuan Lin and colleagues engineered a textured implant material in 2026 that both builds bone and fights gum bacteria. The base is a carbon fibre reinforced plastic used for implants, treated in mixed acids to carve a surface of pores dotted with tiny clusters, best at one acid ratio.

On that surface, bone-forming genes switched on through the Hippo pathway, vessel cells migrated and formed tubes better, bone-eating cells were suppressed, and the gum pathogen P. gingivalis colonised poorly. Rat skull defects confirmed faster bone filling. One surface doing three jobs could cut implant failures from both looseness and infection.
pmc-13351094:
Liancheng Zheng and co-authors reviewed exoskeleton robots in a 2026 mini review, tracing their move from rigid frames toward systems integrated with the body. Wearable robots now serve rehabilitation, mobility help, workplace support, and performance boosting.

The review organises the field by drive systems, control strategies, and human-robot interaction, then by how designs have evolved, what blocks deployment, and where research should head. Papers were picked from major databases for relevance and influence. As devices leave the lab for clinics, factories, and homes, the authors argue design must centre the human wearer rather than machine performance alone.
pmc-13351894:
Serena Malloggi and colleagues test whether a brief re-read before sleep strengthens memory for prose in 2026. Students often skim study material right before bed, but the habit had never been tested. Thirty-four university students studied a short text and recalled it at once, then were split into sleep and wake groups.

Eight hours after study, each student either re-read the text for 1 minute or did not, before an 8-hour gap spent asleep or awake. Sleep and re-reading each helped recall on their own. Only students who re-read and then slept improved over their first recall, while all other groups slipped slightly. A quick bedtime review may give study routines a cheap boost.
pmc-13352394:
Ying Li and Ö Ece Demir-Lira study how parent speech and gesture shape brain synchrony with their child in 2026. Parents guide learning by talking, gesturing, or mixing both, yet the brain side of each style is little known. Parent-child pairs solved a spatial puzzle together while brain activity was recorded from both partners at once with fNIRS hyperscanning.

Mixed speech plus gesture gave the most sustained synchrony, holding high into later stages of the task. Speech alone dipped then recovered strongly late in the task. Gesture alone did not reliably slow the normal fall in synchrony seen without support. Channel checks pointed to links involving the child's right dorsolateral region worth closer study.
pmc-13355194:
Anni Wu and co-authors followed 3,503 older adults in urban China in a 2026 study of how social frailty, mood, thinking, and body frailty move together over time. Data came from a national aging survey run from 2013 to 2018, with three rounds of checks. Social frailty means weak social ties and support, which can harm health in later life.

People with more social frailty tended to have worse mood and weaker thinking, while low mood and body frailty each predicted the other at later rounds. Low mood also came before weaker thinking. The authors urge town health services to watch all four areas together, not in isolation.
pmc-13355394:
Hammad Khan and co-authors followed 220 tuberculosis patients in Peshawar, Pakistan, in 2026 to find who risks liver harm from first-line TB drugs. Liver damage is a major side effect that can derail treatment. Patients on the standard four-drug course had liver and nutrition tests before care and at set points over eight weeks.

About 17 percent developed liver harm, most of it mild. Risk was higher for patients over 45, women, alcohol users, and those with viral hepatitis, with odds roughly doubled or more. Low blood protein markers also raised risk. The authors say these signs can flag patients who need closer liver checks during TB care.
pmc-13356694:
Qi-Shun Wu and co-authors systematically reviewed in 2026 kidney involvement in antisynthetase syndrome, a rare immune disease marked by antibodies against protein-building enzymes. Kidney harm was long thought rare and is poorly mapped. The team searched four databases through January 2026 and kept 38 papers covering 52 patients with proven or defined kidney disease.

Lung disease appeared with or before kidney disease in most cases. Biopsies most often showed a membrane form of kidney filter damage, with other patterns close behind. One antibody class linked to worse kidney peaks and more vessel-type harm. Steroids alone healed about half of mild cases, and a stronger drug helped most stubborn cases.
pmc-13356794:
Huimin Liu and Liqing Li measured in 2026 a new idea in Chinese healthcare, called new quality productive forces, across 31 provinces from 2010 to 2023. The concept blends tech innovation with medical work, reshaping how resources spread. Using weighted scoring and gap and trend tools, they tracked levels, regional gaps, and whether provinces were catching up.

Levels fell at first, then grew steadily to a peak in 2023. The east led and the west trailed, though gaps narrowed over time. Skilled medical labor scored strongest, while medical tools and materials lagged. Provinces showed catch-up patterns but not shrinking spread, so the authors urge region-specific policy and wider digital care.
pmc-13358494:
Michael Mosebetsi Moleka and co-authors report a 2026 study on recovery after keyhole lung surgery. Weak, thin muscles often mean a slower recovery, but the usual muscle checks use belly scans that chest patients may not have. The team tested whether chest muscle size on a normal pre-surgery CT scan can flag risk.

They measured chest muscle at three spine levels in 301 patients and tracked who stayed in hospital more than seven days. A simple measure from scans already on file could help teams plan beds, rehab, and extra support for frail patients. It may also push earlier steps, like food and exercise plans, before surgery.
pmc-13358794:
Yajuan Qian and co-authors study a biopsy technique for chest lymph nodes in a 2026 paper. Doctors pass a needle through the airway wall under ultrasound guidance to sample nodes and judge lung disease. Each needle pass costs time, so knowing what makes a single pass yield enough tissue matters.

They analyzed 636 needle passes into 426 lymph nodes from 219 patients at one center. A scoring system graded how good each sample looked on site. Factors ranged from the needle's path and the operator's experience to node size and stage. The findings can help doctors refine their technique and cut repeat passes.
pmc-13358994:
Derya Yenibertiz and Güzide Tomas grade AI chatbots on a lung disease in a 2026 study. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is a lung disease caused by breathing in substances the immune system reacts to. Patients now often ask chatbots about it first. The team tested how good those answers are for both patients and doctors.

They sent the four most searched patient questions to eight leading chatbots, collecting 32 answers. Four lung professors scored the answers in secret for quality, reliability, readability, and usefulness. Such checks matter because confident, fluent answers can still mislead people facing a complex disease.
pmc-13360094:
Deqing Zhang and co-authors built a 2026 scoring tool to tell two kinds of breast cancer apart before surgery. The tool sorts invasive ductal carcinoma from invasive lobular carcinoma, two types that can call for different care. It uses facts from clinic visits and ultrasound scans. The team drew on records from 803 patients whose cancer type was confirmed by lab tests.

Seven features did most of the sorting work, among them the edge and shape of the lump, its depth, and whether it could be felt by hand. The team turned these into a chart that gives each patient a personal chance of having the lobular type. The chart checked out well in both the group used to build it and a test group. It may help surgeons plan care without extra invasive tests.
pmc-13360694:
Yilin Jiang and co-authors carried out a 2026 genome-wide study of MYB gene switches in maize. These switches control many plant jobs, from flower and pollen growth to seed sprouting and stress defense. Maize knowledge lags behind that for rice and a small model plant, so the team mapped the full maize set. They found 196 MYB switches and grouped them by family ties.

To guess each switch's job, the team matched maize switches to known ones in rice and the model plant. They also read which switches turn on in growing anthers, the pollen-making parts, across several maize lines. That mix pointed to strong candidates for male fertility. Breeders could use the list to improve seed production, since pollen success drives the corn harvest.
pmc-13362394:
Seung Beom Jin and co-authors present a 2026 study on a tool that predicts where a chemical tag called lactylation lands on proteins. The tag affects how cells use energy and switch genes, but finding its sites by lab tests is slow. The team retrained an existing protein model and added a light machine learning layer on top.

They also built the largest checked dataset for this tag so far, with 26,034 samples from nine sources. On blind tests the tool scored about 0.91 for sorting true sites from false ones, matching the best rival tool. Strict checks with no overlap between training and test data held up, so the tool looks fit for real lab use.
pmc-13364394:
Nikolaos Mouziouras and co-workers warn in 2026 that help from a relay station can hurt a multi antenna radio link when the channel facts are off. A relay that reads a weak signal wrong can pass its error on and add noise at the far end. Clean theory hides this flaw.

Their math maps a zone where direct links beat relay help, set by channel doubt and relay slips. A smart switch that mutes weak relays cut error rates in the mid to high signal range. More antennas also made links tougher. The work guides when to trust a relay.
pmc-13364694:
Yasuharu Maeda and co-workers map in 2026 how gut scope scores for ulcer colitis can weigh both how bad and how wide the swell is. Most old scores grade just the worst gut patch, which can miss total load. The team scans two decades of work for scores that add spread, plus new smart scope tools.

Of 21 works kept, most back spread scores: they track lab marks and tissue swell more close than old scores. Smart tools grade spread by code, with fair marks, but proof from new sites is thin. The map shows where scope care should head.
pmc-13369094:
Thalis Asimakopoulos and co-workers pull in 2026 all lot drawn trials of a through skin pulse wave care for long pain. The care sends soft wave pulses with no cut, a draw for folks who shun ops. Their hunt nets eight trials across bone, joint, and nerve pain states.

Pain scores fall in most trials, more clear in sham match ones and at late checks. Act scores rise in step. No grave harms show. Yet trials vary wide in folks, match care, and dose, so the team calls for big, set form trials to fix the care's place.
pmc-13370694:
Vineesh Kappadan and co-workers join in 2026 two fixes for heart light maps of beat hearts: a two hue read and mark free move track. Beat moves blur light maps, so most past work stops the heart, which skews the tale. Their pair reads two hues from one light path and tracks each spot as it moves.

In drug bath rabbit hearts, the joint fix matches tube reads of heart wave spans more close than raw or lone fixes. Share of reads in a tight band jumps from low to most. Live heart maps gain a firm check.
pmc-13372094:
Methavee Poochanasri and co-authors tested a quick body measure for weak muscles in a 2026 study. They worked with 390 older adults who live with type 2 sugar disease. Weak, thin muscles raise the risk of falls and loss of self-care in this group. The measure, called phase angle, comes from a painless body scan.

Low phase angle scores went hand in hand with weak muscles as set by Asian group rules. The scan sorted weak from strong muscles well. Cut points that fit men and women on their own worked best. The team sees the scan as a fast first check, with long-term proof still to come.
pmc-13376794:
Rajiv K Bharti and co-authors scored hand use after wrist nerve surgery in a 2026 study. The nerve pinch in view is the most common of its kind, with numb hands, night pain, and weak grip. A short 11-ask form gives a sound score of arm and hand use.

A total of 35 patients from 2023 to late 2025 were scored before the cut and six months on. Most were women, and most were aged 41 to 60. Score gains log how much daily life came back, in the patient's own words. Such scores let clinics prove gains past the surgeon's own eye.
pmc-13379594:
Sibanda and colleagues explored in 2026 how African Australian young adults see spirituality, religion, and culture shaping their mental health. Fifteen participants aged 18 to 25, with roots in Zimbabwe, Ethiopia, South Sudan, Somalia, and Ghana, shared their experiences in recorded interviews. The study used a method that draws shared meaning out of personal accounts.

Three linked themes emerged: life split between two worlds, healing sought beyond medication, and silence broken. Participants tied distress to migration stress, broken social networks, and clashes between shared cultural duties and personal identity. Faith practices and community networks stood out as strong sources of coping and support. Views of formal services were mixed, since drug-centered care often ignored cultural and spiritual sides of well-being, while care that respected both built trust. The authors urge services to work with, not around, those strengths.
pmc-13383894:
Jianghao Feng and co-authors test whether gut microbes from people with type 2 diabetes can trigger early disease signs in 2026 work. Germ-free mice received pooled microbes from diabetic or healthy human donors, creating two groups watched for ten weeks. Blood sugar handling, insulin, and microbe shifts were tracked over that period.

Mice with diabetic-donor microbes developed worsening glucose tolerance and lower insulin, without sustained high fasting sugar. Their gut communities diverged early and stayed out of balance, with matching shifts in stool and blood chemicals. Two compounds, cholic acid and L-Dopa, fell in both sample types, which the authors link to the early disease pattern.
pmc-13385994:
Stead and colleagues set out a framework in 2026 for the discipline of biomedical informatics, the field that turns health data and knowledge into action. The field is often confused with neighbors such as computer science and biostatistics. The authors trace its rise and sort its work into four domains. These cover how knowledge is found, how it is represented and reasoned with, how it is structured in systems, and how it drives change.

Their central claim is that the field's distinct gift, exposing the structure of biomedical knowledge and making it usable, needs strength in all four domains at once. The field grew by building systems and drawing principles from practice, the authors argue, but must now add hard theoretical work: testing old theories, finding gaps, and coordinating new ones. A precision medicine example shows how the domains combine into abilities no single parent field supplies.
pmc-13389894:
EFSA, the European Food Safety Authority, issues a 2026 scientific report setting safe intake values for trifluoroacetic acid, a breakdown product of concern in food and water. The European Commission asked the authority to revise the acceptable daily intake and the acute reference dose for consumers.

After a targeted call for data in late 2024, a working group weighed the full evidence and judged that the acid and its sodium salt are unlikely to damage genes directly. The group set a daily intake value derived from the available toxicity data. Food safety officials and risk managers across Europe gain updated health-based limits they can apply when judging residues in crops, water, and the wider diet.
pmc-13390294:
Alireza Sadeghpour Teymourlou and colleagues pool, in 2026, evidence on a simple blood ratio as a test for infection around artificial hip and knee joints. Periprosthetic joint infection is a serious failure mode after joint replacement, and a cheap blood clue would aid diagnosis.

Searching PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, the team gathered studies of the platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio and combined their accuracy results. Because studies varied widely, subgroup analyses explored where the ratio performs better or worse. Orthopaedic surgeons gain an updated verdict on this ratio, which comes from a routine blood count. They learn whether it deserves a place beside standard infection markers. They also learn how much weight a single cut-off value can bear.
pmc-13395194:
Leda Sivak and colleagues gather, in 2026, views on video care for country children in Australia with complex needs. Distance and low income block many such families from expert help. A service named Royal Far West offers mental and growth care by screen. The team spoke with eleven carers and twenty-one staff and sorted their answers by theme.

Carers praised the access yet flagged tech faults and hard sessions for some children. Staff valued the reach but noted limits on fine exams and on spotting risk at home. Both groups still called video care a core part of team help. The authors say the lessons will shape service growth and advocacy.
pmc-13396394:
Yuxin Zhou and co-authors published an author correction in 2026 to a Nature Communications study on the genetics of water use and drought resilience in wheat, first issued in September 2025. The study combined several layers of molecular data and singled out a gene, TaMYB7-A1, for its role in how wheat handles dry conditions.

The error sat in Figure 3a, where the side labels for root and shoot samples had been swapped, so counts belonging to roots were printed beside shoots and the reverse. The corrected figure now appears in both the online and PDF versions. Nothing in the correction touches the data or the findings themselves.
pmc-13397394:
Magdalena Gronau examines the scandal that has gathered around physicist Erwin Schrödinger since 2021, and asks what biography itself does to a reputation. Her 2026 paper, written in German, reviews allegations against the Nobel laureate that range from pedophilia to serial sexual abuse.

The debate, she argues, rests on a shaky factual base, with key sources barely accessible and a popular 1989 biography already faulted on release coloring later claims. Gronau works through previously unexamined material, including Schrödinger's diaries, to test what the record supports. Her wider target is the machinery of scandal in science biography: how prejudice and thin sourcing harden into verdicts.
pmc-13398094:
Zainab M Almutairi and Magda Elsayed Abd-Elgawad profile a hardy medicinal shrub across five sites in the Taif region of Saudi Arabia where soil salt levels differ. Their 2026 study of Peganum harmala joins ecology, anatomy, chemistry and genetics in one pass, since links among those layers were poorly known. All soils proved slightly alkaline, with pH between 7.61 and 7.79 as measured across sites, and salt stayed low overall.

Two named sites, Al Ahlam Park and one coded C36, held the least salty ground, while three others ran somewhat saltier. Everywhere, the shrub formed low, spreading domes on sandy, stony soil. Layering soil data against leaf structure, plant chemistry and gene markers shows how one species tunes itself to place.
pmc-13398494:
Essam Arabi and co-authors report a blood-thinner emergency: a chest full of blood in a woman being treated for lung clots. Their 2026 case concerns a 69-year-old who arrived with pleuritic chest pain, a productive cough and growing breathlessness after a fall and a long flight. Scans confirmed pulmonary emboli in segmental branches, and she started therapeutic heparin injections.

On day three she crashed, with sudden low oxygen, left chest pain and a steep haemoglobin drop. Repeat imaging showed a massive left haemothorax (blood filling the chest), a collapsed lung, a shifted mediastinum and hidden right rib fractures from the fall. Doctors stopped and reversed the thinner, transfused blood and drained the chest, balancing clot and bleed in real time.
pmc-13398694:
Reza Kaffash Nayeri and Farshad Banouei report a grim signal of returning bladder cancer: a painful erection that would not subside. Their 2026 case concerns a 59-year-old man, three years past radical removal of bladder and prostate for urothelial carcinoma staged pT3bN0M0. Cancer spread to the penis is rare and carries a bleak outlook, sometimes announcing itself as malignant priapism.

Pelvic MRI showed an infiltrating mass in both proximal corpora cavernosa, and PET imaging lit up several penile lesions with no distant spread found. A core biopsy proved metastatic transitional cell carcinoma, and surgeons performed total penectomy, with chemotherapy advised next. The authors urge vigilance for odd symptoms in bladder cancer survivors.
pmc-13400694:
Franco Moscovicz and colleagues track, in 2026, iron deposits forming in rat brains after a prolonged seizure episode, using a special MRI method. Iron deposits have been found in tissue removed from people with hard-to-treat temporal lobe epilepsy. Iron can fuel a cell death process that may help seizures develop.

Fourteen animals were scanned before the induced episode and at four points over the following three weeks. Deposits appeared in several deep brain regions, including the hippocampus, matching tissue studies, and hippocampal deposits grew over time. Control animals showed none of this. The authors propose that noninvasive iron mapping could become an imaging marker for epilepsy and related disorders.
pmc-13401294:
Khorram-Manesh Amir and Carlström Eric wrote a 2026 analysis comparing two disaster simulation systems, MRMI and the Emergo Train System. They argue that disaster exercises should be treated as system-level interventions. Many exercises, they note, focus on moving casualties through quickly. Success is judged by task completion.

They also drew on past reviews, disaster research, and World Health Organization Emergency Medical Team standards. Side-by-side comparison sorted the design features. The findings were then read through socio-technical systems and resilience engineering lenses. The goal is simulation that reflects disasters as long, disruptive, ethically hard events. It should build learning across the whole organization, not just drill performance.
pmc-13401494:
Luis Velázquez Arenas, Sarahi Garay Enriquez, and Daniela Gómez Guerra report a 2026 case of nevus of Ota treated successfully with a Q-switched ruby laser. The condition is a benign excess of pigment cells in the skin that leaves grey-blue patches on the face, often a real cosmetic burden.

After two sessions she achieved marked clearing of the pigmentation. The authors present the case as further support for the ruby laser as an effective and safe option for this birthmark. Their introduction also notes the pigment can involve the eye and mouth linings, and that affected people face higher risks of glaucoma and uveal melanoma.
pmc-13401594:
Lin-Wen Cheng, Cheng-Ku Yu, Che-Yu Lin, and Shabeh ul Hasson present a 2026 data paper describing fifteen years of minute-by-minute rainfall measurements from Da-Tun Mountain in northern Taiwan. The volcanic massif, about 15 kilometres wide and one kilometre high, sits just inland from the coast and catches heavy rain when tropical cyclones and monsoon winds push moist air against it.

A network of 25 tipping-bucket gauges spread across peaks, slopes, and valleys recorded the rain from 2009 to 2023, and every record passed quality control. Alongside the one-minute data, the authors provide totals aggregated over ten minutes, hours, days, and months. The dense station record serves as a benchmark for studying mountain rainfall processes, characterizing typhoon rain. Correcting radar-based rainfall estimates, among other research and operational uses.
pmc-13401694:
Muna Hassan Warsame and co-authors conducted a 2026 case-control study of severe acute malnutrition in toddlers attending public hospitals in Somalia's Benadir region. Severe malnutrition remains a leading cause of illness and death in Somali children under two.

At two Mogadishu hospitals between February and May 2025, the team enrolled 255 children aged 6 to 23 months: 85 malnourished cases and 170 controls. Large family size roughly doubled the odds of severe malnutrition, and a birth interval under two years roughly quadrupled them. Unprotected water sources more than doubled the odds, while traditional cooking fuel carried the largest association, at over six times the odds. Timing of complementary feeding, whether too early or too late, also differed between groups in the adjusted analysis.
pmc-13402594:
Tao and co-authors develop, in 2026, RenalCLIP, a vision-language foundation model built for kidney cancer, aiming at the overtreatment that follows uncertain scans. Up to 20 percent of removed renal masses prove benign afterward. The model was trained in two stages on 27,866 computed tomography scans from 8,809 patients across multiple centers, aligning image features with the language of radiology reports.

Across ten core clinical tasks, from anatomical assessment to diagnosis and survival prediction, RenalCLIP beat state-of-the-art general foundation models in the reported benchmarks. Its data efficiency stood out: using only 20 percent of the training data, it reached the peak performance that baseline models needed the full set to achieve. The model also showed strong zero-shot detection, image-text retrieval, and report generation. The authors position the system as decision support to sharpen diagnosis, refine prognosis, and personalize management of renal masses before anyone commits to surgery.
pmc-13402794:
Gayeon Kim and colleagues show the plant receptor FERONIA directing new cuticle growth after wounding, which in turn fences in the damage signals that would otherwise sprawl. The cuticle is the waxy first barrier on leaves and stems. When tissue tears, reactive oxygen species spread outward and call in callus growth; what normally stops that spread was unclear.

FERONIA-driven cuticle forming in mesophyll cells beside a wound blocked the reactive oxygen advance, halting disorganized callus beyond the wound edge and switching on orderly cell death right next to the cut. When the cuticle was defective, a NADPH oxidase poured out reactive oxygen without restraint and callus ran wild. The work recasts the cuticle as an active boundary keeper in wound healing, not just a passive skin, with lessons for crop damage repair.
pmc-13403094:
Nataša Joković reviews goniothalamin, a natural compound from Goniothalamus plants, as a selective cancer-killing agent. The compound harms many cancer cell lines while sparing normal cells. Their 2026 review gathers preclinical evidence on its activity, mechanisms, and safety questions across cell and animal studies.

Goniothalamin killed breast, colorectal, liver, leukaemia, and other cancer cells at low micromolar doses, with strength depending on dose and exposure time. It damaged DNA, raised reactive oxygen species, halted the cell cycle, stressed the endoplasmic reticulum, and triggered several cell-death routes including apoptosis. One mirror-image form was stronger in several models, though the other won in some cell lines. It also boosted standard chemotherapy drugs such as paclitaxel and cisplatin. Modified versions improved potency and selectivity, and animal studies showed tumour effects without detectable toxicity, though the authors say absorption and pharmacokinetic studies are still needed.
pmc-13403194:
Hong and co-authors examine, in 2026, whether blue light exposure during sleep tracks with worse blood sugar control and mental health in adults with type 1 diabetes. They use baseline data from 170 participants in a sleep intervention trial. Each person wore a wrist actigraph and a continuous glucose monitor for one week, alongside A1C testing and questionnaires. The group's median age was 37.8 years and 67.6 percent were women in the analyzed sample.

Greater blue light during sleep was associated with less time in the target glucose range of 70 to 180 milligrams per deciliter, with a coefficient of negative 7.30, and more time above range, at 6.95 in their adjusted models. The same exposure tracked with stronger depressive symptoms, coefficient 4.41, and anxiety symptoms, at 2.25, plus worse diabetes quality of life. Light in the hour before sleep related to increased fatigue instead. The authors propose blue nighttime light as a modifiable risk factor worth intervention trials.
pmc-13403594:
Toshihide Takahashi and co-authors tracked a brain tumor in 2026 that grew, then shrank on its own over many years. A 76-year-old woman's back-of-brain mass was found by chance during checks after a head injury. Old scans let the team rebuild about 17 years of change.

Careful slice-by-slice measures showed slow growth first, then a larger phase, then shrinkage without treatment. Calcium deposits inside the tumor grew steadily the whole time. As volume fell, calcium became the main part of the mass. The team reads rising calcium as a sign of tumor aging and wind-down.
pmc-13403694:
Ana Karine Macedo Teixeira and colleagues compared tooth loss in older Brazilians in 2026 across two national surveys, from 2010 and 2023. The samples held 7,619 older adults in the first survey and 9,745 in the second. They sorted results by sex, race, and region to see who gains and who lags.

Having no teeth at all fell from about 53 percent to 36 percent over the span. Working sets of teeth more than doubled as a share. Yet black women still had the worst tooth outcomes, and black men got the least repair care. Use of false teeth among those with few teeth did not improve.
pmc-13403894:
Elin Nyman and co-authors read skin blood flow signals in 2026 to sort people by heart disease risk, with an eye on sex differences. Tiny vessels feed into heart health, yet their role in men and women stays murky. Their data covered 3,177 Swedish adults who wore sensors during a twenty-minute arm squeeze and release test.

A learning model split low-risk from high-risk people with modest accuracy overall. The rebound rush of blood after release carried most of the signal. In men both flow and oxygen measures helped the split. In women oxygen measures did nearly all the work, since flow traces overlapped a lot.
pmc-13404094:
Haibo Yu, Ting Shi, and Hong-Hu Zhu summed up 2025 meeting news in 2026 on three-drug plans for a fast blood cancer in frail adults. A two-drug base of venetoclax plus a hypomethylating agent is now standard for newly diagnosed patients unfit for harsh therapy. Gains from that base still fade at uneven rates.

New triplets add a targeted third drug to the base. One followed study paired a FLT3 blocker with the base in gene-marked disease. Median survival there reached near 29.7 months with long follow-up. Other triplets add menin blockers or fresh agents. Deeper, longer remissions are the goal.
pmc-13404194:
Pritish Raj Shukla and colleagues tested in 2026 whether a soil bacterium can chew through ground waste tire rubber. Vulcanized rubber resists decay thanks to sulfur crosslinks and harsh additives. The team fed two grind sizes of tire rubber to the bacterium for 28 days in a mineral bath.

Fine particles fed growth far better than coarse chunks, with weight loss near 5.8 percent at best. Treated rubber showed surface oxidation, less sulfur and zinc, and looser crosslinks. Breaks fell at random along the main chains, based on their checks. Nearby dump soils held a whole community of kin germs, hinting at team-based cleanup.
pmc-13405094:
The PLOS One editors retract a 2026 article that claimed to detect autism from resting-state brain scans with deep learning. Concerns followed publication about compliance with the journal's authorship policy. The article also closely matched an earlier study it never cited, with near-identical results in two tables despite reporting different brain atlases and methods.

The fourth author accepted the earlier study should have been cited and said the datasets were mislabelled in the tables. Data files supplied could not settle the matter, editors state, and three cited references had themselves been retracted during review. Five authors disagreed with retraction, while others did not respond or could not be reached. The notice removes the article over reliability and policy concerns.
pmc-13406294:
Katja Nowak and colleagues grow human heart surface cells in the lab and watch them change identity, in a 2026 study. The epicardium, the heart's outer layer, helps repair injury, but adult human cells for study were scarce. The team built an immortalised line from cells taken from the heart's auricle.

Blocking TGF-beta signalling kept the cells sheet-like, with strong epithelial markers including WT1 and CRIP1. Adding TGF-beta3 flipped them to a spindle shape with mesenchymal markers, faster movement and remodelling genes. Gene profiling separated the two states cleanly. The paired states give researchers a switchable model of epicardial activation.
pmc-13407794:
Sabri Soussi and Michelle S. Chew review, in 2026, the heart failure that sepsis can trigger, a dysfunction that helps drive circulatory collapse yet still lacks an agreed definition. Sepsis-induced myocardial dysfunction varies in presentation, timing, and reversibility, which frustrates standard criteria and cross-study comparison, so the authors organise newer thinking around subtypes.

The classic definition uses a reversible drop in the heart's pumping fraction. Critics note that the fraction depends heavily on loading conditions. It may not reflect true muscle strength during sepsis. Reversibility is also rarely documented. Most patients are scanned once, early on. Contemporary assessment adds the right ventricle, relaxation function, deformation imaging, and heart-artery coupling. Heart injury markers rise often but explain little alone. Precision critical care, matching treatment to the patient's particular subtype, is the destination proposed.
pmc-13407894:
Qi Jin and co-authors report, in 2026, coaxing carbon dioxide into multi-carbon products even in strongly acidic baths. CO2 conversion in acid usually loses out to hydrogen bubbling. It also rarely links carbons together. The team built a dual-function interface. Copper oxide nanosheets pair with an anchored cobalt porphyrin molecule there. The molecule manages protons and the water structure around them.

The hybrid catalyst channelled protons toward carbon-carbon bond formation instead of wasteful hydrogen release. It reached a multi-carbon efficiency of up to 89.5 percent at current densities above one amp per square centimetre in electrolyte at pH 2, and kept high selectivity even at pH 0.7. Live spectroscopy and calculations showed regulated proton activation building the key coupling intermediates while stabilising the interface.
pmc-13408094:
Yaodong Wu and co-authors create, in 2026, bags of magnetic whirlpools using electric current alone. Skyrmion bags are vortex-like spin textures holding several skyrmions with adjustable topological charge, prized for future computing. They had only been made with magnetic fields. The team therefore drove an iron-germanium nanoplate with nanosecond current pulses and filmed the result live under an electron microscope.

Starting from a warped helical state at zero magnetic field, pulses fractured the pattern, through spin-transfer torque according to theory, into embedded skyrmion bags of varied configurations. Further pulses flipped bags between different charges, stabilising complex three-dimensional patterns with signatures of magnetic monopoles and bobbers. All-electrical control of high-charge spin patterns, a prerequisite for real spintronic devices, is the claim.
pmc-13408594:
Vaida Verhoef, Emma Visser, Karin Smolders, Niki Antypa, and Yvonne de Kort describe in 2026 how new parents actually sleep and meet light across ordinary days at home. Earlier research leaned heavily on mothers, the first weeks after birth, and brief snapshots. The SUNSHINE project instead followed mothers and fathers of infants aged three to nine months for two full weeks.

Wrist sensors and light meters, backed by sleep diaries, showed total sleep that was generally adequate but badly broken, with frequent awakenings and wide variation between nights and between parents. Waking hours were mostly spent in dim light, and brief light exposures during sleep were common. Season, where the baby slept, and who did the night care all seemed to shape the patterns. The authors argue for profiling families before designing circadian-friendly help.
pmc-13409094:
Michael Ekholuenetale and colleagues analyse a nationally representative survey of more than thirty-six thousand Nigerian women in 2026 to learn who received COVID-19 vaccine doses and who was left at zero. The data come from the 2024 Demographic and Health Survey and cover women aged fifteen to forty-nine. Multilevel models separated personal characteristics from community influences.

The headline is stark: nearly three quarters reported no dose at all, and only about one woman in fifty had received more than two. Older age, schooling, health insurance, employment, media exposure, household wealth, and living in a community already willing to vaccinate each raised the odds of a higher dose count. Religious affiliation, marital history, and region mattered too. The authors argue that closing the gap means community-level trust work, not just individual messaging.
pmc-13409294:
Milou Reuvers and colleagues survey in 2026 one hundred fifty-five cancer patients diagnosed between eighteen and thirty-nine whose prognosis is uncertain or poor. Young adults in that limbo carry heavy psychosocial burdens at a life stage meant for building careers and families. Earlier interview work had suggested two coping directions, throwing oneself into life or dwelling on early death, and the team tested whether the split survives in numbers.

Clustering algorithms found patterns, but they separated patients mainly by how much total burden they carried rather than by two cleanly different coping styles. Those with lower burden also reported fewer unmet needs for social support. The authors draw a practical moral: screening routinely for distress and social strain, and aiming help at whoever scores high, beats sorting patients into predefined coping types. Larger, longer studies are needed to confirm the pattern.
pmc-13410694:
Lars Erik Almquist and colleagues study in 2026 how hospital staff who help violently injured patients actually do their work. These violence prevention professionals support recovery and try to stop further harm. Their day-to-day tactics were poorly recorded, and nobody knew which ones travel between workers.

Interviews with 23 professionals were sorted around ten key moments in a patient's recovery path. Cataloging the answers produced 214 distinct tactics. The richest sets covered first meetings with patients, building trust, and guiding people to services. Far fewer tactics dealt with keeping patients engaged or with care after program exit. Sharing the catalog should strengthen training and give new programs a ready toolkit.
pmc-13411794:
Tan and colleagues interview Australians who have lived with spinal cord injury for decades, asking what ageing feels like when a body works around paralysis. Survival after injury has risen, but aged care and disability rarely meet. Their 2026 study holds twenty five interviews: twenty two with people injured before age sixty five and over fifty, plus three carers. Transcripts are read for themes, with a lived experience panel guiding the work.

Three themes carried the title's arc from Superman to barely can. First, compounding vulnerability: ageing felt accelerated, with new losses stacking on old ones. Second, biology met policy gaps, as service rules and staff lacking injury specific knowledge turned decline into crisis. Third, meaning through participation: work, leisure, and self advocacy kept life full where funding and know how allowed. The authors argue ageing well with injury is as much a policy question as a medical one.
pmc-13413494:
Kota Kambara and colleagues sequence in 2026 the genomes of two fungi that wake the seeds of a rare Japanese lady's-slipper orchid. Orchids cannot sprout without a fungal partner feeding them, yet fungal genomes from this partnership stayed scarce. Both isolates came from Cypripedium macranthos var. rebunense and were proven able to trigger germination before their DNA was read and assembled.

Each assembly scored over 95 percent completeness on a standard gene check, signalling high-quality drafts. Family trees placed both fungi in Group IV, an early-branching lineage far from other Tulasnella groups with known genomes. That group carries a distinctive kit of carbohydrate-cutting enzymes and small secreted proteins, which the authors suspect helps it settle into partnership with Cypripedium roots.
pmc-13414394:
Su Jung Park and co-authors film swallowing in 2026 to compare how COVID-19 pneumonia and ordinary aspiration pneumonia each break the act. Past comparisons leaned on rough rating scales, so this team measured residue and throat mechanics frame by frame. Fifty inpatients, twenty-five per disease, swallowed a standardized spoonful of yogurt paste during videofluoroscopy while blinded analysts quantified what lingered and how the throat moved.

COVID-19 patients left more residue pooled above the throat entrance, with a normalized score of 0.20 against 0.13 for aspiration patients. Their upper esophageal opening stretched less wide and the epiglottis folded less far in the measured swallows. Airway invasion scores, by contrast, did not differ significantly. The authors name this an efficiency problem that safety scales alone would miss.
pmc-13414594:
Elena Teona Cosovanu and colleagues report a single newborn case of early listeriosis in 2026. A preterm girl born at 34 weeks arrived at intensive care at 30 hours old with breathing failure. Listeria monocytogenes grew from her blood, stomach fluid, throat, eye, and skin samples.

A gradient strip test suggested the strain resisted ampicillin, a result the authors treat with caution because the confirmatory dilution test was unavailable. Clinicians adjusted her antibiotic mix on day five, and a day nine blood culture stayed sterile. She spent 25 days in intensive care, with low platelets and a small brain bleed among the complications.
pmc-13415794:
Liu and co-authors present, in 2026, UCTLFANet, a neural network for segmenting microalgae in microscope images, segmenting meaning outlining each cell. It supports species analysis, cell counting, and health assessment in marine research. Its novelty is a fine-tuning module from large language model practice: LoRA-FA adjusts the network's weights through low-rank updates instead of retraining everything, slashing compute.

The authors inserted the module into different layer types and found the fully connected layers gave the best segmentation outcomes. Head to head, their model outperformed UNet, UNet++, Attention-UNet, and UCTransNet on their microalgae benchmarks, and bolting the module onto those rival networks improved each of them too, though none caught up. The low-rank approach cuts trainable parameters by 3.6 times in method comparisons, which the authors argue makes the tool practical for marine microbial imaging, where labeled data and hardware are both limited.
pmc-13417494:
Javanshir Isayev and colleagues document traditional medicinal uses of lady's mantle plants in Azerbaijan, in a 2026 field study. Surveys ran across five mountain regions during 2024 and 2025, with interviews and questionnaires from 125 informants. Twenty one Alchemilla species from the rose family were recorded in local practice.

Uses centred on digestive, liver and bile, breathing, and skin problems, plus diabetes care. Agreement among informants was strongest for fever use, while digestive uses drew the most reports overall. Four species scored highest on use and citation measures. Those species are flagged as prime candidates for chemical and drug effect studies.
pmc-13418094:
Hooi Swang Cheng and colleagues survey booster vaccine preferences in Singapore with a choice experiment, published in 2026. An online panel of 1,567 people weighed hypothetical boosters differing in effectiveness, protection length, and cost, against infection risks. A mixed model turned choices into willingness to pay figures and linked acceptance to personal traits.

Longer protection was valued most under high infection and death risk. People would pay modest sums for each extra point of effectiveness and month of protection. Younger adults, women, and people with chronic conditions leaned toward accepting boosters. Prior infection, lower schooling, and higher risk tolerance leaned the other way.
pmc-13421094:
Brändel and colleagues report a 2026 field study of astrovirus infection and gut microbes in a common fruit bat of Central America. Astroviruses can cause severe gut illness in people, yet bats carry them with no clear sickness. The team sampled 234 Seba's short-tailed bats in Panama, in old forest and in farmland forest patches, and profiled their gut microbes.

Infection was more common in the farmland patches than in old-growth forest. Infected bats kept the same count of microbe kinds, but the mix shifted. Helpful bacteria such as Lactococcus dropped, while Helicobacter, a group that includes gut pathogens, rose, and two of its types matched bird-linked forms. Even a symptom-free virus can reshape a bat's gut community, which matters for bat health as farms press into forests.
pmc-13421494:
Yeonjun Sung, Donghyun Jeon and Changsoo Kim present, in a 2026 data paper, the chromosome-scale genome of anise hyssop, an aromatic herb valued in medicine, cooking and gardens. The plant belongs to the mint family and produces a rich chemistry of scent compounds, which a genome sequence can help unravel.

Annotation found 28,193 protein-coding genes, and completeness checks against standard plant gene sets scored high. Leaf RNA data supported the annotation. The authors offer the genome as a foundation for comparative work across the genus and the wider mint family.
pmc-13421594:
Murdhy A. Aldawsari, Saad Jamhan Aldosari, Atef Ismail and Marwa M. Emam introduce DEViTNeXt in a 2026 paper, a hybrid system for classifying mammograms. Their design runs a ConvNeXt branch for local features beside a vision transformer branch for global structure. A fusion layer, tuned by differential evolution, refines attention in both branches. That tuning method borrows its search from evolutionary computation. Prep work sharpens the images, and synthetic malignant cases generated by a GAN help balance the classes. The authors present the framework as a practical answer to mammography's data constraints.
pmc-13421794:
Nichols and co-authors map in 2026 how living in rural Nebraska affects access to durable medical equipment after hospital discharge. Such equipment means the home machines and supplies needed by patients with a tracheostomy, a breathing opening in the neck, or a ventilator.

Only about one in five locations supported invasive ventilation, and fewer than one in five of those stood in rural areas. Tracheostomy support reached about half of locations. Average service areas stretched past 100 kilometers for the most complex care. The authors warn that some patients live more than an hour and a half from a capable supplier. They urge discharge planners to confirm that a nearby company actually stocks the specialized supplies a patient needs.
pmc-13422294:
Gemeda and co-authors recount a near-fatal airway emergency in this 2026 case report from a resource-limited hospital. A healthy 34-year-old man had pulled his lower molar out with a nail. A week later he arrived with Ludwig's angina, a fast-spreading infection of the floor of the mouth. He also had three days of neck swelling and drooling. His oxygen saturation was only 78 percent on room air.

His jaw was locked and standard intubation failed, while a surgical airway through the front of the neck proved anatomically impossible through the swelling. A laryngeal mask airway, a device that sits over the voice box, kept him ventilated as a bridge until surgeons performed a tracheostomy. He suffered septic shock and a cardiac arrest reversed by one round of CPR and a 200-joule shock. Imaging confirmed Lemierre's syndrome, a septic clot in his jugular vein, complicating the infection.
pmc-13423294:
Alain Kuaban, Jurgen Noeske, and Christopher Kuaban examine, in French, drug resistance patterns among patients with rifampicin-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis in Yaoundé, Cameroon. It was most often resistance to isoniazid, at the same share, then ethambutol at about 42%. Fluoroquinolone resistance stayed low at about 3%. Most profiles involved one or two drugs, supporting full testing before treatment.
pmc-13424794:
Chojak and colleagues pool in 2026 where glioblastoma, the most aggressive common brain tumor, comes back after first-line radiation with temozolomide chemotherapy. Knowing whether relapse strikes inside or outside the treated field decides who might qualify for focused salvage treatment.

Distant growth outside the field appeared in about one sixth, with wide variation between studies. After salvage therapy, in-field growth still dominated at about three fifths of cases. A pattern of escape beyond purely local failure was estimated at just under two fifths in the salvage setting. Growth that does not light up on scans was reported so rarely and selectively that the authors treat those numbers as exploratory only.
pmc-13425094:
Earnshaw and colleagues prospectively evaluated an artificial intelligence system, DERM, during its first three months inside a National Health Service urgent skin cancer referral pathway in North West England. They compared the algorithm's verdicts with face-to-face dermatologist diagnoses and with the final tissue diagnosis after biopsy.

Its positive predictive value was lower, however, at 46.5 percent against 62.1 percent for dermatologists judging the same lesions. Across 318 assessments that had no remote human review, the algorithm named the exact diagnosis only 28.6 percent of the time, versus 61.6 percent for dermatologists. Four cancers were found among lesions the AI had classed as benign, prompting caution about removing human review.
pmc-13426394:
Pati and colleagues reported in 2026 on a graphene oxide delivery system that carries neuropeptide Y, a small signalling molecule in the brain, to specific nerve pathways. In a rat model of anxiety, injecting the complex into the amygdala weakened responses tied to context-based fear memory. The effect stayed selective for the target pathways. The authors present the platform as a base for combined delivery tools that keep synaptic precision when treating specific brain conditions.
pmc-13426494:
Na Liu, Wen Wang, and Yuanyuan Wang prioritized nursing improvements for chronic disease outpatients in a 2026 cross-sectional survey of 490 patients at a tertiary hospital. Kano classifications, satisfaction coefficients, and a combined improvement index fed a priority matrix and sensitivity model, with subgroup checks by specialty. Managers receive a ranked improvement list grounded in patient judgment rather than staff assumption. A ranked list keeps scarce funds and staff time from spread too thin, and puts the worst gaps at the head of the queue for work.
pmc-13427194:
Cole J. Wagner and Guangbin Dong report a transition-metal-free method for inserting heteroarenes into carbon-carbon bonds of benzocyclobutenones in a 2026 synthetic chemistry article. Metal-free carbon bond activation widens green options for medicinal chemistry synthesis. The rings that form can be built up step by step, and the parts that come out can be reshaped for new uses in drugs and in crop care.
pmc-13427294:
M. Bindu Malini and colleagues studied eye surface damage and microbes in ventilated intensive care patients in a 2026 prospective hospital study. Their mean age was about 52 years, sepsis was the commonest admission cause at 28 percent, and conjunctival swabs were cultured on days three and seven. Exposure keratopathy, corneal damage from incomplete eyelid closure, appeared in 32 percent of patients.

Organisms differed by damage grade, with Staphylococcus haemolyticus commonest in grade 1, Acinetobacter baumannii in grade 2, and Pseudomonas among higher grades in the findings. Eyes left dry and bare for days on a ward can scar for life, so a short check each day is a small price for sight kept safe.
pmc-13427494:

A random effects model combined reactivation and infection risks across studies for each immune category. Clinicians switching regimens gain quantified risk estimates to plan monitoring and vaccination. Pills that drop one virus but not its twin can let the twin wake and flare, so a swap of drugs must be made with both germs in mind at once.
pmc-13427994:
Santiago Valbuena and colleagues investigate, in a 2026 study, why one brand of neck fusion cage sank into bone more often than expected. Records covered 70 patients treated between 2018 and 2023, with X-ray follow-up near 29 months on average.

Sinking of at least 3 millimeters showed in about 39 percent of patients, a high rate. Statistical modeling found one clear predictor: patients whose main problem before surgery was arm pain from a pinched nerve faced about three and a half times the odds. pmc-13430194:
