In the first case, despite a reassuring balloon test, the larger valve was implanted and expanded poorly at its middle even after further inflation. In the second, the same test pointed the team to the smaller valve, which expanded fully with no rupture or leak. The editorial endorses the balloon observation as a simple tie-breaker algorithm when scans leave sizing genuinely ambiguous.
pmc-13531794:
Haniyeh Khalafinejad and colleagues ask in 2026 whether eating quality tracks with sleep in older Iranians. Baseline data from a Neyshabur aging cohort covered 2,026 adults aged 60 and over. A food questionnaire fed a healthy eating score, while a standard index graded sleep quality and length.

Women reported worse and shorter sleep than men. Across all participants, eating score showed no firm link with either sleep quality or sleep length after adjustment. Among women alone, the highest eating group hinted at less short sleep, just short of statistical confidence. The authors suggest other health factors may dominate the diet-sleep tie.
pmc-13531894:
Albert Roberts, Solon Fountzopoulos, and Terun Desai review in 2026 trial evidence on oral cannabidiol for blood pressure in adults. Four databases were searched in September 2024 for randomized trials in people with normal or high pressure. Wide differences in dose and reporting blocked pooled math, so results were summarized in words.

Only four trials with 120 people qualified. Every trial found lower systolic pressure than placebo, strongest at the highest daily dose and under stress or during sleep. Two trials also found lower diastolic pressure. Side effects stayed mild to moderate, yet tiny samples and short runs demand larger trials.
pmc-13534194:
Urszula Nowacka and colleagues run in 2026 a pilot trial of home heart tracing for pregnancies with late-onset fetal growth restriction. Babies growing too slowly late in pregnancy need close checks, which often means frequent hospital visits. In Warsaw, 120 women were split between home tracing with safety scans and standard hospital checks.

Newborn condition at birth was alike in both groups, with no rise in poor outcomes. The home group had fewer emergency caesarean births, lower anxiety at delivery, and fewer clinic visits. The authors call the results early signals, not proof of full clinical benefit.
pmc-13534494:
Dajane Kana Darkushe develops in 2026 strategies for sustainable stormwater control in Dambi Dollo Town in Ethiopia. Flooding grows when runoff overwhelms drains, a common problem in fast-growing towns. Field checks, surveys, interviews with officials and residents, and policy review mapped current practice.

Current practice proved largely reactive, with weak drains, few green spaces, no stormwater-specific policy, and low public awareness. Proposed plans stress green infrastructure, actions at plot to catchment scales, and strong stakeholder roles. Readers in resource-limited towns gain a practical frame for safer, greener water control.
pmc-13536594:
Rong Sun and colleagues weigh in 2026 how much weather factors and air pollution each add to childhood allergic disease in Chongqing, China. Their relative roles were poorly known in subtropical climate settings. Records held over 1.5 million child hospital visits from 2014 to 2019 and 2023 to 2024.

Heat showed the strongest links, raising nose allergy and asthma visits while cutting eczema visits. Single air pollutants mattered far less than heat in the models used. Seasonal peaks differed by disease, so the authors urge season-aware prevention that pairs climate adaptation with clean-air work.
pmc-13538394:
Wei Shi, Qiang Zhou, and Yan Song examine social connectedness and climate doubt in China in a 2026 survey study using national social survey data. Doubt weakens public action on climate change, yet Chinese patterns differ from Western accounts. Learning models ranked correlates of doubt, while mediation models traced middle pathways through worldview, risk awareness, and policy views. Regional differences were also mapped.

Stronger social ties tracked with lower climate doubt overall, though the link varied by tie type. Human-centered beliefs, risk awareness, and policy views each carried part of the association, with pathways differing by doubt type. Regional variation ran large, warning against one-size advice. The authors present connectedness as a subtle lever for resilience that must be tuned to local context.
pmc-13538694:
Zhengyi Yu and colleagues track asphalt damage under combined sunlight aging and freeze-thaw cycling in a 2026 materials study. Half-round bending tests measured air voids, bending strength, stiffness, failure movement, and fracture energy in aged and unaged specimens across rising cycle counts. A damage index and correlation analysis ranked which measures best capture the coupled harm.

More cycles raised air voids while strength and fracture energy slid steadily. Sunlight-aged specimens fared worse than freeze-thaw-only peers at equal cycles, though aging also stiffened the mix somewhat. Bending strength proved the most sensitive damage signal, followed by fracture energy and air voids. The authors recommend strength and early fracture energy as key gauges for pavement in harsh climates.
pmc-13539894:
Achmad Syawqie and three colleagues present a 2026 scoping review of sensor devices that might catch oral cancer early from saliva, without cutting tissue. Early detection matters because mouth cancers are often found late, when treatment works less well.

Searching five databases for work published between 2019 and 2025 left nine original studies to chart. Most devices read electrical or light signals, or used tiny transistors, aiming at markers such as interleukin-8 and a cytokeratin fragment. Several reached extremely low detection limits in the laboratory. Reporting of testing time, sample size, and accuracy against real diagnoses varied widely, so the authors ask for standard validation and larger clinical studies.
pmc-13540294:
Sarah Abdel-Gawad leads a 2026 dental materials study asking whether newer all-in-one bonding glues for fillings actually beat the versions they replaced. Manufacturers update universal adhesives often, and claims of progress deserve checking after the bond has aged.

One hundred eighty human molars were bonded with three updated adhesives, their predecessors, or a multistep reference glue, then stored in water for six months. Two updated products merely matched their older versions, and one performed worse than its predecessor. Microscope images showed interface patterns and film thickness varying by application method. The authors conclude that commercial updates do not reliably improve dentine bonding.
pmc-13541894:
M Bosch-Ramírez and seven colleagues follow, in a 2026 prospective study, older adults treated for faecal incontinence with gentle electrical stimulation of a nerve at the ankle. The condition affects up to half of institutionalised older people, yet treatment evidence in this age group is thin.

Sixty-one community-dwelling patients, median age seventy-one and mostly women, received stimulation in phases over twelve months with checks out to three years. About two thirds were strong responders by the end, and most kept their gains at thirty-six months. Severity scores fell sharply, while quality of life improved only in the depression domain. Older age itself predicted response.
pmc-13542194:
Xiangyu Gao and four colleagues explore, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, whether blood phosphorus levels track with muscle mass in people with type 2 diabetes, a group prone to early muscle loss. Just over a thousand inpatients had muscle measured by dual-energy X-ray scans.

Low muscle mass affected about a fifth of men and a smaller share of women. Higher phosphorus was linked with lower odds of low muscle mass in both sexes after extensive adjustment. The relationship with the muscle index rose only up to a threshold near one millimole per litre, then flattened, with slightly different cut points for men and women. Longitudinal validation is requested by the authors.
pmc-13542494:
Huang and colleagues report a new disease-causing variant in acrogeria, an extremely rare premature-ageing skin disorder first described in 1940, and review how LMNA gene variants map onto its family of diseases. Acrogeria thins the skin and fat of the hands and feet and ages patients far beyond their years. Their 2026 case concerns a 32-year-old man whose mottled pigmentation had spread since childhood. Genetic testing found a previously unreported change in LMNA, the gene that builds the nuclear scaffolding proteins lamin A and C.

The variant, a single letter swap altering amino acid 591, joins the catalogue of acrogeria mutations, and the authors note possible accompanying heart abnormalities worth watching in this patient. Their literature review sorts genotype-phenotype patterns across the laminopathies, the family including Hutchinson-Gilford progeria and muscular dystrophies, where the same gene produces wildly different diseases depending on where the change lands.
pmc-13543494:
Qianting Deng, Chongyun Wu, and Luodan Yang reviewed classroom physical activity breaks in 2026 for university students. Long sitting through lectures dulls thinking, and breaks are well studied in schoolchildren but barely in adults at university. The team searched major databases to May 2025, screened thousands of records, and kept twenty studies on engagement, academic emotions, attention, or grades.

Breaks were steadily tied to better sustained attention, stronger emotional engagement, and more upbeat academic emotions. Evidence for selective attention, social engagement, and relief of negative emotions was mixed, and grade effects stayed unsettled, with one study even finding a small negative effect on selective attention. Since breaks do not eat teaching time, the authors judge them a viable, low-cost tactic, while stressing that the university evidence base remains thin beside schools.
pmc-13543694:
Danielle Amaral e Silva's team compared cocoa in 2026 from two Brazilian Amazon ecosystems: seasonally flooded floodplains, a long-used growing setting, and plain uplands. Beans from both systems were checked for shape, chemistry, stimulant compounds, and antioxidant levels, and chocolates made from each were put to consumer tasting.

Floodplain fruits were oval with thick husks and smaller beans. Their beans carried more fibre and far more total polyphenols, but less protein and lower antioxidant capacity than upland beans. They also held more caffeine and theophylline, with a stimulant ratio like fine Criollo cocoa. Both bean lots fermented well, and tasters liked the two chocolates about equally, each with fine-flavour notes. Distinct chemistry with equal appeal, the authors argue, supports selling floodplain cocoa as a regional specialty rather than a lesser grade.
pmc-13544094:
Combes and colleagues ask what shapes the gut microbes of young broiler chicks: the place where they hatch, or early contact with an adult hen. Their 2026 poultry study compared chicks hatched on the farm with chicks hatched in a conventional hatchery, with each group raised either with or without a hen for the first 15 days. A fifth group received antibiotics instead, and all birds later faced transport, temperature swings, crowding, and vaccination.

At 20 days of age, hen contact clearly drove development of the cecal microbiota, the microbes living in a gut pouch, raising levels of Bacteroides, Parabacteroides, and several other bacterial groups. The hatching system by itself changed nothing, although it strengthened the hen effect. Antibiotic chicks fared worst, losing diversity as Escherichia-Shigella took over, alongside higher inflammatory gene activity in gut tissue. By 56 days most early microbial differences had faded.
pmc-13546594:
Lingran Zhao and co-authors reviewed in 2026 the two-way relationship between long-term psychological stress and stomach cancer. Anxiety and depression are common in people with this cancer, and the review asks whether stress also helps the disease progress, not just the other way around. Searches of major databases gathered clinical, population, and laboratory studies focused on stomach cancer specifically.

The findings point both ways: cancer acts as a lasting stressor, while chronic stress may feed tumor growth through hormone systems, inflammation, weakened immune control, and changes in gut microbes. The authors judge the link clinically meaningful but not yet proven causal. They call for prospective studies and trials that build stress care into cancer treatment.
pmc-13547194:
Lijeong Hong and Min-Shik Kim tested in 2026 whether people unconsciously learn social patterns the way they learn repeated layouts when searching a scene. In three experiments, volunteers searched for a target face among other faces while the spatial layout was shuffled every trial, removing the usual cue. What stayed consistent instead were social features: which faces appeared together, the overall mood of the crowd, or which way pairs of faces turned.

Search ran faster when the social pattern stayed consistent than when it changed, even though participants barely knew the patterns existed. The crowd mood cue worked strongest of the three. The authors conclude that the mind quietly picks up social structure and uses it to guide attention, much as it uses physical layout.
pmc-13547394:
Sujata Singh and co-authors simulated in 2026 a two-layer solar cell that stacks a lead-free perovskite on top of silicon to catch more of the spectrum than either material manages alone. The top layer uses a cesium germanium iodide perovskite, avoiding toxic lead, sandwiched between charge-selective layers of zinc oxide and copper oxide. The team swept thickness, doping, defect levels, and band gap in software to hunt for the best combination.

The optimized stack reached a simulated efficiency above 37 percent, past the ceiling for a single-layer cell, with strong current and voltage figures. Because the work is entirely computational, the numbers describe what the design could deliver if fabrication matches the model. The authors frame it as a route to higher output with a smaller carbon footprint.
pmc-13547894:
Ta and colleagues review in 2026 a side effect of intravenous iron that doctors increasingly recognize: hypophosphataemia, a drop in blood phosphate that can weaken muscles and soften bone. Iron infusions transformed iron deficiency care, and some formulations trigger this drop often.

Reported rates reach above nine in ten patients for the highest-risk formulations, though most cases are mild and pass quickly. In vulnerable patients the drop can be deep and symptomatic, causing lethargy, weakness, and muscle pain. Rarely it brings heart rhythm problems or bone disease, sometimes needing hospital care and phosphate replacement. The review illustrates the range with five cases and offers a management pathway. Spot high-risk patients early, choose lower-risk iron formulations for prevention, and correct phosphate together with the other minerals the condition disturbs.
pmc-13548494:

The new approach adds annotation from the EggNOG database to the domain data, building a mixed feature set for each genome.

Every one of the top fifty features was already a known movement-related gene or domain, and most of the top hundred had experimental support. The authors argue that tighter taxonomic limits can backfire by shrinking the training set. Readers get a faster route to short, testable gene lists for other complex bacterial traits.
pmc-13548594:
Junyuan Feng and colleagues present a deep learning system that reads brainwave recordings to detect infantile epileptic spasms syndrome, in a 2026 methods paper. This severe infant epilepsy shows chaotic brainwave patterns, and reading the traces by eye is slow and error-prone, delaying treatment. Their system, SinTransNet, splits each recording into five frequency bands, extracts features with wave-shaped convolutional filters, and lets a transformer weigh relationships across bands.

Testing used 129 recordings containing close to two thousand spasm events from the team's own collection. The system reached average accuracy near eighty-six percent, catching about four fifths of true cases while keeping false alarms low. The authors argue that automated reading of this kind could speed diagnosis in pediatric neurology wards, giving infants a better chance at early treatment before developmental harm accumulates.
pmc-13548694:
Youyou Xie and colleagues create radiation-resistant cervical cancer cells in the laboratory to learn how a nuclear protein helps tumors shrug off radiotherapy, in a 2026 study. Resistant disease is a major reason treatment fails. A growth pathway downstream, mTOR, linked the two effects. Patient tissue echoed the pattern: tumors from people whose cancers resisted radiation showed high HMGB1 and low activated AMPK. The authors nominate the HMGB1 to AMPK axis as a drug target, while noting patient validation is still thin.
pmc-13551694:

The authors propose the pairing for further development.
pmc-13551794:

Direct clinical evidence in sexual dysfunction remains limited, so the review charts a research agenda.
pmc-13555994:

Timeliness, openness, and trust appeared often, while fairness, public involvement, and handling false information were put into practice less often. The comparison shows where regional plans match what studies show and where they still fall short.
pmc-13557794:

Specific bile acids correlated with iron transport measures across the group. The authors suggest that this capacity measure may flag a preclinical disturbance that links iron handling, bile acid metabolism, and low blood sugar before anaemia appears. Larger studies would be needed to confirm the pattern.
pmc-13558594:

Simulations reported authentication accuracy above ninety-five percent and packet delivery near ninety-seven percent, with lower delay and longer network life than rival blockchain schemes. Attack tests covered active and passive threats.
pmc-13558694:

Four finalists bound stably and tightly, with low drift across the simulations and strong computed affinity. All results are computational, with no cell or animal testing yet. The authors offer the four leads and the AI workflow as a starting kit for tumour-specific SCD-1 drug development.
pmc-13559594:

pmc-13560294:

The authors urge caution, since five small trials form a thin base for ranking treatments.
pmc-13560394:

Four themes emerged. Students knew core ethics rules such as consent and not copying others' work yet felt shaky applying them to authorship, fieldwork, and data reading. Questionable practices, including unfair authorship, cherry-picked reporting, and bent readings of data, came across as normal shortcuts. Guidance from seniors worked as ethical support when mentors stayed engaged, but rank sometimes hushed questions. Workplace pressure for output, thin hands-on training, and no safe reporting routes rounded out the picture. The authors stress they show perceptions, not causal links, and they aim the findings at training reform.
pmc-13562194:

Their 2026 study mines cancer atlas data, validates in public datasets and single-cell sequencing, then tests the gene in cells and in tumors grown in mice. pmc-13563794:

Their 2026 multicentre study gathered 203 patients treated between 2017 and 2024, with 153 for training and 50 for validation. Inputs joined texture features from PET/CT scans, metabolic readings from the same images, and blood biomarkers pulled from records. Seven model types were trained and compared under nested cross-checks.

The authors say automated scan reading and wider validation stand between the tool and the clinic.
pmc-13569094:

A larger-volume, later-sampled culture method lowered rates further, and a light-based pathogen reduction treatment produced the lowest rates of all. pmc-13569194:

Every service used travel-based deferral of donors, while only half used pathogen reduction, mostly for selected products. Just nine respondents screened donations for any such virus, all for West Nile virus, and no transfusion-transmitted cases were reported that year. The patchwork shows wide global variation and a thin screening base against future virus threats.
pmc-13571394:
Miyazaki and colleagues presented in 2026 a detailed anatomy guide to the right ventricular outflow tract of the heart. Neighbouring structures include both coronary arteries, the left atrial appendage, and the chest wall, all at risk during procedures. The authors present the atlas as a safety resource: knowing the real layout should cut complications in rhythm and valve interventions.
pmc-13572394:

Resistant cells showed high levels of a stress protein and strong shields against damage. Blocking those byproducts in cell powerhouses saved the cells, which points to where the damage starts.
pmc-13572494:

The authors say pairing both routes makes best use of scarce tissue.
pmc-13573494:

Five themes emerged from the talks: caregiver drive, meaningful participation, skill mastery, thriving beside peers, and hopes for the future. pmc-13574894:

Scans showed an 8 millimetre osteoid osteoma in her shin bone, a small tumour that often responds to anti-inflammatory drugs.

Those drugs were not safe options late in pregnancy, and plain pain relief plus opioids gave little help. A team spanning radiology, maternal-fetal medicine, and anaesthesia used ultrasound and CT guidance to burn the tumour away with radiofrequency ablation, a needle-based heat treatment. Her pain resolved, the radiation dose stayed well within accepted limits for pregnancy, and she later delivered at term without problems.
pmc-13575094:
Hangli Wang and three colleagues describe a portable heart tracing system with built-in diagnosis in a 2026 paper. Electrocardiograms, or ECGs, are central to spotting heart disease early. Older monitors tend to be bulky or rely on simple reading methods.

Their terminal measures only 80 by 100 millimetres and weighs about 150 grams, sending data by Wi-Fi to a host computer. A neural network mixing widened convolutions with attention steps sorts heartbeats into standard classes. Tests gave 99.28 percent accuracy per beat, with heart rate readings within two percent at rest. Filtering kept signals clean despite noise. The authors present the system as a step toward carry-anywhere cardiac checks.
pmc-13576094:
Jordana Lopes Carvalho leads a 2026 comparison of moral distress among doctors and nursing staff in surgical care at a public university hospital in Brazil's south. Moral distress arises when staff feel blocked from doing what they judge right. Surgical units combine hard choices, tight rules, and team friction, making them a sharp test case.

The survey covered 245 professionals, 167 physicians and 78 nursing staff, and used a validated Brazilian scale. Groups differed on several dimensions, among them working conditions and how far staff can defend values and rights while keeping care safe. Across both groups, feeling recognised and holding a clear professional identity sat at the centre of the distress pattern. Overall structures looked similar, with some paths stronger in one profession. The authors advise managers to tailor responses by role rather than apply one fix.
pmc-13576594:
Delphine Gastineau leads a 2026 multicentre study of surgery for a rare liver cancer, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, asking whether how the operation is done changes benchmark success. Cutting the tumour out is the only cure, and quality is judged by clear margins plus removal of nearby lymph nodes. Open surgery is standard, while keyhole and robotic routes are growing amid doubts about their cancer quality.

Records covered 240 patients treated from 2010 to 2024. Only 38.8 percent hit both benchmarks, with open surgery highest at 51.1 percent, robotic at 44.4 percent, and keyhole at 14.5 percent in the same ranking. Death at 90 days was 5.0 percent overall with no clear gap by route. Oddly, keyhole surgery linked to the best survival after adjustment, despite the lowest benchmark rate. The authors flag a disconnect between benchmark scores and long-term outcomes.
pmc-13578294:
Georgios Theocharidis and co-authors build a 2026 system that reads brain scans to flag who may later develop Alzheimer's disease. Catching the disease before symptoms start could open a window for early care. Their system works only with standard structural scans, the kind many hospitals already take, and studies five slices from each brain.

A network first trained on photos pulled features from each slice. Three classic learning models then voted together on the risk call. The data held just over a thousand people whose thinking was normal at scan time, split so no person leaked across test groups. Across two hundred repeat runs the blend scored well on sorting future cases from stable ones, which the authors offer as a low cost screening aid.
pmc-13578594:
Dimitri Martel and colleagues check whether MRI maps of fat makeup around the human knee give the same answer a week later, in a 2026 study. Fat chemistry near joints may shift with joint disease, so a steady measure is needed before it can track change. Ten healthy adults, half of them women, were scanned twice, one week apart, on a strong research scanner.

Eight fat depots around the knee were traced, from bone marrow to the fat pads behind and beside the kneecap. Total fat share repeated best, with tight spread across all sites. Saturated fat held nearly as steady. One class of unsaturated fat swung widely, above all in the small fat pads. The authors back the steady measures for future studies and flag the shaky one.
pmc-13583394:
Ana Paula de Andrade Silva and colleagues review capsaicin for burning mouth syndrome in this 2026 paper. The syndrome causes a daily burning feeling inside the mouth with no visible cause, and it mostly affects women over 50. Capsaicin, the hot compound in chili peppers, can be applied in the mouth or swallowed, yet doctors disagree on whether it truly helps.

Searching seven databases, the reviewers found 782 papers and kept only four that fit their rules. Doses and study lengths varied widely, but every kept study reported lower pain scores after capsaicin use. Three trials carried a moderate risk of bias and one a critical risk, so the proof behind the benefit rates as low. The authors urge caution until stronger trials are done.
pmc-13584394:
Zhu, Guo, and Zhang published a 2026 study on a scoring tool for artery hardening risk. Calcium buildup in the belly aorta warns of heart events and early death. No simple tool existed to flag who should get closer checks. The team built a paper scoring chart from a national health survey.

Five plain inputs feed the chart: age, weight index, heart disease, pressure, and smoking. The chart sorted risk well in both its building and checking groups. Predicted chances matched real outcomes closely across the risk range. Decision checks showed the chart helps across many cutoff choices. Clinics could run it with facts already in most charts. Early flagging could steer scans toward those at highest risk.
pmc-13584494:
Xuefan Yang and colleagues present a rare cancer case alongside a review of past reports in this 2026 paper. The cancer grew inside a urethral diverticulum, a small pouch off the urine channel in a woman. Such cancers are so rare that no standard treatment path exists, and their vague symptoms often pass for a simple urine infection.

Their patient was a 46-year-old woman with two years of frequent, urgent, and painful urination. Scans found a growth about five centimeters wide around the urethra, and a biopsy showed papillary carcinoma. Surgeons removed the front pelvic organs, rerouted urine through a piece of bowel, and rebuilt the vagina. Final tests showed a high-grade cancer that had reached the bladder wall muscle. The authors press for careful exams and wider sharing of cases.
pmc-13585394:
Ribeiro-Silva and colleagues examine in 2026 whether the weather around a young infant affects how long mothers breastfeed exclusively, using a nationwide Brazilian cohort. Climate change makes both heat and cold exposures a growing concern for infant feeding.

The study linked records for 397,239 children under six months from the national food and nutrition surveillance system, covering 2015 to 2019. It matched them with daily gridded temperature data. Statistical models that account for delayed effects found no national link between cold and stopping exclusive breastfeeding. Heat, by contrast, was associated with about a ten percent higher risk of interruption, and that increase looked similar across infant ages, sexes, and levels of local deprivation. Cold effects may still vary by age and deprivation, the authors note, even though the national picture showed none.
pmc-13588194:
Henrique Nogueira Pinto and colleagues link a lab-grown blood-brain barrier to a human brain organoid on a single chip. The barrier guards the brain but also blocks most medicines, and animal models mimic it poorly. Their platform grows a flow-through, vessel-like barrier from human stem cells beside an open chamber holding a mini brain organoid, joined by a gel interface with no artificial membrane in between.

The two parts coexisted stably on the chip. Star-shaped support cells from the organoid reached out, crossed toward the barrier, and touched its vessel cells directly, copying the real neurovascular unit's layout. Because both sides stay open to testing, a candidate drug's crossing and its effect on brain tissue can be read in one run. The authors offer the chip as a human-first stand-in for animal barrier studies.
pmc-13591694:
Essa M Rafique and three colleagues review, in 2026, how Tamil Nadu, an Indian state once heavy with HIV, reversed its epidemic early and kept it down. They weigh state data from 2000 to 2024 against peer states and strong global performers. The review credits nimble administration: quick program shifts, joined up TB and HIV care, and services folded into normal clinics rather than kept in stand alone silos.

New infections fell by 94 percent across the period, and adult prevalence dropped to a small fraction of its 2000 level. The state also first in India met the world mark for ending mother to child spread. Rafique and the team offer the model as a transferable plan for other low resource settings.
pmc-13592594:
Lia Brigante and seven colleagues argue that the European Union's first update of midwife qualification rules in 21 years must match world standards. The directive sets minimum training rules for midwives across EU and EEA states, and its reach echoes worldwide because other nations copy EU norms. Midwives, when trained and licensed to global standards, can deliver about ninety percent of essential care for women and newborns, the authors note.

Training and practice standards have moved on over two decades while the law stood still, they say. Aligning the update with current science, global professional standards, and World Health Organization guidance would protect care quality, let midwives work to their full scope, and ease movement across borders. Brigante and the team frame the revision as a global policy moment.
pmc-13592794:
Alexander Muacevic leads a team tracing where stroke deaths happen across the United States from 2020 to 2024. Hospital stroke care has leapt ahead, yet deaths outside hospitals form a blind spot. National mortality records for adults over forty five were sorted by urbanization level and place of death. Smoothed state ratios and inequality indices measured how concentrated deaths were in space.

Deaths shifted outward: medium and fringe suburbs posted the largest relative gains, big city cores stalled, and rural areas dipped slightly. Home deaths spiked in 2021, and hospice deaths kept climbing. Both home and hospital deaths clustered heavily in space, with inequality scores near one half. Muacevic and the team urge folding such maps into stroke surveillance to target emergency care.
pmc-13593694:
Philipp Friedrich Georg Ried and Roland Seifert surveyed German dentists about gum overgrowth caused by medication, a side effect in which the gums swell over the teeth. Their 2026 online survey reached dentists through regional associations, though only 118 usable replies came back from a very large invited pool.

The blood pressure drugs amlodipine and nifedipine, plus the immune suppressant ciclosporin, were named most often as triggers, and affected patients showed no pattern by sex. About seven in ten respondents had treated the condition successfully, most often by teaching better oral hygiene, switching the causative drug, or trimming the gum surgically. Published figures for how often each drug causes the problem vary widely. The authors therefore advise quoting only a narrow range. Readers should check the source data closely before trusting any single number.
pmc-13593794:
Catherine Paterson heads a fifteen-author review of programs that support the minds and daily lives of children and teenagers with cancer, from diagnosis through survivorship. Searching five databases without date limits, the team gathered thirty-four studies from seventeen countries covering nearly two thousand young patients, and combined their results statistically.

Programs that trained thinking skills gave the clearest gains, improving memory and related abilities by a moderate margin. Play and creative therapies, animal-assisted sessions, self-management teaching, and physical activity together improved psychological outcomes such as anxiety and pain. Several of the same approaches lifted quality of life scores as well. Benefits for depression, coping, and fatigue were less consistent. The authors conclude that psychosocial care earns its place across the whole cancer journey, not only during treatment.
pmc-13594394:
Xiaoqian Duan and co-authors report a 64-year-old man with high-risk Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia. He could not undergo a stem cell transplant. Yet he stayed in remission for over three and a half years on an unusual maintenance plan. His leukemia carried a gene deletion linked to relapse and had already returned once during targeted drug treatment.

One intensive cycle of the immune engager blinatumomab combined with dasatinib drove the disease to a deep molecular remission. He then switched to brief monthly outpatient infusions of the same antibody at reduced intensity. Daily dasatinib and regular interferon injections completed the plan. Leukemia transcripts stayed undetectable for nearly three years, with only one brief low-level blip that settled without escalation. He had no unplanned hospital stays and no severe nerve side effects, suggesting gentler intermittent dosing can hold this disease while sparing the patient.
pmc-13594494:
Muhammad Usman Ghani and co-authors review how artificial intelligence might predict atrial fibrillation after coronary artery bypass surgery. The complication strikes fifteen to thirty percent of patients. It also lengthens hospital stays. Their 2026 narrative review gathered nine studies from 2020 onward that combined machine learning with clinical, blood, genetic, and metabolic information.

Across those studies, modern algorithms scored well at separating patients who would develop the rhythm problem from those who would not, beating traditional clinical risk scores. The catch, the authors note, is unfinished homework: few models have been tested outside the hospitals that built them, calibration is rarely checked, and bias remains possible. They argue that pairing explainable algorithms with biomarker data could eventually let teams target preventive care at the patients most likely to benefit.
pmc-13595794:
Mia C Somenzi leads an eleven-author team modeling the human blood-brain barrier in a dish to watch how the parasite Toxoplasma gondii, carried by roughly a third of humanity, attacks it. Their 2026 study used brain-like vessel cells grown from human stem cells, a system that mimics the barrier's tight seals.

Infection drove the cells to pour out CCL2, a signal that summons immune cells, and the signal itself turned out to damage the barrier, a previously unrecognized role. The immune messenger interferon-gamma pushed back on both fronts, limiting CCL2 release and protecting the barrier from parasite-driven breakdown. The authors describe this as a defense built into the barrier cells themselves, not merely help arriving from immune cells. The work lays groundwork for understanding how the parasite threatens the brain and where protection might be reinforced.
pmc-13600394:
Mach and colleagues use aged mice to study frailty, many drugs at once, and drug cuts. Older people often take five or more drugs. Stopping some may help, but effects are hard to trace. Mice got one drug, a mix of drugs, or plain food from mid life. At late age, half of each group had drugs slowly stopped. A smart cage then tracked each mouse for close to a full day. It logged rest, moves, and grooming.

Drug mixes changed daily acts in ways single drugs did not predict. Some changes reversed when drugs stopped. Others stayed, and new ones showed. Frailty paths split into four clear groups.
pmc-13602094:
Eun Jeong Kim and four colleagues map body shape variation in the stone flounder from Korean coastal waters in 2026. The stone flounder is a commercially valued flatfish of nearshore seabeds. The team measured 81 body indices and applied geometric shape analysis to wild fish from two coastal regions. They weighed the influence of size, sex, and capture site together rather than one at a time.

Classical measurements pointed to body size and sex as the main shape drivers, while site effects were smaller and context-dependent. Geometric analysis agreed, and still detected clear separation between sites. Size and sex each bent the growth trajectory, while site did not. Mitochondrial DNA showed moderate genetic difference between the regions, weakly but significantly tied to shape distance. The authors present a baseline for managing this fishery species and future breeding work.
pmc-13609194:
Peiqi Yan and four colleagues follow the gut microbiome across the stages of coronary artery disease. Gut imbalance is linked to heart disease, but how it shifts from mild narrowing to heart attack was unmapped. The team analyzed bacterial gene data from 306 people: healthy controls plus patients with mild coronary stenosis, stable angina, unstable angina, and heart attack. Diversity analysis, machine learning, and network modeling worked over the same data.

The microbial community changed most sharply at the heart attack stage. Three bacteria emerged as stage markers: Veillonella for mild stenosis, Intestinimonas for stable angina, and Streptococcus for unstable angina and heart attack. Network connections thinned from mild disease through unstable angina, then flipped to an antagonism-dominated web during heart attack. Machine learning separated the stages well, and the marker bacteria stayed significant after accounting for major clinical factors. Stage-specific stool markers could aid staging, the authors propose.
pmc-13612194:
Muhammad Ibrar Ahmad leads a seven-author team pooling trials of mixed exercise in women with breast cancer. Pairing aerobic training with resistance work might improve both metabolic health and quality of life during and after treatment, but single trials are small. Their systematic review and meta-analysis searched four databases and kept 37 randomized trials, standardizing outcomes and grading bias risk.

Combined exercise produced a large improvement in overall quality of life and in the breast-cancer-specific FACT-B score. Metabolic markers moved selectively: HDL cholesterol rose, insulin resistance fell, and diastolic blood pressure dipped. Glucose, insulin, triglycerides, LDL cholesterol, and systolic pressure did not change significantly. Studies varied a lot underneath the averages, which the authors flag. Secondary analysis hinted that bigger exercise doses bought bigger gains. They call for dose-finding trials to pin down how much combined training is enough.
pmc-13612994:
Nikolaos D. Tantaroudas leads a team describing a low-cost platform for watching the health of rural bridges, built under the Horizon Europe FUTURAL project. Old bridges in country areas can be unsafe, yet standard monitoring gear costs more than small regions can pay. Their answer combines passing vehicles, cheap internet-linked sensors, and a phone app called FUTURAPP that pairs with small motion sensors plugged into smartphones.

Readings flow to cloud computers for safe storage and handling. A neural network trained on shaking patterns in the 2 to 15 hertz range learns each bridge's normal behaviour and flags changes that may signal damage. Computer models of the bridges, built with ANSYS software, help the team judge what the sensor data mean. The goal is bridge checks that rural towns can actually afford to run.
pmc-13613794:
Adebiyi Adesina, Meltem Odabaş, Heidi Quinn, Moazzam Ali, and Elizabeth A. Sully estimate in 2026 how much money task-sharing could save in family planning across 128 low- and middle-income countries. Task-sharing trains a wider range of health workers to give services once kept to a few cadres, easing staff shortages. The team applied World Health Organization guidance to a large model of contraceptive care built for the year 2024.

They priced six methods, from condoms and pills to implants and intrauterine devices, under two futures: current rules on who may provide each method, and wider sharing under the global guidance. Comparing the direct costs shows where savings are largest and which methods gain most. For health planners short of both staff and cash, the numbers show a concrete route to reaching more people with the same budget.
pmc-13614194:
Reem Nsouli leads a team building a tunable light reactor that lets chemists screen 24 reactions at once while setting the light for each well on its own. Light-driven chemistry can build bonds in gentle new ways, yet most screening rigs fix one light setting for the whole plate. That blind spot slows the hunt for new light catalysts and reactions.

In the new device, colour, brightness, and exposure time can each be set per well. The team proved it with iron, cerium, and copper chemistry where visible light splits molecules apart. Being able to vary light itself, like any other ingredient, turns a hidden factor into a measured one. Labs can now learn which light recipe a reaction truly wants instead of settling for whatever lamp hangs over the bench.
pmc-13614294:
Bar Chen leads a large team reporting in 2026 on a transistor-based sensor that can tell living bacteria from dead ones, a skill current low-cost sensors lack. Knowing whether bacteria are alive decides whether contamination is still a threat. The device uses many tiny conducting channels linked to a sensing surface coated with antibodies that grab E. coli bacteria.

Tests ran in droplets of just half a microlitre of rich bacterial broth, with no washing or sample prep before measuring. The sensor picked up even a single bacterium, gave readings in real time without labels, and rose in a clean straight line with bacterial counts. It also separated live from dead cells. Food plants and water testers could gain a fast on-site check that answers the question that matters most: is this contamination still alive?
pmc-13614994:
Henrique Fernando Lopes-Araujo and colleagues examine a puzzle in Brazil's HIV record from 2015 to 2024 in a 2026 study: new HIV infections rose while AIDS cases and deaths from AIDS fell. Brazil is praised worldwide for its public response to the epidemic. The team tracked infection and illness rates, time from diagnosis to starting treatment, immune cell counts at diagnosis, and how fully treatment suppressed the virus.

Starting treatment within 30 days rose from 28 percent of patients to 63 percent, while starting more than six months late fell from 35 percent to 10 percent. Faster, stronger treatment explains much of the fall in illness and death. The rising count of new infections points the other way, toward gaps in prevention. The study shows policy makers exactly where the next effort belongs.
pmc-13615594:
Ang and colleagues compare two trifocal lens implants for cataract patients with mild corneal astigmatism, an uneven curve of the eye front. Trifocal lenses split light for near, mid, and far sight. One type also corrects astigmatism, while the other does not.

Records covered one hundred sixty-seven eyes seen six to twelve months after surgery. Sight scores without glasses were much the same across lens groups. The astigmatism-correcting lenses left less leftover focusing error after surgery. Gains stood out most in eyes with against-the-rule astigmatism, where the steep curve runs sideways. No extra glare or halos were reported with the correcting lenses.
pmc-13617094:
Luis Martínez-Heredia and thirteen colleagues examine immune cell patterns in hypophosphatasia, a rare inherited disorder where a missing enzyme, tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase, weakens bones and teeth. The enzyme also seems to influence inflammation, so the team compared forty-seven genetically confirmed patients with thirty healthy controls. Blood tests, inflammation markers, stool markers, and detailed immune cell profiling were combined.

Patients showed lower levels of the enzyme on T cells, B cells, neutrophils, and monocytes, along with shifts in several cell ratios. Immune-mediated inflammatory diseases were common in this clinic group and came with lower enzyme activity and higher gut inflammation markers. Certain cell patterns tracked with having such a disease. Because the study is a single snapshot, the authors stress it cannot prove the enzyme shortage causes inflammation, only that the two travel together.
pmc-13618394:
Shouyu Wu and nine colleagues demonstrate a way to sculpt with light at the nanoscale in three dimensions, using a single femtosecond laser pulse split into thousands of focal points. Three-dimensional micro and nano manufacturing usually forces a trade among resolution, speed, and quality. Their method pairs a multi-layer noise threshold filtering algorithm, which cleans up focal quality, with an over-sampling algorithm that packs foci more densely across layers.

A dual spatial light modulator system generated up to five thousand four hundred laser foci across six layers, and processing runs reached twenty-four million points per second. The smallest isolated feature measured about fifty nanometers, and the approach worked across inorganic, organic, and hydrogel materials. The authors present the strategy as a precise, scalable route to high-quality three-dimensional manufacturing for photonics, optical storage, and beyond.
pmc-13620194:
Meaghan Furlano, writing alone, takes up a live sociology debate: do professions still form a category apart from other occupations? Drawing on neo-Weberian work by Adams and Saks, the article argues that professions are social constructions, always shifting with place and time. New kinds of job insecurity in Anglo-American work might look like the end of professional privilege.

Furlano reads that insecurity differently, as the latest round of an old effort to keep status. Professions still enjoy state-backed legitimacy, barriers that close ranks against outsiders, and a cultural image that makes their elevated standing seem like common sense. Some surface traits now overlap with ordinary occupations, yet the economic and symbolic advantages persist. The conclusion is that professions are not in crisis but mid-reconstruction, rebuilding their distinct place once again.
pmc-13620294:
Lorenzo Sabatino and eight colleagues propose a compact code for classifying sinus infections that start from the teeth. Odontogenic sinusitis needs dentists and ear, nose, and throat surgeons to work together, and mixed messages cause failures. Their system, named TEBOF, scores five features: timing, cause, foreign body presence, blockage of the sinus drainage path, and any open channel between mouth and sinus.

The team applied the code to 124 consecutive patients at a Rome hospital. Chronic disease and classic dental causes dominated, while foreign bodies, blockage, and open channels each appeared in a large minority. Combined sinus and oral surgery was the commonest treatment, and overall success reached about ninety-seven percent, with only four patients needing a second operation. The authors argue a shared five-letter shorthand can steer the whole team to the right operation the first time.
pmc-13623094:
Fatima Umar and colleagues catalogue a gene family called ITPK in bread wheat, a crop where the family had been little studied. These genes help make phytic acid, the main phosphorus store in seeds. Phytic acid matters for plant growth and stress defence, but too much of it locks away iron and zinc in food, lowering its value.

Scanning the wheat genome turned up fifteen ITPK genes spread across four chromosomes and all three of wheat's sub-genomes. Family trees placed the wheat genes in three of four groups, and the genes shared building blocks that hint at shared jobs. Computer analysis predicted partnerships with two other genes in the same pathway. Expression data showed the genes switch on in tissues and growth stages, after flowering, and lab checks found levels shifting when iron or zinc was added. The authors offer the catalogue as groundwork for breeding better wheat.
pmc-13623294:
Natasha de Lima Monteiro leads an integrative review of dengue infection in kidney transplant recipients, a group whose immune systems are suppressed by medicine. Dengue is a mosquito-borne virus common in the tropics, and transplant patients may react in unusual ways. The review gathers case reports and cohort studies found through a literature search run in August 2025.

Twenty-two studies from dengue-endemic countries met the rules, infections striking from days to years after transplant. Fever, muscle pain, and headache led the symptom list, much as in other patients. Low platelet counts were common, blamed on the virus and on the anti-rejection drugs. Bleeding appeared more often when infection came soon after surgery, hinting at more severe disease. Kidney graft loss stayed low at four percent, and most patients recovered. No study checked whether dengue stirs up anti-donor antibodies, a gap the authors flag.
pmc-13623794:
Andreas Frodl and colleagues systematically review a practical question in children's fracture care. After fixing a broken arm bone with thin Kirschner wires, should the wire ends be buried under the skin or left poking out?? Buried wires may infect less but need a second anaesthetic to remove. Exposed wires are cheaper and simpler yet raise infection worries.

Twelve studies covering 1,977 patients under sixteen were pooled. Buried wires did show lower overall infection rates. Deep infections needing another operation, however, did not differ between the two styles, and neither did wires slipping out of place or bones breaking again. Exposed wires caused far less skin irritation. Geography mattered: the infection gap was strong in Asia and Africa but absent in Europe and the United States. Weighing cost and the avoided anaesthetic, the authors favour exposed wires for most children in temperate climates.
pmc-13623994:
Sebastian Böhme and co-authors published a German-language health economics analysis of patient cost-sharing as a steering tool in European care. Germany debates charges such as the old practice fee as a way to curb doctor visits. The authors test that idea against institutional design and evidence from four countries: Germany, the Netherlands, France, and Denmark.

Their synthesis says cost-sharing works when three conditions line up: the type of service, the behavioural design of the charge, and the surrounding system. Flat charges fall hardest on low incomes and do not steer well. Reviving the former practice fee in its old shape is explicitly not recommended. Better, they argue, are charges aimed where misuse is documented, such as leaving a coordinated care pathway without cause, shaped with income differences in mind. Used that way, charges could guide patients without endangering normal access to care.
pmc-13631594:
Samhitha Urs and a large team review in 2026 the least understood part of factor VIII, the blood clotting protein missing in hemophilia A. Their focus is its large middle section, the B domain, which is cut away when the protein activates and is left out of many replacement products.

Combining computer models of the full-length protein with microscope imaging, the team shows the B domain shields key regions of the molecule. That cover prevents early activation and blocks inhibitor antibodies from binding. Its sugar decorations and cutting sites also guide folding and release from cells. The authors argue that keeping or mimicking parts of this domain could improve future hemophilia treatments, making them last longer and provoke fewer immune reactions.
pmc-13631894:
Cong and colleagues published a 2026 study on smoking, a risk gene, and dementia in Britain. The APOE ε4 gene variant raises dementia risk in its carriers. Smoking also raises dementia risk, but their joint effect was unclear. The team tracked 173,366 dementia-free adults in the UK Biobank.

Smoking tracked with higher dementia risk across the full group overall. Surprisingly, the smoking link ran stronger in people without the risk gene. Among current smokers, risk rose clearly only in noncarriers in pooled data. A check across past studies, over 200,000 people, backed the pattern. Body inflammation and vessel pathways may carry the effect, they propose. Risk models should weigh smoking and gene status together, they advise.
pmc-13631994:
Levy Faber and colleagues reported in 2026 the first case of fungal empyema caused by Aspergillus niger after a chest wound in a healthy young soldier. Empyema is pus collecting around the lung, and fungal causes are rare. The twenty-two-year-old soldier was shot through the chest in combat and sent home after eight days.

Months later he developed worsening chest pain and breathlessness on effort. Scans found a complex pocket of fluid around the right lung, and surgery revealed a trapped lung under a thick peel of scar-like tissue. Surgeons freed the lung, and cultures from both the fluid and tissue grew the black mold Aspergillus niger, with no other germ found. Six months of antifungal medicine followed, with a good recovery. The authors urge testing for fungi in odd post-injury chest infections.
pmc-13633094:
Hadiqa Anum and four colleagues published this 2026 review of using cold to deepen crop colors in indoor farms. Anthocyanins are the pigments behind red, purple, and blue produce, and shoppers link them with freshness and health value. Brief cold exposure before harvest can push plants to make more of these pigments. The review pulls together molecular evidence across major crop families and turns it into practical guidance for plant factories, where every condition can be dialed in.

Responses to cold differ by species and even by variety. The authors weigh the settings that matter most: how cold, how long, and how close to harvest. End-of-cycle cooling and day-night temperature swings can raise pigment levels while holding yield steady, especially when paired with tuned lighting. Too much cold costs growth and energy. Their decision framework aims to balance color, nutrition, and efficiency for each crop.
pmc-13637094:
Nanda Kleinenberg-Talsma and four colleagues published this 2026 mixed-methods study of how residents of one Dutch neighborhood prepare for old age. Preparing early could delay frailty, yet towns need to know what residents actually do and want. The team surveyed adults in Groningen's Oosterpark district in 2023 about nine preparation themes, from money and housing to friendships and fitness. Six group discussions and two interviews added depth to the numbers.

One hundred thirty-four questionnaires came back. Respondents scored themselves well prepared on fitness and relationships, and poorly on housing and leisure. Talk added a tenth theme the survey had missed: the neighborhood itself. Many people worried often about aging yet prepared actively for very little. Others simply did not know how to start or where to ask. The authors advise local bodies to offer plain, reachable help points rather than waiting for citizens to find their way.
pmc-13647094:
Alice Roe and four colleagues test how teenagers at high risk of mood disorders remember their own past, in a 2026 study. Two hundred one adolescents at high risk and 117 at low risk, aged sixteen to eighteen, completed a task about good days and bad days. The task measured how easily positive and negative memories come to mind, how specific those memories are, and how fast their emotional charge fades.

Healthy-minded teenagers showed two protective tilts: good events came to mind more easily than bad ones, and the glow of positive memories faded more slowly than the sting of negative ones. At-risk teenagers showed weaker versions of both tilts and recalled more negative events. Memory specificity, by contrast, did not differ between groups. The authors say these recall biases may help explain how mood disorders take hold, and point to memory-based exercises as a possible early intervention.
pmc-13647994:
Rania Sihem Boussa and eleven colleagues read the genes of parasites taken from people with cystic echinococcosis in Algeria. This disease grows tapeworm cysts in the liver, lungs, or other organs. Cyst samples came from 31 patients who had surgery at referral hospitals between 2022 and 2024.

The team drew DNA from cyst fluid, wall, and lining, then ran two kinds of gene tests and read three markers. Samples from 29 cases gave clear reads. Nearly all proved to be one type, called G1, of the species Echinococcus granulosus sensu stricto. One case was a close type, G3, and one was a distinct species type. Knowing the main type helps shape local control work.
pmc-13650694:
Tingyi Zhao and four colleagues, publishing in 2026, report a paradox: boosting an antioxidant enzyme made human cells more vulnerable to oxidative attack. The enzyme, glutaredoxin 1, normally repairs oxidized protein bonds using the cell's glutathione system, so extra copies were expected to protect the cervical cancer cells used in the study.

Instead, engineered cells carrying extra enzyme survived and multiplied worse than controls under radiation, peroxide, or heat shock. Their internal oxidant levels ran higher after stress, and DNA assays showed more single-strand and double-strand breaks, plus more of the chromosomal damage seen in micronuclei. Recovery of a key reducing cofactor lagged, signaling a redox system knocked off balance, and a major stress-response factor dropped. The authors conclude that antioxidant defense works as a tuned system, and that overshooting one component can deepen damage rather than relieve it.
pmc-13651194:
Aiman Javed and eight colleagues, publishing in 2026, chart a quarter century of American deaths where Alzheimer's disease and diabetes appeared together. The two conditions share pathways and frequently coexist in older adults, yet their combined death trend had not been mapped, so the team turned to the national mortality database.

Between 1999 and 2023, more than two hundred thousand such deaths were recorded among people over forty-five. Age-adjusted rates climbed from under three to well over four per hundred thousand people, peaking around the late twenty-teens before easing, with a sharp pandemic-era rise that the authors flag. Rates rose in both sexes and stayed higher in women. White decedents formed most deaths, while Black and Hispanic populations carried higher adjusted rates, and the West and non-metropolitan areas showed the heaviest burden. The authors call for public health strategies aimed at this overlap.
pmc-2600394:
Lanciotti, Kosoy, Laven, and co-authors characterise the Zika virus tied to an epidemic on Yap State, Micronesia, in 2007. Zika was then a little-known virus, and the Yap outbreak gave a rare chance to study it closely. The team determined the full protein-coding sequence of the virus.

They also studied its properties in blood tests, which show how the immune system responds. Knowing the sequence and test behaviour helped labs distinguish Zika from related viruses such as dengue. That groundwork proved vital years later, when Zika spread widely and was linked to birth defects.
pmc-3418594:
Pearce, Salotti, Little, and co-authors study radiation exposure from CT scans in childhood and later risk of leukaemia and brain tumours. CT scans are very useful clinically. Their ionising radiation, though, may carry cancer risks, in particular for children, who are more sensitive to radiation than adults.

The team followed a cohort of children and young people who had scans, tracking later cancers. Their retrospective study gave some of the first direct estimates of excess risk after childhood CT. The results inform how doctors weigh scan benefits against dose in young patients.
pmc-5491694:
Omata, Cheng, Kokudo, and their co-authors updated Asia-Pacific guidelines in 2017 on hepatocellular carcinoma, the main form of liver cancer. There is great geographical variation in this cancer's distribution. The majority of cases worldwide are found in the Asia-Pacific region, where it is a leading public health problem.

The guidelines cover how to detect, stage, and treat the disease in light of regional realities, including widespread hepatitis infection. Updates matter because imaging, surgery, and drug options keep changing. Shared regional guidance helps hospitals offer consistent, evidence-based care. It also supports screening programs for people at highest risk, such as those with chronic liver disease.
pmc-5499094:
Williamson, Altman, Bagley, and their team published the COMET Handbook in 2017. Picking the right outcomes is key when a trial is designed, so that the effects of rival treatments can be compared head to head. Outcomes must also matter to patients and to those who fund and use care.

COMET backs core outcome sets: a small agreed set of outcomes that every trial in a field should measure. The handbook shows how to build such a set with patients, doctors, and researchers at the table. When all trials report the same core outcomes, their results can be pooled and judged as one body of proof. That cuts waste and speeds firm answers for practice.
pmc-6061794:
Wouter De Coster, Svenn D'Hert, Darrin Schultz, and coauthors described the NanoPack tool set in 2018. Long-read sequencers from Oxford Nanopore and Pacific Biosciences produce very different data from older machines. Users need plots and filters tuned to long reads.

NanoPack gathers small Python tools that chart read length and quality and trim poor data. Reports can be built for a single run or compared across runs. The tools are free under an open license. Labs adopting long reads use them as a first check before assembly, since bad input quietly ruins downstream results.
pmc-7566194:
The Global Burden of Disease 2019 Risk Factors Collaborators measured in 2020 how much illness and early death can be traced to eighty-seven risk factors worldwide. The analysis spans more than two hundred countries and territories over three decades, from 1990 to 2019. It sits inside the wider Global Burden of Disease Study, which applies one set of methods to every country so results can be compared.

The risks covered range from smoking, high blood pressure, and air pollution to unsafe water and poor diet. For each, the team estimates the share of deaths and lost healthy years it explains. Rankings like these show health ministries where prevention buys the most health, and how those priorities shift as countries grow richer or older.
pmc-8005494:
Peng Yu and co-authors reviewed in 2021 pyroptosis, a fiery form of programmed cell death tied closely to the immune system. Unlike quiet cell death, pyroptosis makes the cell swell and burst, spilling signals that summon inflammation. Interest in the process grew sharply after the discovery of the gasdermin family, proteins that punch the holes that finish the cell.

The review explains the machinery step by step, from the sensors that detect danger to the gasdermins that carry out the rupture. It then surveys the many diseases this process can influence, including infections, inflammatory disorders, and cancer. Knowing how to trigger or block this death pathway could give doctors a new lever over illnesses driven by inflammation.
pmc-8023694:
Maxime Taquet and colleagues studied in 2021 the brain and mental health outcomes that follow COVID-19, using electronic health records for well over two hundred thousand survivors. Early reports had raised concern about lasting neurological and psychiatric effects, but firm numbers were scarce. The team tracked which new diagnoses appeared in the six months after infection.

They estimate how often conditions such as stroke, dementia, anxiety, and mood disorders occurred, and how the risks compared with those after other illnesses. Their large scale records gave some of the strongest early evidence that COVID-19 can leave a measurable mark on brain health. The results helped clinics plan follow up care and set priorities for longer studies.
pmc-8810394:
The Global Burden of Disease 2019 Dementia Forecasting Collaborators estimated in 2022 how many people live with dementia now, and how many will in 2050. Populations are growing older around the world, which pushes dementia numbers upward on its own. At the same time, solid evidence links several changeable risk factors to the disease.

The team models the expected rise country by country, separating the part driven by aging from the part that risk factor trends could soften. Their forecast shows cases climbing steeply by mid century, especially in lower income regions. The analysis gives governments a planning horizon: care systems, budgets, and prevention campaigns all need to be ready well before 2050 arrives.
podcast-joerogan-36NpaOg5594:
Comedian Brian Simpson joins Joe Rogan for episode 2491. Simpson rose fast with a sharp, cool style and dry wit. Late-night sets made his name among comic peers.

Rogan explores his path from foster care and service to the stage. Simpson tells his story with calm, cutting humor. They talk about craft, luck, and staying sane in comedy. The episode gives new fans a full intro to a rising voice. His mind works in clean lines, and the talk shows why peers rate him so high. His rise feels earned, and he knows it.
podmore-apparitions-thought-transference:
Frank Podmore weighed the proof for thought leaps in Apparitions and Thought-Transference, his study of 1894. The book draws on the great case hoard of Phantasms of the Living. Podmore sifts those cases with a doubt man's care. He asks which tales stand when fraud, flaw, and chance are cut from the count.

His sums are strict, yet he grants a strange rest that won't fade. The book is the core of the great work in brief, sharp form. It shows how the new field tried to be a science. Its care is its claim.
pyramid-texts-maspero-1894:
Spells carved inside Egyptian pyramids more than four thousand years ago are the oldest church texts in the world. The Pyramid Texts, in Gaston Maspero's French rendering of 1894, gives them whole for the first time. Maspero was the French scholar who opened these tombs' walls to print.

The spells speak to the dead king, ward off snakes and foes, and lift his soul to the stars. They name old gods, rites, and foods for the life beyond the grave. No older body of religious writing survives on earth. Maspero's version first let the modern world read that dawn of faith.
saxo-grammaticus-danish-history-elton-18:
Saxo Grammaticus, a Danish clerk of the twelfth century, wrote the Gesta Danorum, the Deeds of the Danes, a vast Latin history of his people. Oliver Elton translated the first nine books into English in 1894. Saxo wrote to give Denmark a past as grand as Rome's, and he filled it with kings, heroes, and gods grown into men.

Amleth, the brooding prince who feigns madness, walks here in his first form, the seed of Shakespeare's Hamlet. Wars with the Wends, sea kings, shield maidens, and the feuds of the royal house crowd the books. Saxo's Latin is rich and rolling, a skald in a clerk's robe. His history is the great well of Danish legend.
sbe-36-milinda-part-2-1894:
Volume 36 of The Sacred Books of the East appeared in 1894, with T W Rhys Davids translating Part 2 of The Questions of King Milinda. The Milinda is a dialogue between King Milinda, a Greek ruler in India, and the monk Nagasena. Part 1 had appeared earlier in the series.

Nagasena answers the king's hard questions on the soul, rebirth, and karma with famous images, such as the chariot that is no single part. Part 2 presses into finer points of Buddhist teaching. Rhys Davids, a leading scholar of Pali, gave the text full notes. This volume completed the fifty-volume Sacred Books of the East, a landmark of world religious publishing.
spr-proceedings-vol10-1894:
A single long part, number twenty six, makes up volume ten of the Proceedings in 1894. The Society for Psychical Research devoted the year to weighty reports. Results from the census of hallucinations reached print around this period. Telepathy experiments appear with their ledgers of hits and misses.

Trance mediumship keeps its place, with sittings reported almost word for word. Physical phenomena get brief, wary notices beside the mental evidence. The society's leaders argue in print over what the mass of cases proves. Volume ten is a compact sample of the whole enterprise. It suits readers who want one year of the archive entire. The standards of proof are the real subject.
spr-proceedings-vol9-1893-1894:
Parts twenty four and twenty five form volume nine of the Proceedings, for 1893 and 1894. The Society for Psychical Research carries its inquiries into a second decade here. Telepathy work continues, though the glow of the first trials has cooled. Reports on apparitions still arrive, sifted by committee standards.

Mediumship investigations fill long sections, with trance sittings written out in detail. The society also prints studies of hypnotism and allied states of mind. Every claim meets investigators trained to suspect error first. Volume nine keeps the archive's steady rhythm of case, check, and argument. Historians of the occult and of science both use it. Plain primary evidence is its strength.
stoever-life-linnaeus-1794:
Dietrich Stoever wrote the life of Carl Linnaeus, the great Swede who named the kinds of life. Joseph Trapp turned the book into English in 1794. Linnaeus had died not long past, and tales of his life were still fresh. One tale in the book draws fans of strange lore.

In 1735, at Hamburg, Linnaeus saw a famed seven-headed hydra on show. He found the thing a fake, made from skins and parts of beasts. The show men fled the town when his word spread. The tale shows the great name giver at work as a fraud hunter.
the-alchemical-essence-and-the-chemical-: The Alchemical Essence and the Chemical Element, 1894. The essence and element. This book preserves that episode. Later readers can locate it. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Time has kept the file intact.
the-forsyte-saga-volume-2-pg2594: Volume two of the Forsyte Saga: the family chronicle continues through changing England. Soames, Irene, and the new generation in Galsworthy's masterly hands. The saga deepens. The Forsytes face the new century with old values.
the-hermetic-and-alchemical-writings-of-: The Hermetic and Alchemical Writings of Aureolus Philippus Theophrastus Bombast, 1894. The Paracelsus writings. This book preserves that collection. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
the-new-pearl-of-great-price-a-treatise-: The New Pearl of Great Price, 1894. The precious treatise. This book preserves that work. Tomorrow's readers will find it. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Those who study the era will use it.
tob-0094:
Jean Bodin, the French thinker famed for his work on the state, wrote four books on the madness of sorcerers in 1580. De Magorum Daemonomania argues that witchcraft is real, deadly, and far more common than judges admit. Bodin demands the harshest response: death for witches, and punishment for those who defend them.

He sets rules of evidence so loose that denial itself becomes a sign of guilt. Coming from a mind of the first rank, the book gave the witch hunts learned cover across Europe. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. It remains a chilling read.
tob-0194:
Dudley Wright reconstructed the Eleusinian Mysteries, the secret rites of Demeter and Persephone celebrated near Athens for well over a thousand years. Initiates were promised a blessed lot after death, and the central acts were kept secret on pain of death. What happened inside the Telesterion hall is still argued among scholars.

Wright gathers the ancient testimony: hymns, inscriptions, hostile Christian reports, and archaeology, then narrates the festival's procession, fasting, and revelations as far as evidence reaches. V1 evidence calls his account the best plain tale of antiquity's most famous secret. Readers get both the known outline and an honest view of where the secrecy still holds.
tob-10794:
Georg Ebers could read Egypt's old hieratic script, a rare skill he put to work in Uarda, subtitled A Romance of Ancient Egypt. Ebers set his novel in ancient Thebes under the pharaohs. At its center stands Uarda, whose story entangles court plots, priestly power, and a love that crosses ranks.

Real learning fills the grand scenes: temples, medicine, festivals, and daily crafts are rendered from Ebers's Egyptological research. For nineteenth-century readers, Uarda was a favorite window on pharaoh-era Egypt, offering scholarship disguised as romance. Modern readers can enjoy both the melodrama and a period picture of what Europe then knew about ancient Egypt.
tob-4094:
Hermann Jacobi translated the Jaina Sutras for volume forty-five of the Sacred Books of the East, and part two holds two major Jain scriptures. The Uttaradhyayana gives monastic discourses on the disciplined life. The Sutrakritanga argues against rival schools and defends the Jain path.

Jain teaching prizes non-violence above all, extending care to the smallest living things. Monks and nuns bind themselves to strict vows of truth, poverty, and harmlessness. Jacobi, a leading scholar of Jainism, equips the texts with full notes. Checked from the 1919 edition, part two completes the series' Jain canon for English readers.
tob-4166-36794:
Volume two of Lang's Myth, Ritual and Religion presses his case against the solar-myth school. Lang explains rituals as acts tied to real belief, not as faded sun worship. He traces fairy tales back to older, rougher originals shared across continents.

Case after case, he sets Greek myth beside the lore of peoples his rivals ignored. The sun theorists get brisk, witty answers throughout. Lang also defends the view that some peoples held a high-god belief very early, a claim that stirred lasting debate. Readers who enjoy learned argument at full stretch will find volume two as sharp as the first.
tob-4194:
Leo Tolstoy, in his religious crisis, cut the four Gospels into one harmony and called it The Gospel in Brief. Published in the 1890s, it strips away miracle and church doctrine to leave the Sermon on the Mount as Christ's true teaching. Non-resistance to evil stands at the center of Tolstoy's reading.

The Russian church excommunicated him, which only spread the book. Gandhi read Tolstoy and carried the ethic of non-resistance into another century's struggles. Tolstoy retells the story in plain, urgent prose, as if copying out orders for his own life. Verified from the 1919 edition, the harmony shows the novelist turned prophet at his starkest.
tob-4294:
James Haughton Woods published his Yoga-System of Patanjali with Harvard in 1914, and the academic study of yoga in the West dates from it. Woods translates the Yoga Sutras and prints the classical commentaries with them, so the root text arrives with its oldest interpreters in attendance.

Aphorism by aphorism, readers can test the short sayings against centuries of gloss. Woods writes as a philologist: exact, patient, and clear about hard places. Verified from the 1919 edition, his volume introduced yoga thought to universities. Teachers who want Patanjali with scholarly ballast still start on Woods's pages.
treaty-of-tordesillas-1494:
Spain and Portugal signed the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494. The pact draws one line down the Atlantic Ocean's wide map. Lands west of the line fall to Spain, east to Portugal.

The line runs 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands. A papal grant stands behind the bargain of the two crowns. Brazil's bulge falls on Portugal's side, a fact of lasting weight. Neither power asks the peoples who live on those lands. The treaty that split a new world still shapes its tongues and maps. Portuguese in Brazil and Spanish elsewhere trace back to this line.
un-ga-res-194:
Palestine's refugees stand at the heart of Resolution 194, adopted by the UN General Assembly on 11 December 1948, months after the war that created the state of Israel. The text first honors the late UN mediator, Count Folke Bernadotte, killed while working for peace. It then sets up a three-state Conciliation Commission to take over his task in Palestine.

The commission is told to help the sides reach a final settlement of all open questions. The resolution is best known for its stand on the refugees who had fled or been driven from their homes. It says those wishing to return and live in peace should be let back, and those who do not return should be paid for lost property.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 194 (III), adopted on 11 December 1948, addressed Palestine after the first Arab-Israeli war. The Assembly thanked the late United Nations Mediator, who had given his life in the work. It set up a three-state Conciliation Commission. The commission was to take over the search for a final settlement between the parties.

The text gave Jerusalem and its area special treatment under United Nations control, with protection for holy places and the freest possible access. Its best known passage states that refugees who wished to return home and live at peace should be let to do so at the earliest workable date. It states that pay should be made for lost or harmed property.
un-sc-res-1094:
Guatemala's peace accords gained military verification in January 1997. The final accords signed at Guatemala City on 29 December 1996 ended the long internal war. A definitive ceasefire signed at Oslo on 4 December would take force once a United Nations mechanism stood ready. MINUGUA had verified human rights in the country since 1994.
